## Heaven and Hell as Relationship, Not Place
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/heaven-and-hell-in-orthodox-thought.html
Summary: Orthodox theology describes heaven and hell less as two locations than as two ways of receiving the same God. The love that is joy to those who have learned to love it is torment to those who have not, as the same sunlight that gladdens the eye wounds one that cannot bear it. St Isaac the Syrian calls the suffering of hell a scourging by love. Hell is not God's absence but his presence, refused.
==============================================================================

### The question underneath the question
People who ask where heaven is are usually asking something else. They want to know what God is like, and whether the God who is called love in one breath can be the God who sends people to unending fire in the next. It is a fair question and a very old one, and the Fathers of the Church did not answer it by softening either half.
What they did instead was to shift the question from geography to relationship. Heaven and hell in this account are not two rooms in a large building, with the doors locked from the outside. They are two ways of standing in the presence of the same God, who does not change his mind about anyone, and whose love is not withdrawn from the damned.

### Not a set of co-ordinates
Orthodox writers are noticeably careful about spatial language here. Fr Seraphim Rose gave a section of The Soul After Death to what he called the location of heaven and hell, and argued that they are entirely real without being places in any crude sense that a map could handle. The soul that leaves the body does not travel a measurable distance.
This carefulness is not modern embarrassment about a pre-scientific picture. It is much older than the telescope. The Church has always used the language of height and depth, of ascent and of the abyss, and has always known it was using images for something that images cannot contain. Liturgical poetry is free with such pictures precisely because nobody was expected to take out a compass.
Dropping the spatial frame does not make the subject vaguer. It makes it sharper. A place can be reached by accident or by administrative error; a relationship cannot. If what is described is a way of standing towards God, then nothing arbitrary decides it, and nothing external can be blamed for it. The teaching becomes less like a sentence passed on someone and more like a diagnosis of what he has made of himself.

### One love, two experiences
The patristic move is to locate the difference in the receiver rather than in God. Scripture already speaks this way: the letter to the Hebrews says, in the wording of the King James Version, “For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29), quoting Deuteronomy, and the same fire in Scripture is warmth and light and glory as often as it is destruction. What differs is what the fire meets.
St Isaac the Syrian, a seventh-century bishop of Nineveh whose Ascetical Homilies are read across the Orthodox world, states it as sharply as anyone. He teaches that those who suffer in hell are scourged by love, and that the power of love works in two ways at once, tormenting those who have set themselves against it while delighting those who have lived in accordance with it. The instrument of torment, on this reading, is not a divine anger but a divine affection that the sinner cannot bear.
Fr Lawrence Farley, summarising the Fathers on this point, uses the comparison of sunlight and blindness: the light shines on everyone equally, and what a person gets from it depends on the condition of the eye. The comparison is not original to him. It runs through the tradition, and it is why Orthodox writers so often say that the fire of hell and the light of heaven are the same fire and the same light.

### Where the image comes from
The picture is drawn from a series of scenes rather than argued from first principles. Moses sees a bush that burns without being consumed. The three young men walk unharmed in the Babylonian furnace while the flame kills the men standing outside it. On Mount Tabor the disciples see an uncreated light coming out of Christ's own body, and are told to say nothing about it until later.
Worship carries the same instinct. Before communion the Church has its people pray that the Mysteries may be for healing rather than for judgment and condemnation, which only makes sense if the gift itself is one thing and its effect on the receiver is another. The bread and wine do not become two different substances for two different sorts of people. Something in the person decides how the same gift lands.

### What this does not mean: universalism
It would be easy, and dishonest, to slide from here into the claim that everyone is saved in the end because the love never stops. Orthodoxy has not taught that. The Fifth Ecumenical Council in 553 condemned the Origenist doctrine of the pre-existence of souls, and the wider Origenist scheme of a final restoration of all things has never been received as the teaching of the Church.
Matthew 25 keeps the same adjective for the life of the righteous and for the punishment of the others, and the Church has kept it too, without explaining it away. What Orthodoxy does hold is that the refusal is the creature's and not God's, and that the Church may pray for anyone, including those it has no grounds to hope for, because it does not know the end of any story but its own. Hope of that kind is a long way from a doctrine that all will certainly be saved.
There is a related caution about St Isaac himself. He is venerated as a saint, his Ascetical Homilies are treasured, and certain eschatological passages attributed to him have been discussed and disputed for centuries. The scourge-of-love teaching is quoted approvingly across the Orthodox world; the question of how far his other speculations may be pressed is a separate matter, and an unsettled one.

### What this does not mean: a caricature of the West
Orthodox writers sometimes set this teaching against a Western picture in which God punishes sinners because his justice requires satisfaction, and the contrast is usually drawn too sharply. The legal and courtroom language of salvation is not a Western invention imposed on the Gospel. It is in Romans, it is in the Psalms, and it was used by Greek Fathers as freely as by Latin ones.
Anselm in the eleventh century, and the Reformed theologians who developed penal substitution after him, were trying to say something serious about the cost of sin and about why the cross was necessary rather than merely moving. Christians who hold that account are not describing a petty God. They are taking guilt seriously, which is a mark of moral realism and not of cruelty.
Where Orthodoxy differs is in which language it treats as primary. Its dominant grammar is medical rather than forensic: sin as a sickness that disfigures the one who has it, salvation as healing, God as the physician, hell as the condition of a person who will not be healed. Both sets of images are in Scripture. Which one governs the others changes how the whole picture looks, and that difference is worth stating plainly rather than dissolving into a claim that everyone means the same thing.

### What follows in practice
If hell is love refused rather than love withheld, then the Christian life looks less like assembling a case for the defence and more like training an eye to bear light. That is what Orthodox practice is for. Fasting, confession, almsgiving, forgiving people who have not apologised, standing through long services: none of it earns anything, and all of it slowly changes what a person is able to receive.
Forgiveness deserves a line of its own here, because it is the hardest of these and the most exactly related to the teaching. A person who will not forgive is practising, in a small way, the very refusal the Fathers describe: love arrives and is not admitted. Orthodox services keep pressing the point, most obviously on the evening before Great Lent begins, when everyone in the church asks forgiveness of everyone else, face to face and by name.
It also puts a limit on religious harshness, which is the point at which this teaching bites its own believers. Someone who is doctrinally exact about the nature of divine love, and cold to the person standing next to him, has understood nothing about it. Fr Seraphim Rose, an American convert who spent his last years warning other converts about exactly this, put the priority in a sentence.

> Being correct is the external side of Christianity. It's important, but not of first importance.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, talk on simplicity, 1979, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works* (St. Herman Press, 2003), ch. 87

### A door left open
Readers from other Christian traditions will notice that this article has stated differences rather than blurred them. That is deliberate, and it is not meant as a rebuke. An account of heaven and hell that turned out to be identical to everyone else's would be of no use to anyone, and pretending otherwise would insult a reader who came here to find out what the Orthodox actually hold.
Fr Seraphim Rose, who came to Orthodoxy out of a Protestant family and never stopped writing for people like them, was asked in 1980 by a catechumen whether she could go on calling her Protestant and Roman Catholic relatives Christians. He answered at length and without evasion, holding the Orthodox claim about the Church while refusing to pronounce on anybody's soul, and he ended with a formula he credited to Fr Dimitry Dudko.
He added a parenthesis immediately afterwards, to the effect that this would carry more weight if the Orthodox themselves gave a better example. That seems the right note to end on. The teaching described here is not a threat held over anyone. It is an account of what love does when it meets a person, and an invitation to find out whether it is true.

> We should view the non-Orthodox as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been revealed, as people who are potentially Orthodox
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works* (St. Herman Press, 2003), ch. 84

### Common questions

Q: Does Orthodoxy teach that hell is God's absence?
A: Not in the usual sense. The more characteristic Orthodox account is the opposite: hell is God's presence experienced by someone who cannot bear it. The divine love is not withdrawn from anyone, and the Fathers speak of the same fire that is glory to the saints being torment to those set against it. What is absent is not God but the capacity to receive him as joy.

Q: What is St Isaac the Syrian's scourge of love?
A: St Isaac, a seventh-century bishop of Nineveh, teaches in his Ascetical Homilies that those suffering in hell are scourged by love. Love's power, he says, acts in two ways: it torments those who have set themselves against it while delighting those who have lived in accordance with it. The phrase is quoted across Orthodox writing as a compressed statement of the whole teaching.

Q: Is this the same as saying everyone will eventually be saved?
A: No. Orthodoxy has never received universal salvation as doctrine. The Fifth Ecumenical Council condemned the Origenist teaching on the pre-existence of souls, and the associated idea of a final restoration of all things has not been accepted as the Church's faith. Orthodox Christians may pray for anyone and hope widely, but hope is not a promise, and the Church has kept the language of Matthew 25 unaltered.

Q: Are heaven and hell places?
A: Orthodox writers treat the spatial language as imagery for something real. Fr Seraphim Rose argued that heaven and hell are entirely real without being locations in any crude sense, and the Church's hymns use height and depth freely while never suggesting a map could show them. The emphasis falls on relationship to God rather than on position, though nothing in this makes the reality less serious.

Q: How does this differ from Western Christian teaching on hell?
A: Chiefly in which language governs. Western accounts, particularly after Anselm and in Reformed theology, often make justice and satisfaction primary, and that language has genuine scriptural roots. Orthodoxy uses the same scriptural material but gives priority to images of sickness and healing, with God as physician. Both traditions affirm judgment and the reality of hell; they describe what is happening in it differently.

Q: If hell is love, why should anyone fear it?
A: Because the teaching makes the stakes personal rather than administrative. Nobody is condemned by a clerical error or spared by one. What decides the experience is what a person has become over a lifetime of small choices, and that is a more searching thought than a verdict handed down from outside. Orthodox practice exists to work on exactly that, which is why it is concrete and daily.

### Sources
- Fr Lawrence Farley, “The Fathers and the Fire”: https://orthochristian.com/90103.html
- Fr James Guirguis, “How Will We Be Judged?”: https://orthochristian.com/128777.html
- Deacon Pavel Serzhantov, “The Most-Discerning Abba Isaac the Syrian”: https://orthochristian.com/100934.html
- Fr James Thornton, “Saint Isaac the Syrian, Bishop of Nineveh”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/general/frjames_stisaac.aspx
- Meatfare Sunday: The Last Judgment: https://orthochristian.com/77222.html
- An Orthodox Understanding of the Atonement: https://orthochristian.com/105429.html
- Fr Seraphim Rose, The Soul After Death (English text at azbyka.ru): https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/the-soul-after-death/
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works, ch. 87: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_87.aspx

## Sola Scriptura and Holy Tradition
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/sola-scriptura-and-holy-tradition.html
Summary: Sola scriptura is the Reformation principle that Holy Scripture is the final and sufficient rule of Christian faith. The Orthodox Church holds a different account: Scripture is the written heart of Holy Tradition, the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church, which also carries the creed, the councils, the liturgy and the Fathers. Orthodoxy reads the Bible inside the community that received it, citing 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and 1 Timothy 3:15.
==============================================================================

### A question worth asking slowly
Someone raised in an evangelical or non-denominational church who begins attending an Orthodox liturgy usually arrives at the same question within a month or two. The Bible is carried in procession, censed, kissed and read aloud at every service. Standing alongside it, however, are councils, canons, Fathers and a great deal of inherited custom. Where does authority actually sit? The question is a fair one and it deserves a straight answer rather than a slogan.
Two answers are on offer. One is the Reformation principle usually called sola scriptura. The other is the Orthodox account of Holy Tradition. They are genuinely different, and this article will not pretend otherwise. But the first has to be stated the way its own best defenders state it, because a position knocked over in caricature has not been engaged at all.

### What sola scriptura actually claims
The principle holds that Holy Scripture is the final and sufficient rule for Christian faith and life: everything necessary for salvation is either set down plainly in Scripture or may be drawn from it by sound and necessary reasoning. The Westminster Confession of 1646 puts it in close to those words in its opening chapter. No council, bishop or custom may bind the conscience as Scripture binds it.
Notice what the claim is careful to say. It concerns the last word, not the only word. Scripture is the court of final appeal; other authorities may teach, advise and persuade, and they are expected to do so. What they may not do is overrule the text to which they are all themselves answerable.
The passages most often cited are 2 Timothy 3:16-17, where Scripture is called God-breathed and profitable so that the man of God may be complete and equipped for every good work; Acts 17:11, where the Bereans search the Scriptures daily to test what the apostle has told them; and the Lord's rebuke in Mark 7 to those who set aside the commandment of God in order to keep a custom of their own. These are serious texts and no Orthodox reader should wave them away.

### Why it was formulated when it was
The principle did not arrive out of nowhere. It was hammered out in a Western Church that had lived through the papal schism that began in 1378, when rival claimants excommunicated one another and for a period three men each called himself pope; through a long argument about whether a council stood above a pope; and through a traffic in indulgences that struck many sincere people as the sale of what cannot be sold.
In that setting, asking where the court of appeal lies is not an academic exercise. If the visible authorities contradict each other, and some of them are plainly for hire, a Christian needs ground to stand on that is not simply the assertion of whoever holds office this year. The Reformers found that ground in the text of Scripture. Whatever one finally concludes about their answer, the pressure that produced it was real and the men who felt it were not frivolous.

### What its best defenders do not mean
It is often assumed that sola scriptura means the Bible and nothing else, interpreted by me. Its more careful exponents have consistently denied this. The historian Heiko Oberman distinguished two late-medieval attitudes to tradition, one treating Scripture and tradition as a single stream and the other as two independent sources, and argued that the Reformers meant to recover the first rather than to abolish tradition as such.
Keith Mathison's study The Shape of Sola Scriptura, published in 2001, built on that distinction and argued at length that individualist biblicism, in which every believer is his own final court, is a later mutation rather than the Reformation position. Calvin quotes Augustine on almost every page of the Institutes. The Lutheran confessions appeal to the Fathers. Reformed and Anglican churches confess the Nicene Creed. Most Protestant readers of this page received their doctrine of the Trinity from a fourth-century council and will say so if asked.
So the disagreement is narrower and sharper than it first appears. It is not tradition against no tradition. It is a disagreement about what tradition is, and about whether the Church's handing-on of the faith is itself part of how God gives that faith, or only a record of a gift completed elsewhere.

### What Orthodox Christians mean by Tradition
Tradition, in Orthodox usage, is not a shelf of old opinions. The word renders the Greek paradosis, a handing-over. What is handed over is the whole life of the Church as the Holy Spirit lives in her: the Scriptures, the creed, the councils, the liturgy, the prayers, the icons, the fasts, the lives of the saints, and the way in which all of these are understood together.
St Paul uses the word without embarrassment. “So then, brethren, stand firm and hold to the traditions which you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15, RSV). Spoken teaching and written teaching sit in one sentence, under one verb, with no hint that the second has replaced the first. The Orthodox Church has never found a reason to separate them.
Writing in the 370s, St Basil the Great made the same point with a list of examples. In On the Holy Spirit he asks who taught us in writing to sign ourselves with the cross, to turn east at prayer, to bless the water of baptism and the oil of chrismation, to baptise with three immersions. His answer is that these things reach us from the unwritten teaching of the apostles, and that to discard everything lacking written warrant would injure the Gospel in its very vitals.

### Scripture as the written heart, not a rival
None of this demotes the Bible. In the Orthodox account Scripture is not one authority among several jostling for position; it is the written heart of the whole. Nothing else in Tradition may contradict it, and everything else exists to carry it, guard it and open it. The Gospel book rests on the altar. It is carried in procession, censed and kissed. No canon and no custom is treated that way.
The other half of the picture is 1 Timothy 3:15, where the apostle tells Timothy how to behave “in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth” (RSV; the King James has “the pillar and ground of the truth”). That image is architectural. The Church is what holds the truth up where it can be seen. Read this way, Scripture and Church are not competitors but one gift in two aspects: a book that came out of a worshipping community and is still read inside it.
Which is why Orthodoxy has never developed anything resembling an office that can issue new doctrine. Tradition, as Orthodox Christians understand it, has no power to add; its entire claim is to have kept. When the Seventh Ecumenical Council defended icons in 787, the argument was not that a fresh insight had arrived but that the practice was as old as the faith and followed from the Incarnation.

### The honest worry: does tradition become a licence?
Here is the objection, and it is a good one. If the Church may appeal to unwritten apostolic teaching, what stops anything at all from being introduced under that heading a thousand years later and declared ancient? The Reformers believed they had watched exactly this happen, and they built their principle to prevent its happening again. A reader who raises this is not being awkward. He is being careful, and the Orthodox answer had better be a real one.
Tradition, in the Orthodox account, is not a mechanism for adding but a test for recognising, and it is a demanding test. St Vincent of Lérins, writing in Gaul in 434, gave the rule that is still quoted: hold the faith “which has been believed everywhere, always, by all”, which he unpacked as universality, antiquity and consent. A teaching that cannot show all three has not shown itself to be Tradition, whatever its age and whoever its champions.
Orthodoxy also distinguishes sharply between Holy Tradition and local custom, and the Fathers were blunter about bad custom than many of their modern admirers. A phrase associated with St Cyprian of Carthage runs that custom without truth is simply error grown old. Usages come and go: a Greek parish and a Russian parish in the same city will differ in a dozen visible ways without either supposing that the faith is at stake.
Fr. Seraphim Rose, an American convert raised in a Protestant family, warned about the same danger from inside. Introducing the life of St Paisius Velichkovsky, he described Christians who follow an unexamined custom and absorb whatever has come down to them without ever asking where it came from.
He counted that as a serious danger rather than a small one, and his prescription was a return to the sources, Scripture and the Fathers, rather than an appeal to whatever people happen to be doing. That instinct is not far from the one the Reformers were acting on. The two accounts differ over where each expects to find the sources still intact.

> The followers of unenlightened custom are themselves innocent; they merely accept what has been 'handed down' to them.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, Introduction to *Blessed Paisius Velichkovsky: The Man Behind the Philokalia* (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, 1994 [1976])

### Where the two accounts genuinely part
They part over one question: whether the Church that received and recognised the Scriptures can be trusted as their keeper and interpreter. Sola scriptura answers that she cannot be trusted finally, because she has erred and may err again, and that the text must therefore stand over her. Orthodoxy answers that Christ promised the Spirit would guide her into all truth, and that the promise was never made conditional on her officers behaving well in any given century.
Each answer carries a cost, and both sides know it. The Orthodox position asks a great deal of trust in a visible community full of sinners at every level, and Orthodox Christians have given the world ample reason to ask hard questions about that. The other position has to account for sincere readers of one sufficient text reaching incompatible conclusions about baptism, the Lord's Supper and the ordering of the Church. Thoughtful Protestants have wrestled with that difficulty honestly for four centuries. Neither problem is a debating point; each is a real weight.
State the difference plainly and it stops being frightening. Orthodoxy does not hold that Scripture is insufficient, and Protestantism does not hold that history is worthless. The parting is over the standing of the Church herself, and everything else follows from that.

### A door left open
Nothing written here is meant to close a conversation. Fr. Seraphim held the traditional Orthodox conviction that the Church is one and that her sacraments are given within her; he said so plainly and it would be dishonest to soften it. He also refused, firmly and repeatedly, to pronounce on where any particular person outside the Orthodox Church stands before God, and he thought that when others fail to see Orthodoxy some of the fault lies closer to home.
In a letter of November 1980 to an enquirer who had asked whether she might go on calling her Protestant and Catholic family Christians, he passed on a formulation he credited to Fr. Dimitry Dudko: that we should regard the non-Orthodox as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been revealed, as people who are potentially Orthodox. That is the sentence this parish would rather end on than any argument.
If you have read this far and disagree, you are welcome at the Sunday liturgy in Kovan all the same, and welcome to bring the disagreement with you. The Gospel is read aloud in the middle of the church, facing the people, before anything is said about it. You can watch what the Orthodox actually do with their Bible and judge from there.

> perhaps it is our fault for not living and teaching the Orthodox Faith in a way they can understand
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works* (St. Herman Press, 2003), ch. 84

### Common questions

Q: Does the Orthodox Church believe the Bible is inspired?
A: Yes, without qualification. The Orthodox Church holds Scripture to be inspired by the Holy Spirit and treats it as the highest thing she possesses: the Gospel book rests on the altar, is carried in procession and is kissed by the faithful. What Orthodoxy adds is that the same Spirit who inspired the writers is still at work in the community that received, preserved and reads them, and that the book is meant to be read inside that community.

Q: Is Holy Tradition the same as the traditions Jesus condemns in Mark 7?
A: No. In Mark 7 and Matthew 15 the Lord condemns human customs used to evade the commandment of God, which is a specific abuse rather than the handing-on of apostolic teaching. The same Greek word appears positively in 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and 1 Corinthians 11:2, where St Paul commends the traditions he delivered. Orthodoxy makes the distinction the New Testament itself makes, and the Fathers criticised bad custom sharply when they met it.

Q: Can the Orthodox Church add new doctrines?
A: Orthodoxy claims no such power. Tradition, as Orthodox Christians understand it, is the preservation and unfolding of what was given once, not a channel for additions. When councils defined the Trinity or defended the icons, they argued that they were stating what the Church had always believed rather than announcing something new. A teaching that cannot show ancient, widespread and consistent use is not regarded as Tradition at all.

Q: Do Orthodox Christians regard Protestants as Christians?
A: Fr. Seraphim Rose, writing in 1980, held that Orthodox Christians can properly call other Christians by that name and live on good terms with them, and he thought the word heretic was used far too freely in his day. He also held the traditional Orthodox teaching that the Church is one and her sacraments are given within her, and he declined to judge where any individual stands before God. This parish follows him on both counts.

Q: What is the practical difference on a Sunday morning?
A: Less than you might expect in one respect and more in another. Both an Orthodox and an evangelical service read Scripture aloud and preach from it. The Orthodox service also assumes a fixed lectionary shared worldwide, a creed recited by everyone, prayers largely composed between the fourth and eighth centuries, and hymns stitched mostly out of biblical phrases. The reading is corporate and inherited rather than freshly chosen each week.

### Sources

- St Vincent of Lérins, Commonitory (434): https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3506.htm
- Orthodox Church in America, The Orthodox Faith: Holy Tradition: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/doctrine/sources-of-christian-doctrine/tradition
- Orthodox Church in America, The Orthodox Faith: The Bible: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/doctrine/sources-of-christian-doctrine/bible1

- Fr. Seraphim Rose, Introduction to Blessed Paisius Velichkovsky: http://orthodoxinfo.com/phronema/intro_bpv.aspx

## Who Decided Which Books Are in the Bible?
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/who-decided-the-canon-of-the-bible.html
Summary: No single council handed the Church a finished Bible. The books read aloud in the churches gradually proved themselves; St Athanasius of Alexandria listed the present twenty-seven New Testament books in his Festal Letter of 367, and local councils in the following decades confirmed similar lists. Orthodox Christians therefore say that the Church recognised and received the Scriptures rather than created them, which is a narrower claim than it is often taken to be.
==============================================================================

### Why people ask this question
The question usually arrives with an edge on it, from one side or the other. Someone wants to show that the Bible is a committee product and may therefore be set down. Someone else wants to show that the Church made the Bible and therefore outranks it. The documentary record supports neither ambition particularly well, which is one good reason to tell the story carefully and let the dates do the work.
What follows is a summary of what can actually be shown, with the sources given at the end so that any reader can check them. Where the evidence is thin or genuinely contested, this article says so rather than smoothing it over.

### First there was reading, not a list
For most of the second century there was no list and no felt need for one. Congregations read the letters they had been sent and the Gospels they had received, and they read them at the Eucharist. A book functioned as Scripture in practice long before anyone argued about whether it was Scripture in principle. Justin Martyr, writing around the middle of the second century, describes the memoirs of the apostles being read on Sunday alongside the writings of the prophets.
Pressure to be explicit came from two directions at once. Marcion, in the 140s, published a severely reduced collection consisting of one edited Gospel and ten letters of Paul. Meanwhile other groups were circulating new writings under apostolic names. Once a subtraction and an addition were both on offer, the churches had to say aloud what they had been doing quietly all along.
The Muratorian Fragment, a damaged Latin list discovered in the eighteenth century, is usually dated to the late second century, though a minority of scholars place it considerably later. On either dating it shows a community with a nearly complete New Testament, a firm core, and a handful of uncertainties around the edges.

### Eusebius takes stock, around 325
The clearest early snapshot comes in the Church History of Eusebius of Caesarea, book three, chapter twenty-five. He sorts the books into groups. Acknowledged: the four Gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul, the first letter of John, the first of Peter and, in his careful phrase, “if it really seem proper”, the Revelation of John. Disputed but recognised by many: James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John.
Rejected, in his third group, are the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Apocalypse of Peter, the letter of Barnabas, the Teaching of the Apostles, and again the Revelation of John, which some reject and others class with the accepted books. Revelation appears twice because Eusebius is reporting a live disagreement rather than resolving it. That is what the situation looked like three centuries after the Resurrection: a settled core, a contested margin, and no council on the subject.

### Athanasius, Easter 367
Bishops of Alexandria sent out an annual festal letter announcing the date of Pascha and adding pastoral instruction. The thirty-ninth of these, sent by St Athanasius the Great in 367, contains the earliest surviving list of exactly the twenty-seven books of the New Testament as they stand today, with Revelation included. He calls them fountains of salvation and says that no one should add to them or take anything from them.
The letter is more interesting than its reputation. Athanasius adds a second category: books “not indeed included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read” by those newly joining the Church. He lists the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd. Esther stands in the second list, not the first.
A tidy account in which 367 settles everything does not survive an actual reading of the letter. What Athanasius gives is one bishop's authoritative ruling for his own vast see, in a form that later proved persuasive elsewhere. That is considerable, and it is not the same thing as a universal decree.

### The local councils
Councils then confirmed, region by region, what was already in use. The African councils at Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 issued a list; the text most easily consulted today survives in the canonical collection of the Council of Carthage of 419, whose canon on the subject names Tobit, Judith, Esther, two books of Maccabees, the five books of Solomon and the Revelation of John, and closes by saying that these are the things received from the fathers to be read in church.
The Synod of Laodicea in Phrygia, in the fourth century, produced a list in its sixtieth canon which gives twenty-six New Testament books and omits Revelation. The standard English edition of the canons carries an editorial note that this particular canon is of questionable genuineness. Both of those facts belong in an honest account, and leaving either out would be a form of tidying.
In 692 the Council in Trullo, meeting in Constantinople, confirmed a long series of earlier canons, among them those of Laodicea and of Carthage together with the canonical letters of Athanasius, Gregory the Theologian and Amphilochius of Iconium. Those lists do not agree with each other at every point. The council ratified them together regardless, which says something about how the Church has carried the question.

### Revelation, and the books long argued over
The Apocalypse took longest. It was doubted across much of the Greek-speaking East for centuries, in part because groups appealing to it had drawn strange conclusions from its imagery. The Syriac Peshitta, the standard Bible of the Syriac churches from the early fifth century, contains twenty-two New Testament books: it omits 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. That was not rebellion. Those were simply the books that community had received.
Even now Revelation is the one New Testament book with no appointed place in the Byzantine lectionary. It is fully canonical in the Orthodox Church and it is not read at the public services. That combination looks odd if the canon is imagined as a list voted through in a single session, and looks entirely ordinary if the canon grew out of what was actually read.
The disputed letters, James and Jude and 2 Peter and the shorter letters of John, were argued over for something like three hundred years before the argument quietly stopped. Hebrews was doubted in the West for a long period on grounds of authorship. None of these books was contested because anyone disliked what it taught; the uncertainties were about origin and circulation.

### More than one Old Testament
The Old Testament is where real differences persist to this day. The Greek-speaking Church used the Septuagint, which contains Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the books of Maccabees and longer forms of Daniel and Esther. Jerome, translating into Latin around 400, preferred the shorter Hebrew reckoning and described the additional books as useful for edification rather than for establishing doctrine, while continuing to translate them.
Reformation Bibles followed Jerome's instinct and printed the disputed books separately as the Apocrypha; most later Protestant editions dropped them. The Council of Trent defined the longer list for Roman Catholics in 1546. The Orthodox Church did neither. She has continued to print and read those books, calling them anagignoskomena, things that are read, and has never treated their exact enumeration as requiring a definition of that kind.
Variation runs wider still. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church receives a broader canon that includes 1 Enoch and the Book of Jubilees. Nobody in this history is being careless. Each community is transmitting what it actually received, and the differences sit almost entirely at the margins rather than at the centre.

### Why 'the Church decided' is a simplification
It is the usual Orthodox shorthand and it is not quite right. Nobody in the fourth century imagined that a synod could make a book apostolic. The bishops and councils were doing something more modest and rather more interesting: they were reporting, and then ratifying, what the churches had found themselves unable to stop reading.
Recognition is the better word. A congregation discovered over generations that certain books fed it, matched the faith it had been taught and carried the ring of the apostles. Where that experience was uniform, agreement came quickly. Where it was patchy, as with Revelation in the East and Hebrews in the West, agreement took centuries. The shape of the process is not legislative. It is closer to the slow way a household learns which books never leave the table.
Fr. Seraphim Rose, an American convert who spent his life republishing neglected Orthodox sources, thought that going back and looking at what was actually there was the central task of his own time. Writing about St Paisius Velichkovsky, the eighteenth-century monk whose disciples produced the Optina revival, he located his importance precisely there.

> he redirected the attention of Orthodox Christians to the sources of Holy Orthodoxy
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, Introduction to *Blessed Paisius Velichkovsky: The Man Behind the Philokalia* (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, 1994 [1976])

### What this implies, and what it does not
The implication Orthodox Christians draw is limited but real. If the Scriptures reached us through the reading, worship and discernment of a concrete community over several centuries, then that community is not an optional accessory to the Bible. The same tradition that carried the books also carried a way of reading them: the creed, the liturgy, the commentaries of the Fathers.
What does not follow is that the Church stands above Scripture, or may correct it, or holds some reserve of information withheld from the text. Orthodoxy claims none of those things, and Orthodox writers who reach for a stronger claim are overreaching. The relation is closer to that of a witness than of an author. Nothing in the fourth-century record will bear more weight than that.
It is also worth saying that the arguments at the edge of the canon have never been the load-bearing ones. Every community named in this article read the same four Gospels and the same Paul. Luther, who placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his New Testament and wrote slightingly of James in his preface of 1522, printed all four books. The canon has proved a good deal more durable than the disputes about it.
If this history makes you want to look at how the Orthodox Church reads the book she received, rather than at what she says about herself, that would be the right next step. Fr. Seraphim, speaking to an American audience in 1980 about why Protestants were becoming Orthodox, put the burden of proof where this parish thinks it belongs.

> If we have the true Christianity, there should be something in our midst that someone who sincerely loves the truth will see and want.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, lecture 'Orthodoxy in the USA', *The Orthodox Word* no. 94 (1980), in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works* (St. Herman Press, 2003), ch. 86

### Common questions

Q: Did the Council of Nicaea decide the canon of the Bible?
A: No. The Council of Nicaea in 325 addressed the divinity of Christ, the date of Pascha and a set of disciplinary canons. Its acts say nothing about which books belong in the Bible. The story that bishops piled books on a table and watched the genuine ones leap up comes from a much later legend and has no standing as history. The canon was settled gradually, through usage and then through local councils.

Q: Why does the Orthodox Old Testament contain more books?
A: Because the Greek-speaking Church used the Septuagint, which contains Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, Maccabees and longer forms of Daniel and Esther. Orthodox Christians call these the anagignoskomena, the things that are read. Most Protestant Bibles follow the shorter Hebrew reckoning that Jerome preferred and printed the others as Apocrypha before largely dropping them. Both practices are ancient, and neither appeared out of nowhere in the sixteenth century.

Q: Which book took longest to be accepted?
A: Revelation, in the Greek-speaking East. Around 325 Eusebius could still list it both among the accepted and among the rejected books, and the list attributed to the Synod of Laodicea omits it entirely. Athanasius included it in 367 and it was eventually received throughout the Orthodox Church. It remains the only New Testament book with no appointed reading in the Byzantine lectionary, which is a trace of that long hesitation.

Q: If the Church recognised the canon, does the Church stand above the Bible?
A: Orthodoxy does not draw that conclusion. Recognising is not authoring, and the fourth-century councils believed they were reporting which books the churches had always read rather than conferring authority on them. What Orthodox Christians do conclude is narrower: that the community which received the books also received a way of reading them, and that the two were never intended to be separated from each other.

Q: How reliable are the dates given in this article?
A: The main dates are firm and checkable: the Festal Letter of Athanasius in 367, the African councils of 393 and 397 with the surviving list preserved in the collection of 419, and the Council in Trullo in 692. Two points are genuinely uncertain and have been flagged as such in the text: the dating of the Muratorian Fragment, and whether the sixtieth canon of Laodicea is original to that synod.

### Sources

- St Athanasius, Festal Letter 39 (367): https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2806039.htm
- Canons of the Synod of Laodicea: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3806.htm
- Council of Carthage (419), canon on the canonical Scriptures: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3816.htm
- Council in Trullo (692), canon 2: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3814.htm
- Orthodox Church in America, The Orthodox Faith: The Bible: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/doctrine/sources-of-christian-doctrine/bible1
- Fr. Seraphim Rose, Introduction to Blessed Paisius Velichkovsky: http://orthodoxinfo.com/phronema/intro_bpv.aspx

## Reading Scripture with the Church Fathers
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/how-the-church-fathers-read-scripture.html
Summary: The Church Fathers read Scripture as one book whose subject is Christ, tested against the rule of faith handed down from the apostles. They read the Old Testament typologically, as the Lord himself did on the road to Emmaus. Orthodox Christians read with them, not because any Father was infallible, but because reading without a community stretched across time tends to lose its bearings without noticing.
==============================================================================

### Who counts as a Father
The phrase can sound like a club with a rope across the door. It is looser than that. The Fathers are the teachers whose writing the Church has found, over long use, to express her own mind: Irenaeus in Gaul, Athanasius and Cyril in Alexandria, the three Cappadocians, John Chrysostom in Antioch and Constantinople, Maximus the Confessor, John of Damascus, and others down to writers as recent as Ignatius Brianchaninov in the nineteenth century.
No list was ever promulgated and nobody sat an examination. What made a writer a Father was reception: his works kept being copied, read at the services, cited at councils and found useful by people trying to pray. That is a slow and rather unglamorous process. It is also, as it happens, much the same process that produced the canon of Scripture itself.

### The rule of faith
The first thing the Fathers brought to Scripture was not a technique. It was a summary of the faith received at baptism, the regula fidei or rule of faith, which is the ancestor of the creeds. St Irenaeus sets it out around 180 in Against Heresies, book one, chapter ten: one God, one Christ incarnate, one Spirit, one coming judgement, confessed in the same terms by churches in Germany, Spain, Gaul, the East, Egypt and Libya.
In the preceding chapter he explains why this matters, with an image nobody forgets. A skilled artist makes a mosaic portrait of a king out of precious stones. Someone else takes the stones apart and refits them into the shape of a fox, then points to the jewels as proof that this is the king. Every piece is genuine. The arrangement is not.
That is his charge against the Gnostic readers of his day: each verse they cite is in the Bible, and the picture they assemble from the verses is not the one the apostles handed down. The rule of faith is what tells a reader whether he is looking at the king or at the fox. It is not an addition to Scripture. It is the shape Scripture takes when it is read whole.

### Typology, or reading the Old Testament as Christ read it
On the road to Emmaus, “beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27, RSV). The Fathers took that verse as both permission and instruction. The Old Testament is not a separate religion with a Christian appendix attached; it is one story, told in advance and in figures.
The apostles had already begun. St Paul says of Israel in the wilderness that these things happened to them as types, and identifies the rock that followed them with Christ (1 Corinthians 10:1-11). St Peter reads Noah's ark as a figure of baptism (1 Peter 3:20-21). The Lord reads the bronze serpent of Numbers as a figure of the Cross (John 3:14) and Jonah as a figure of the three days (Matthew 12:40).
Once you have noticed it, it is everywhere in the services. Paschal hymns sing the crossing of the Red Sea as baptism. The Great Canon of St Andrew of Crete, chanted in the first week of Great Lent, works through the whole Old Testament applying each figure to the soul of the person singing it. Orthodox typology is not principally an academic method. It is what the Church does aloud every year.

### Alexandria: the sense beneath the letter
Two emphases developed and are usually labelled by city. Alexandria, a Greek intellectual capital with a long habit of reading Homer allegorically, produced readers who looked for the spiritual meaning underneath the surface of the text. Origen, in the third century, proposed three senses corresponding to body, soul and spirit, and read a great deal as pointing beyond itself.
That tradition continued through Didymus and, in a far more restrained form, through St Cyril of Alexandria, whose commentaries are among the treasures of the Church. At its best the Alexandrian instinct kept Christians from reading the Old Testament as the mere chronicle of a small nation. At its worst it could float away from the text altogether.
Reception here was uneven and it is worth saying so. Origen's exegetical influence was immense and much of it was absorbed gratefully, while a body of doctrine associated with his later followers was condemned in the sixth century. St Vincent of Lérins, writing in 434, chose him as the chief example of how a gifted and holy teacher can be admired and still be wrong.

### Antioch: the history first
Antioch pushed the other way. Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, St John Chrysostom and Theodoret insisted that the plain historical sense comes first, and that the spiritual meaning must grow out of it rather than replace it. Their word for that contemplative reading was theoria, a seeing through the history rather than past it.
Chrysostom's homilies show what the approach looks like in a parish. He works verse by verse, explains the customs, notices who is speaking to whom, and then turns without warning to the congregation in front of him and asks what they intend to do about the poor man outside the door. It is exegesis for people who will be at work in the morning.
Here too the reception was uneven. Theodore of Mopsuestia, the most rigorous of the Antiochenes, was condemned at the Fifth Ecumenical Council in 553. Chrysostom is one of the three Holy Hierarchs and the most widely read preacher in the Orthodox world. The Church kept the method and did not keep every conclusion reached by everyone who used it.

### Why the Church kept both
The two emphases are often presented as rivals, and modern scholars have increasingly qualified how sharp the division really was. Alexandrians could be literal and Antiochenes could be figural, and the same writer frequently does both on one page. Still, the tension is genuine, and the interesting thing is that the Church never resolved it by choosing.
She kept both because each corrects the other. Without the Antiochene discipline, allegory becomes a machine for finding whatever the reader brought with him. Without the Alexandrian eye, the Bible flattens into ancient history with morals attached. Holding the two together is uncomfortable, and the discomfort is much of the point: the text is being read by people who expect it to exceed them.

### Consensus is not unanimity
A common misunderstanding needs clearing away here. Orthodoxy does not teach that every Father is right about everything, or that they agree verse by verse. They do not. They contradict one another on chronology, on the identity of minor figures, on the meaning of particular passages and occasionally on more than that. What the Church looks for is the consensus patrum: agreement that is ancient, widespread and consistent, on the things that carry weight.
St Vincent of Lérins described both halves of this. His famous rule is to hold the faith “which has been believed everywhere, always, by all”. Less famously, in the same book, he insists that real progress in understanding is not merely permitted but required, so long as it is growth “in the same doctrine, in the same sense, and in the same meaning” rather than a change into something else.
Reading a Father is therefore a skill and not simply an act of submission. Fr. Seraphim Rose, an American convert raised in a Protestant family, wrote a whole book to demonstrate what that looks like. The Place of Blessed Augustine in the Orthodox Church argues against two currents at once: an inflated estimate of Augustine drawn from Western sources, and a fashion among some Orthodox writers of the 1970s for calling him a heretic. What he asked for instead was neither.

> a balanced appraisal of him with due credit given both to his unquestioned greatness and to his faults
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *The Place of Blessed Augustine in the Orthodox Church* (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, 1983), ch. I, p. 8

### Reading a Father critically, and reverently
Fr. Seraphim did not defend Augustine's doctrines of grace and predestination. He described himself elsewhere as no great admirer of them and thought them overly logical. What he defended was the man's piety, the contrition and love for Christ that fill the Confessions, and he judged that demolishing Augustine's reputation would take that piety down along with it.
The rule cuts in both directions, and it should be turned on modern teachers as readily as on ancient ones. A reviewer in the journal Orthodox Tradition called Fr. Seraphim's treatment of Augustine more balanced than most, and in the same notice pointed out that he had misattributed one patristic reference and that, working largely from Russian sources, his citations of the Greek Fathers are not always faithful to the Greek. Reading a teacher reverently includes checking him.
For an enquirer this is freeing rather than unsettling. Nobody is asking you to accept a body of writing uncritically, and nobody in the Orthodox tradition ever has. What is asked is that you read with the Church rather than against her, assume that people who prayed for decades saw things you have not yet seen, and hold your own conclusions a little more loosely than the accumulated judgement of centuries.

> I myself fear the cold hearts of the 'intellectually correct' much more than any errors you might find in Augustine.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter to Fr. Michael, 26 June 1981, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works* (St. Herman Press, 2003), ch. 86

### The heart before the mind
One further element belongs here, and in the Fathers it comes first rather than last. They did not think Scripture yields its meaning to cleverness. Purification precedes illumination: the reader is expected to be praying, fasting, confessing and giving alms, on the understanding that the obstacle to understanding is more often the condition of the reader than the difficulty of the text.
Fr. Seraphim put the same conviction to a room of Californian students in the spring of 1981, in a lecture that became a small book. He had spent years in Eastern philosophy before he came to Christ, and what he told them was not a technique.
Whether that claim is true is something each reader has to settle somewhere other than in an article. But it explains a good deal about Orthodox practice: why the Psalter is put into the hands of beginners while the harder commentaries wait, and why a monk who has read very little is not regarded as a poor reader of Scripture.
In practice all of this comes to something unremarkable. The Orthodox Christian reads the Bible daily from a fixed lectionary shared with every other Orthodox parish that day. He hears it sung and chanted at the services, where most of the hymns are themselves stitched out of biblical phrases. He reads a commentary, Chrysostom on Matthew being the usual starting place, and he asks his priest when he is stuck.
None of that substitutes for reading; it is a way of not reading alone. The difference from a private devotional habit is not that one side is serious and the other is not. Many Protestant readers put Orthodox Christians to shame in sheer diligence with the text, and Fr. Seraphim said as much about the Protestants he knew and admired. The difference lies in the assumption that the book belongs to a community stretched across twenty centuries, and that the community's reading has a claim on mine.
That claim can be declined, and declining it is a coherent position held by sincere Christians for reasons they can state. If you would rather test it than argue about it, the simplest experiment is to read one Gospel for a month alongside Chrysostom's homilies on it and see what happens. Our parish in Kovan will lend you a copy and ask nothing in return.

> God's revelation is given to something called a loving heart.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *God's Revelation to the Human Heart* (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, 2nd edn, 2014), §2 'Revelation'

### Common questions

Q: Do Orthodox Christians believe the Church Fathers were infallible?
A: No. The Fathers disagree with one another on many points and no individual Father is held to be free from error. What Orthodoxy trusts is the consensus patrum: agreement that is ancient, widespread and consistent on matters of substance. St Vincent of Lérins gave the test in 434, namely what has been believed everywhere, always and by all. Individual opinions outside that consensus are read with respect and with judgement.

Q: What is typology?
A: Reading a person, event or object in the Old Testament as a real historical thing which also prefigures Christ. The New Testament does this constantly: St Paul calls Israel's wilderness experiences types (1 Corinthians 10:11), St Peter reads the flood as a figure of baptism (1 Peter 3:21), and the Lord reads the bronze serpent and Jonah as figures of his Cross and burial. The Fathers extended a method they had inherited from the apostles.

Q: What is the difference between the Alexandrian and Antiochene schools?
A: Broadly, Alexandria emphasised the spiritual meaning beneath the letter while Antioch insisted that the historical sense comes first. Modern scholars have qualified the contrast, since writers on both sides did both. The Orthodox Church never chose between them: Cyril of Alexandria and John Chrysostom are both great teachers. Each emphasis restrains the other's characteristic failure, whether allegory untethered from the text or history with nothing beyond it.

Q: Can I read the Bible on my own?
A: Yes, and Orthodox Christians are expected to. The daily lectionary exists precisely so that everyone reads. Reading with the Church means reading with help and with a check: hearing the text at the services, reading a Father such as Chrysostom alongside it, and asking a priest when a passage resists. The aim is not to restrict reading but to keep it from drifting without anyone noticing that it has.

Q: Where should someone begin with the Fathers?
A: St John Chrysostom's homilies on Matthew or on Genesis are the usual first recommendation, since he is clear, practical and addressed to ordinary congregations. St Athanasius' On the Incarnation is short and formative. After those, St Basil's Hexaemeron and the Confessions of Blessed Augustine. Read slowly, and alongside the biblical text rather than instead of it, which is how the Fathers themselves expected to be used.

### Sources
- St Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.8 (the mosaic of the king): https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103108.htm
- St Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.10 (the rule of faith): https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103110.htm
- St Vincent of Lérins, Commonitory (434): https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3506.htm
- Orthodox Church in America, The Orthodox Faith: The Church Fathers: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/doctrine/sources-of-christian-doctrine/the-fathers
- Review of The Place of Blessed Augustine, Orthodox Tradition XIV.4: http://orthodoxinfo.com/inquirers/bless_aug.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 86, 'Orthodoxy of the Heart': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 87, 'Simplicity': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_87.aspx
- God's Revelation to the Human Heart, publisher's page: https://www.sainthermanmonastery.com/God-s-Revelation-to-the-Human-Heart-p/grhh.htm

## What Are the Seven Ecumenical Councils?
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/what-are-the-ecumenical-councils.html
Summary: The seven ecumenical councils are Nicaea I (325), Constantinople I (381), Ephesus (431), Chalcedon (451), Constantinople II (553), Constantinople III (680-681) and Nicaea II (787). Each answered a single pressing question about the Holy Trinity, the person of Christ, or the honouring of icons. In Orthodox understanding a council is ecumenical not because an emperor summoned it, but because the whole Church afterwards recognised its own faith in what the council said.
==============================================================================

### A council is what the Church does when a question cannot be left open
Councils are not the ordinary way the Church teaches. Most of the time the faith is handed on by baptising, preaching, burying the dead and serving the Liturgy, and nobody writes anything down. A council happens when something has gone wrong: when a bishop begins saying something his own congregation cannot recognise, when two cities are no longer praying the same faith, when the question being asked will not go away by itself.
The pattern is older than any of the seven. In the fifteenth chapter of Acts the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem over whether Gentile converts must be circumcised, argue it out, and send a letter beginning, in the RSV, "For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28). Every later council is an imitation of that meeting: men in a room, speaking plainly, believing the Spirit is present in the speaking.
What follows sets out the seven in order, with the question each faced and the answer it gave. The dates are firm; the debates behind them were not always dignified. Bishops were exiled, mobs gathered, emperors interfered. It is worth knowing that the definitions Christians now recite calmly were hammered out by tired men in difficult rooms.

### Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381): who God is
Nicaea I met in 325 in Bithynia, summoned by the Emperor Constantine. The question was put by Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, who taught that the Son is the first and highest of God's creatures — that there was a time when the Son was not. If Arius was right, the Christian who worships Christ is worshipping a creature. The council answered that the Son is begotten, not made, of one essence with the Father, using the Greek word homoousios. It also settled the reckoning of Pascha and issued twenty canons on church order.
Constantinople I met in 381 under the Emperor Theodosius I, with about one hundred and fifty bishops and no representation from the West. The question this time concerned the Holy Spirit. A party sometimes called the Pneumatomachi, the Spirit-fighters, granted the Son's divinity but treated the Spirit as a creature. The council confessed the Spirit as Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.
A point of honesty here. The creed sung on Sundays is called Niceno-Constantinopolitan and is associated with these two councils, but historians still discuss how directly the council of 381 produced the text we have; it is first explicitly ascribed to the hundred and fifty fathers in the acts of Chalcedon, seventy years later. The faith it states is not in doubt. The documentary history is untidier than the label suggests.

### Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451): the one Christ
Ephesus met in 431, called by Theodosius II. Nestorius, Archbishop of Constantinople, had objected to calling the Virgin Mary Theotokos, God-bearer, and preferred Christotokos, Christ-bearer. Behind the word stood a question about Christ: is the child born of Mary one and the same person as the eternal Word, or are there two who are somehow associated? The council deposed Nestorius, upheld Theotokos, and approved St Cyril of Alexandria's second letter to him. The title had been in Christian prayer long before it was in a decree.
That council was disorderly. Cyril opened the sessions before the bishops from Antioch had arrived; when they came they held a rival meeting and deposed him in turn. The breach was repaired two years later by the Formula of Reunion of 433. Ecumenical status was not conferred by good manners.
Chalcedon met in 451 under the Emperor Marcian. Eutyches, an archimandrite in Constantinople, had swung to the opposite error from Nestorius, teaching that after the union there is only one nature in Christ; a council at Ephesus in 449, later known as the Robber Council, had supported him. Chalcedon's Definition confesses one and the same Christ, made known in two natures without confusion, without change, without division, without separation, each nature keeping its own properties and concurring in one person.
Reception also failed in part at Chalcedon. The Armenian, Coptic, Syriac and Ethiopian churches did not accept its wording, though they reject Eutyches as firmly as anyone. A joint theological commission of Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox representatives issued agreed statements in 1989 and 1990 reporting a shared faith in Christ expressed in different terms. Communion has not been restored, and the reception of those statements is itself still argued over.

### Constantinople II (553) and Constantinople III (680-681): finishing the sentence
Constantinople II met in 553 under Justinian I. Its question was how Chalcedon was to be read. Many Christians in Egypt and Syria heard the Definition as a concession to Nestorius, and the empire was splitting along that fault. The council condemned the Three Chapters — the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, the writings of Theodoret against Cyril, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa to Maris — and set out fourteen anathemas affirming that the one who suffered in the flesh is one of the Holy Trinity.
Origen is also named among those condemned, and the Seventh Council later recalled the Fifth as having anathematised "the fables of Origen, Evagrius, and Didymus". Scholars continue to debate whether the fifteen anathemas directed specifically against Origenism were issued by the council itself or by a synod shortly before it. Pope Vigilius resisted the council and afterwards assented to it.
Constantinople III sat from 7 November 680 to 16 September 681, convoked by the Emperor Constantine IV. The question was whether Christ has one will or two. Monothelitism had been proposed as a formula that might bring the non-Chalcedonians back, and it was politically attractive. The council answered that Christ has two natural wills and two natural operations, the human will not opposed to the divine but freely subject to it.
This was not hair-splitting. If Christ has no human will, there is no human "nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done" in Gethsemane, and nothing human has been healed by being taken up. St Maximus the Confessor, who had argued this at the cost of his tongue and his right hand, died in exile in 662. The council vindicated him nineteen years after his death, and condemned Sergius, Cyrus, Pyrrhus, Paul, Peter, Macarius of Antioch and Pope Honorius.

### Nicaea II (787): the icons and the Incarnation
The seventh council met at Nicaea in 787 under the Empress Irene and Patriarch Tarasius, after some sixty years of imperial iconoclasm and an iconoclast council held at Hieria in 754. Its question was whether images of Christ, his Mother and the saints may be made and honoured at all. The council answered that they may and should, and drew a distinction it thought essential: icons receive salutation and honourable reverence, in Greek timetike proskynesis, and not the true worship of faith, latreia, which belongs to the divine nature alone.
Its reasoning is about the Incarnation rather than about art. The God whom no one has seen has taken flesh and been looked at, touched and painted; to deny that he can be depicted is, in the council's reading, to flinch from saying that he really became man. In the words of the Definition, "the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents", so that what is venerated is never the wood and pigment.
The matter was not closed in 787. Iconoclasm returned under the emperors from 815 and was ended only in 843, a day the Orthodox Church still keeps as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. In the West the decree reached the Frankish court in a poor Latin translation that made it say something close to the opposite, and the Frankish bishops reacted against it at Frankfurt in 794. Unease about Nicaea II is a great deal older than the Reformation.

### What makes a council "ecumenical"
Here is the part that surprises most enquirers. Nothing about the way a council is convened makes it ecumenical. Emperors summoned councils that the Church afterwards rejected: Ariminum in 359, the Robber Council of Ephesus in 449, Hieria in 754. The Council of Ferrara-Florence of 1438-39 was large, learned, attended by the Eastern patriarchs' representatives and signed by most of the Greek delegation — and it was not received in the East. Numbers, imperial backing and even signatures settle nothing on their own.
What makes a council ecumenical, in Orthodox understanding, is reception: the whole body of the Church, bishops and priests and monastics and ordinary believers, over time recognising in the council's words the faith they were already living. The Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs of 1848 puts it bluntly, arguing that neither patriarchs nor councils can introduce novelty because the guardian of the faith is the whole body of the Church, the people themselves. Constantinople I is the clearest illustration: a regional Eastern gathering with no Western bishops present, received later as the voice of the universal Church.
Two things follow. The first is that there is no mechanism for deciding in advance; reception is slow, and it cannot be organised. The second is that the number seven is a convention rather than a closed door. Some Orthodox writers have argued that the Council of Constantinople of 879-880 under St Photius, and the fourteenth-century Constantinopolitan councils on St Gregory Palamas, carry the same authority. That discussion is live among Orthodox theologians and has not been settled.

### Where Protestant Christians stand, and why the divide is not simple
Most Protestant Christians hold more of this than is often assumed. The classical Reformers accepted the first four councils explicitly; Lutheran and Anglican confessional documents keep Nicene and Chalcedonian language; the Nicene Creed is recited or sung weekly in a great many Protestant congregations. The substance of the christological councils — one person, two natures, two wills — is ordinary teaching in evangelical theology, whether or not Constantinople III is ever mentioned by name.
Nicaea II is the usual point of difficulty, and it deserves to be treated as a real conviction rather than a lapse. A Christian formed on the second commandment, who has been taught to see carved and painted images as exactly what God forbade, is not being obtuse when the veneration of icons troubles him. The Frankish bishops of the eighth century felt the same difficulty. Orthodoxy's answer is the one the council gave: God has become visible, and honour given to the image is not worship and does not stop at the image.
There is a further difference of principle worth naming plainly, because blurring it would be no kindness. A Christian who holds Scripture to be the final authority may accept the councils because he judges their teaching to be scriptural — the council is confirmed by the Bible. Orthodoxy receives the councils as the voice of the Church in which the Bible is read, and does not treat the two as separable. Two people can recite the same creed, mean every word, and still not agree about where its authority comes from.
That difference is real, and Orthodox Christians should not pretend otherwise. What is not permitted is turning the councils into something to win an argument with. Fr. Seraphim Rose, himself raised a Protestant, wrote in print against exactly that habit among converts.

> Even when it is worded in a theologically correct manner, this attitude is spiritually wrong
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, "In Defense of Fr. Dimitri Dudko", *The Orthodox Word* no. 2 (1980), p. 131, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Why seven councils matter on an ordinary Sunday
In our parish in Kovan the creed is sung by everyone, in several languages at once, most of the congregation not thinking about Bithynia at all. That is the point. The councils did not produce a syllabus; they produced the words a fisherman's widow and a university lecturer can say together without either of them meaning something different. Four Greek syllables in homoousios cost a century of exiles and reversals, and they are now sung in under two seconds by people who will never hear the word explained.
A council is a fence rather than a map. Each of the seven marks the place where the Church said: past this line you are talking about someone other than the Christ we know. Within the fence there is a great deal of room, and the Orthodox tradition has never pretended that every question has been answered. Enquirers are welcome to come and stand inside it for a while before deciding anything.
Fr. Seraphim Rose spent years outside the Church before he entered it, was raised in a Protestant home, and never forgot either fact. Writing to a catechumen who was distressed by the way some Orthodox converts spoke of other Christians, he passed on a formulation he credited to the Moscow priest Fr. Dimitry Dudko. It is the right note on which to leave the councils, which were called to guard the faith and not to give anyone a stick.

> We should view the non-Orthodox as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been revealed, as people who are potentially Orthodox
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Common questions

Q: What are the seven ecumenical councils in order?
A: Nicaea I in 325, on the divinity of the Son; Constantinople I in 381, on the Holy Spirit; Ephesus in 431, on the unity of Christ's person and the title Theotokos; Chalcedon in 451, on the two natures; Constantinople II in 553, on how Chalcedon is to be read; Constantinople III in 680-681, on the two wills; and Nicaea II in 787, on the holy icons.

Q: Who decides that a council is ecumenical?
A: In Orthodox understanding, no single office does. A council is recognised as ecumenical when the whole Church receives it — when bishops, clergy, monastics and lay believers across time recognise in its definitions the faith they already hold. Several councils convened as ecumenical were afterwards rejected, including Ariminum in 359, Ephesus in 449 and Hieria in 754, which is why convocation alone settles nothing.

Q: Do Protestants accept the ecumenical councils?
A: Many do, in substance. The classical Reformers accepted the first four; Nicene and Chalcedonian language is preserved in Lutheran and Anglican confessional texts, and the Nicene Creed is used weekly in many Protestant congregations. The christological content of all seven is widely held. The seventh council, on the veneration of icons, is the point most often not accepted, and that hesitation is a serious conviction about the second commandment rather than carelessness.

Q: Why does the Orthodox Church stop at seven?
A: Chiefly by convention. Nothing in Orthodox theology forbids another ecumenical council, and some Orthodox writers argue that the Constantinopolitan council of 879-880 under St Photius, or the fourteenth-century councils concerning St Gregory Palamas, already carry that authority. The discussion continues among Orthodox theologians. Because reception by the whole Church cannot be arranged in advance, the question cannot be closed administratively.

Q: What did the Seventh Council actually say about icons?
A: It defined that icons of Christ, the Mother of God, the angels and the saints should be set up in churches and honoured, receiving salutation and honourable reverence but not the true worship of faith, which belongs to God alone. Its reasoning was about the Incarnation: the God who has taken flesh can be depicted. The Definition adds that the honour paid to the image passes on to the one whom it represents.

Q: Were the councils politically manipulated?
A: Emperors convoked them, paid for them and sometimes leaned hard on them, and the sessions were often turbulent. Ephesus in 431 saw two rival assemblies deposing each other. Orthodoxy does not deny any of this. It holds that what settles a council's standing is not the tidiness of its proceedings but whether the Church afterwards recognised its own faith in the result — a test that several imperially sponsored councils failed.

### Sources
- The Seven Ecumenical Councils: First Council of Nicaea (325), canons and creed: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3801.htm
- First Council of Constantinople (381), canons: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3808.htm
- Council of Chalcedon (451), the Definition of Faith: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3811.htm
- Second Council of Constantinople (553), the anathemas: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3812.htm
- Third Council of Constantinople (680-681), the definition on the two wills: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3813.htm
- Second Council of Nicaea (787), the Definition on the holy icons: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3819.htm
- Second Agreed Statement of the Joint Commission of the Theological Dialogue between the Orthodox Church and the Oriental Orthodox Churches, Chambesy 1990: https://www.ecupatria.org/documents/second-agreed-statement-1990/
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works, ch. 84 'Pastoral Guidance': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
