## Apostolic Succession, and Why It Matters
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/apostolic-succession-explained.html
Summary: Apostolic succession means that every Orthodox bishop was ordained by bishops who were themselves ordained by bishops, in a line traced back to the apostles. What Orthodoxy believes is handed on is the apostolic ministry itself: authority to ordain, to preside at the Eucharist, and to teach as a witness. It is not a guarantee of a bishop's personal holiness or of his orthodoxy, and the Church has deposed bishops who held it.
==============================================================================

### What the phrase actually describes
Apostolic succession sounds abstract until you have watched it happen. At the consecration of an Orthodox bishop, other bishops stand around the man, open the book of the Gospels over his bowed head, and lay their hands on him while the prayer is read. Those bishops were made bishops the same way, by men who were made bishops the same way, and so on backwards, out of living memory, through the centuries, to the apostles.
The Church has always insisted that this be done by more than one man. The first of the collection known as the Apostolic Canons says simply: "Let a bishop be ordained by two or three bishops." The fourth canon of Nicaea in 325 asks for all the bishops of the province where possible, and at minimum three meeting together with the written consent of those absent, with the ratification left to the metropolitan. Nobody may make himself a bishop, and no single bishop may make another one alone.
That detail matters more than it looks. A bishop is not a man who has acquired something and can pass it on privately. He is received by a college of bishops into a ministry that is not his, on behalf of a particular community that has asked for him. Even the canonical arithmetic is designed to prevent anything resembling a private transaction.

### The laying-on of hands in the New Testament
The gesture runs through Acts and the pastoral epistles without ever being explained, in the way that habits people share are never explained. The eleven replace Judas by choosing Matthias (Acts 1:15-26). The apostles pray and lay hands on the seven (Acts 6:6). The church at Antioch fasts, prays and lays hands on Barnabas and Saul before sending them out (Acts 13:3). Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in every church (Acts 14:23), and Titus is told to appoint elders town by town (Titus 1:5).
Two verses to Timothy are the clearest. In the RSV: "Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophetic utterance when the elders laid their hands upon you" (1 Timothy 4:14), and "I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is within you through the laying on of my hands" (2 Timothy 1:6). Something is described as given through hands. Timothy is warned not to be casual about giving it himself: "Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands" (1 Timothy 5:22).
None of this is offered as proof-texting. It is the ordinary texture of the apostolic churches, and the question is simply whether that texture was meant to continue after the apostles died, or whether it was a feature of the founding generation only.

### What the second century took for granted
The generation immediately after the apostles answers that question without appearing to think it controversial. Writing from Rome to Corinth around the end of the first century, St Clement says that the apostles appointed their earliest converts as bishops and deacons, and gave directions that when those men died, other approved men should succeed to their ministry. He is not arguing for succession; he is appealing to it as something both churches already accept.
St Ignatius of Antioch, writing on his way to martyrdom around 107, assumes bishop, presbyters and deacons in each city as a matter of course, and tells the churches to do nothing pertaining to the Church apart from the bishop. Seventy years later St Irenaeus of Lyons, in the third book of Against Heresies, meets the Gnostic teachers by listing the bishops of Rome in order and pointing to Polycarp of Smyrna, who had been taught by the apostle John and whom Irenaeus had heard as a boy.
Honesty requires a qualification. In the New Testament the words for presbyter and bishop are sometimes used of the same men — compare Acts 20:17 with Acts 20:28, or Titus 1:5 with Titus 1:7 — and historians argue about how quickly the threefold pattern of bishop, presbyter and deacon became universal. Orthodoxy reads the New Testament vocabulary in the light of what the churches demonstrably did within a generation or two. A reader who finds that move too quick is raising a fair question.

### What Orthodoxy believes is transmitted
The thing handed on is the apostolic ministry: authority to ordain other clergy, to preside at the Eucharist, to receive people into the Church and to reconcile them, to teach as an accountable witness of what the Church has always taught. When Christ breathed on the disciples and gave them the Spirit with the power to forgive sins (John 20:22-23), Orthodoxy understands him to be equipping a ministry that would outlast the men in that room.
Notice what this is not. The grace at work in a sacrament is Christ's, not the bishop's. He is not a reservoir that has been filled and from which a measure can be drawn; he is a steward, and the prayers of ordination say so. Nor is a bishop ordained in the abstract: he is ordained for a diocese, a named community of real people, and a bishop without a flock is an anomaly the canons struggle to describe.
It follows that succession is not a chain of magic. Nothing passes down it automatically in the way that voltage passes down a wire. What is given is a commission within the Church, and it is exercised inside the Church's life, under her canons, answerable to the other bishops and to the faithful who will notice soon enough if their bishop starts teaching something strange.

### What is not transmitted
Personal holiness is not transmitted. This needs saying plainly, because a great deal of misunderstanding starts here. Judas was one of the Twelve and had been sent out to preach and to heal. Bishops in the Arian party had been consecrated by hands as properly as anyone. Nestorius was Archbishop of Constantinople. The iconoclast patriarchs held real sees by real ordinations, and several of them were learned and personally austere.
Correct teaching is not automatically transmitted either. The Orthodox Church has deposed, condemned and anathematised bishops who stood in the line, and has kept doing so. A bishop who begins teaching what the Church does not hold is not protected by the hands that were laid on him; the Church's response has been to remove him. Succession secures the office, not the man in it.
This is why it is wrong to speak as though the Orthodox claim were a claim about pedigree. Nobody is saved by being in a lineage. What the lineage does is much more modest: it means that there is a visible, traceable, accountable continuity between the community gathered in a hall in Kovan on a Sunday morning and the community that gathered in Jerusalem in the first century, and that the continuity can be checked.

### The Protestant conviction: succession of doctrine
Many thoughtful Christians hold that what genuinely has to be handed on is the apostolic message, not the apostolic hands, and they have a text to hand. Paul writes to Timothy, in the RSV: "what you have heard from me before many witnesses entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2). Hands are not mentioned. Teaching is. A line of bishops that no longer teaches what the apostles taught, on this view, is a line that has ceased to be apostolic in the only sense that counts.
The argument is serious and it is not a dodge. Orthodox history supplies some of its best evidence: for several stretches in the fourth century the majority of sitting bishops in the East were Arian or semi-Arian, and the faith was being defended by a deposed and exiled Athanasius and by monks with no office at all. A reader who concludes from that episode that hands alone settle nothing has read the episode correctly.
It is also worth saying that this is not a Protestant idiosyncrasy. Many Protestant bodies, including Anglicans and several Lutheran churches, retain bishops and set store by continuity of office; and every Orthodox bishop would agree that the office is worthless if the teaching is abandoned. The disagreement is narrower and more precise than the usual shorthand suggests.

### Why Orthodoxy holds the two together rather than choosing
Consider how Irenaeus actually argued. His opponents claimed a secret apostolic tradition passed to initiates. He did not answer by producing a lineage instead of a doctrine; he answered that the apostles' teaching is public, that anyone can go to Ephesus or Rome or Smyrna and find out what the church there has been taught continuously, and that the succession of bishops is what makes that check possible. Succession, for him, is the accountability of the teaching, not a substitute for it.
Put the other way round: a doctrine needs an address. If apostolic teaching is handed on by whoever has understood it rightly, the question of who has understood it rightly has no way of being settled except by each generation's judgement, and sincere people who read the same Bible reach different conclusions. If, instead, a visible community is charged with the teaching and can be held to it, the claim becomes checkable and the standard becomes public.
So Orthodoxy declines the choice. The hands without the faith produce an Arian bishop, and the Church deposes him. The faith without the hands produces a teaching with no one accountable for it, which in practice fragments. Held together, they amount to a single claim: the Church that hands on the apostolic faith is the same Church, continuously, and you can go and look at it.
There is one more strand. The bishop ordains, but he does not ordain in private. Historically an election involved the clergy and people of the diocese, and the congregation's acclamation, axios — he is worthy — still survives in the service as their part. The continuity Orthodoxy claims runs through a whole body, not only through a line of men.

### Saying the Orthodox position plainly
Enquirers usually want to know what all this implies about other Christians, and they deserve a straight answer rather than a diplomatic one. The Orthodox Church holds that she is the Church founded by Christ and that the sacraments are given in her. That is not a recent hardening or a Russian peculiarity; it is the traditional position, and Fr. Seraphim Rose, an American convert from a Protestant family, stated it without softening.

> In the Orthodox Church alone is grace given through the sacraments
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### And saying plainly what Orthodoxy does not claim to know
In the very same letter, written to a catechumen troubled by Orthodox Christians calling her Protestant and Catholic relatives heretics, Fr. Seraphim set a limit that is as much part of the Orthodox position as the sentence above. He would not pronounce on where any individual stands before God. He added, in that letter, that he had met people whose lives were entirely changed by meeting Christ, and that he could not deny their experience because they were not Orthodox.
Two claims, then, and they do not cancel each other. The Church makes a definite claim about herself and about where the sacraments are given. She makes no claim at all about the eternal standing of the Christian down the road who loves Christ, reads Scripture daily, and has never once been told what an Orthodox bishop is for. Those are different questions, and confusing them has done a great deal of damage.
If you have read this far from a Protestant background, nothing here asks you to conclude that your pastor is a fraud or that your grandmother's faith was empty. It asks a narrower question: whether the community that Christ founded was meant to be visible and continuous, and if so, where that continuity is to be found. Come and see how it looks from inside before deciding. The doors in Kovan are open on Sunday mornings, and nobody will ask you to sign anything.

> it is not for us to define the state of those who are outside the Orthodox Church
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Common questions

Q: What is apostolic succession in simple terms?
A: It is the continuous handing on of the apostolic ministry by the laying-on of hands. Every Orthodox bishop was ordained by other bishops, who were ordained by other bishops, in a traceable line reaching back to the apostles. Orthodox canons require at least two or three bishops for a consecration, so that no one can make himself a bishop and no single bishop can create another privately.

Q: Does apostolic succession guarantee that a bishop is holy or orthodox?
A: No, and Orthodoxy has never claimed it does. Judas was one of the Twelve. Arian and iconoclast bishops held valid ordinations. The Church has deposed and anathematised bishops standing in the succession, and continues to do so. Succession secures the office and its accountability; it does not sanctify the man holding it, nor does it protect him from error.

Q: Is apostolic succession in the Bible?
A: The phrase is not, but the practice is described repeatedly. Matthias is chosen to replace Judas (Acts 1), hands are laid on the seven (Acts 6:6) and on Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:3), elders are appointed in each church (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5), and Timothy is told that a gift was given him through the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6) and to be unhurried in doing the same.

Q: Isn't succession of doctrine more important than succession of hands?
A: Orthodoxy agrees that succession of hands without the apostolic faith is worthless, and the fourth-century Arian crisis proves it. The Orthodox answer is that the two belong together rather than competing. St Irenaeus appealed to the line of bishops precisely because it made the apostolic teaching publicly checkable against secret Gnostic claims. The hands give the teaching an address; the teaching gives the hands their purpose.

Q: Does Orthodoxy say Protestant ministers are not really ministers?
A: The Orthodox Church holds that she is the Church Christ founded and that the sacraments are given in her, and she does not recognise ordinations performed outside her. That is a statement about the Church's own order, not a verdict on anyone's sincerity, love of Christ or standing before God. Fr. Seraphim Rose put the limit firmly: it is not for us to define the state of those outside the Church.

Q: How can a line of hands be traced over two thousand years?
A: Not by a single unbroken written register for every see. What exists is a continuous institutional record: episcopal lists from the second century onwards, conciliar signatures, diptychs, ordination records and the mutual recognition of the autocephalous churches. Orthodoxy's claim is that the community has continued visibly and can be examined, not that a complete genealogical document survives for every bishop in every century.

### Sources
- The Apostolic Canons, canon 1: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3820.htm
- First Council of Nicaea (325), canon 4: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3801.htm
- St Clement of Rome, Letter to the Corinthians, chs. 42-44: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1010.htm
- St Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Smyrnaeans: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0109.htm
- St Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies, Book III ch. 3: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103303.htm
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works, ch. 84 'Pastoral Guidance': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works, ch. 86 'Orthodoxy of the Heart': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
- Parish of the Dormition of the Mother of God, Singapore: https://orthodox.sg/

## Does Christian Doctrine Develop, or Is It Preserved?
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/does-doctrine-develop-or-is-it-preserved.html
Summary: Orthodoxy holds that the apostolic faith was given whole and is guarded rather than improved. What changes is language: words like homoousios and Theotokos were coined or defended to protect a faith already held. St Vincent of Lerins allowed real growth provided it stays the same teaching in the same sense. Orthodoxy is wary of theories of development because they can justify teaching the early Church did not hold.
==============================================================================

### The question behind the question
Ask an Orthodox priest whether Christian doctrine develops and you will usually get a hesitation before the answer. The hesitation is not evasion. It is the recognition that the word carries two quite different meanings, and that agreeing or disagreeing too quickly will mislead whoever asked.
One instinct governs the Orthodox side of this conversation, and it is worth stating before anything else. The faith is received, not composed. St Jude writes of "the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 3, RSV), and Orthodoxy has taken that phrase with great seriousness: bishops and councils are stewards of something already given, not a standing committee empowered to improve it. Whatever else is true, the Church does not hold that she may teach in the twenty-first century what she could not have taught in the second.
But the Church plainly says things now that nobody said in the year 60. The Nicene Creed uses a Greek philosophical term that is not in Scripture. A council defended a title for the Virgin Mary that Scripture does not use in that form. Something has happened between then and now, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The question is what.

### Two things the word can mean
When a Roman Catholic theologian says doctrine develops, he usually means that the Church's understanding of a revelation given once can genuinely unfold over time, so that what was implicit becomes explicit and may be defined as binding. When an Orthodox theologian denies that doctrine develops, he usually means that the content of the faith cannot be added to, and that the Church's task is to state the same faith in whatever words each crisis requires. Stated that way, the two positions overlap considerably and disagree about something narrow and important.
Fr. Seraphim Rose made a methodological observation in the middle of an entirely different argument, about creation and evolution, and it applies here exactly. His complaint was that two parties can spend years exchanging fire while using a shared word for two different things, so that neither side ever hears what the other is claiming. Anyone entering the argument about doctrinal development should establish first which of the two questions is being asked, because the answers run in opposite directions.

> Many of the arguments between 'evolutionists' and 'anti-evolutionists' are useless, for one basic reason: they are usually not arguing about the same thing.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter to Dr Alexander Kalomiros, in *Genesis, Creation and Early Man*, Part Two, "A Clear Definition" (St. Herman Press)

### St Vincent of Lerins and his canon
The classic text on this question in the Christian tradition was written around 434 by a monk of the island monastery of Lerins, off the coast of Provence, under the pen-name Peregrinus. His short book is usually called the Commonitory, and he wrote it to answer a practical problem: when a new teaching appears and its defenders quote Scripture for it, how does an ordinary Christian tell truth from novelty?
His answer, in the second chapter, is the sentence that has been quoted ever since. Christians should hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all", and the rule is observed by following "universality, antiquity, consent" (Commonitory ch. 2, in the translation of C. A. Heurtley). Universality means what the Church confesses across the world, antiquity what was held by the fathers before us, consent what the great majority of them agreed in teaching.
It is a better rule than it is sometimes made to sound, and also a harder one to use. Applied with a ruler, it would exclude a good deal that every Christian accepts, since almost nothing has been taught in identical words by literally everyone from the beginning. Vincent knew this. Most of the Commonitory is devoted to the cases where the rule is difficult, and it is precisely because he knew it that he wrote the chapter that follows.

### Vincent's own answer: growth, not alteration
The twenty-third chapter of the Commonitory is headed, in Heurtley's rendering, "On Development in Religious Knowledge", and it is not what a reader expecting a flat denial of change would predict. Vincent asks whether there is then no progress in the Church of Christ, and answers that there is, and that it should be very great. What he refuses is the substitution of one thing for another. In his words: "Progress requires that the subject be enlarged in itself, alteration, that it be transformed into something else."
His image is a body. A child grows into an adult and acquires size, strength and proportion, yet no new limbs appear; the joints of the grown man were already framed in the infant. So the Church may understand more, explain better, and defend more precisely, provided it is the same teaching "in the same doctrine, in the same sense, and in the same meaning". That last phrase, in eodem sensu eademque sententia, is the load-bearing one, and it is the test Orthodoxy still applies.
So the Orthodox instinct is not hostility to growth as such, and it is worth noticing that the tradition's most quoted defender of antiquity was the one who said so. What Vincent rules out is transformation dressed as maturity. What he permits is a Church that understands its own confession more deeply, states it more exactly, and defends it more capably, because someone has denied it and the denial has to be answered.

### New words in the service of an old faith
Take homoousios, the word at the centre of Nicaea in 325. It is not a biblical term. Worse, later writers report that it had been rejected at a synod at Antioch in the 260s, in connection with the condemnation of Paul of Samosata, so the fathers at Nicaea adopted a word with an awkward history. St Athanasius spent a treatise defending the use of a non-scriptural term, arguing that the word was needed because Arius and his supporters could sign every scriptural formula while meaning by it something the Church did not mean.
That is the pattern. The word added nothing to the faith; it closed a door that had been propped open. Christians had worshipped Christ as God for three centuries without the term, and the term was coined so that they could go on doing exactly what they had been doing without being told that it meant something else. New vocabulary is a defensive measure, and the Church has generally adopted it reluctantly.
Theotokos works the same way. The title was in use in Greek Christian prayer well before Ephesus defined it in 431; the ancient prayer known in English as "Beneath thy compassion" survives on a Greek papyrus usually dated to the third or fourth century, though the dating has been argued over. The council did not invent the word. It refused to let the word be taken away, because what the word protects is a statement about Christ: the one born of Mary is the eternal Son, and not a man associated with him.

### Newman's proposal, taken seriously
John Henry Newman published An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine in 1845, as he was leaving the Church of England for Rome. The book deserves better than the caricature it often receives, and an Orthodox reader who has not read it is arguing with a rumour. Newman was facing a genuine difficulty with complete honesty: the Church of the fourth century said things the Church of the first century had not said in those words, and appeals to antiquity alone did not seem to him to account for it.
His proposal was that a living idea in a living community behaves like a living thing. It is turned over, tested, applied to new circumstances, and what was implicit in it becomes explicit. He knew perfectly well that this could be used to justify anything, so he offered seven notes for distinguishing a true development from a corruption — among them preservation of type, continuity of principles, power of assimilation, and conservative action upon its past. The care is real. Newman was not looking for a licence.
He also drew, pointedly, on Vincent of Lerins. Both men use the image of bodily growth. That is the measure of how close the two accounts can stand, and it makes the remaining distance worth identifying accurately rather than rhetorically.

### Why Orthodoxy hesitates
The first hesitation is about where the burden of proof sits. On a developmental account, a teaching can be justified by showing that it follows from principles the Church has always held, even if no one taught it for many centuries. Orthodoxy wants something more stubborn: the witness of the Church's actual prayer, preaching and practice. A doctrine that cannot be found in what Christians were doing on their knees is, on Orthodox terms, unproven however elegant the line of inference.
A second hesitation concerns the early Church. If doctrine unfolds, then believers in the second century possessed the faith in a less complete form than believers today, and Orthodoxy is reluctant to say that. The martyrs of Lyons in 177 had the whole faith. What they lacked was not truth but vocabulary, and vocabulary was only needed later because the truth was later attacked.
The third hesitation is historical and should be stated without heat. Newman's theory was framed in part to account for teachings that Orthodoxy does not accept — among them the universal jurisdiction and the personal infallibility of the Bishop of Rome, defined in 1870, and the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854. Orthodox Christians do not hold those doctrines and have said so for centuries. The theory of development is not the reason for that disagreement, but it is the framework that made the disagreement easier to describe.
Orthodox theologians are not entirely of one mind here. Some have argued that the gap between a carefully stated theory of development and the Orthodox account of unfolding expression is narrower than the vocabulary suggests, while others regard the whole category as foreign. Anyone who tells you that the Orthodox tradition speaks with one voice on this particular question is tidying up.

### Guarding is not the same as repeating
There is a way of holding all this that is faithful in form and dead in substance: to keep the formulas and lose the thing the formulas were made to protect. Orthodoxy is not immune from it. Fr. Seraphim Rose, writing in the 1970s about a narrowness he saw growing among converts and Western-born Orthodox, thought this the real danger rather than laxity.

> the chief danger is something much deeper—the loss of the savor of Orthodoxy
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 63 "Super-Correctness" (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Where this leaves an enquirer
For a Protestant reader, much of this will feel familiar from an unexpected direction. The Reformers' appeal to antiquity, the suspicion of teachings that appear late without early witnesses, the instinct that the Church is accountable to something she did not invent — these are Orthodox instincts too, and the overlap is not accidental. Where Orthodoxy differs is in locating the guarded thing in the continuous life of a visible Church rather than in the text alone, and that difference is real and should not be smoothed over.
Preservation, understood properly, is not a filing system. It is closer to what a family does with a language: the grammar does not change, the vocabulary grows as it must, and the whole thing dies the moment nobody speaks it at home. The councils coined words because the faith was being spoken, and was being contradicted, by people who cared enormously. A tradition that had stopped caring would not have needed homoousios at all.
Which is why the last word here should be about temperature rather than precision. Fr. Seraphim spent his final years defending Blessed Augustine of Hippo, whose errors on grace and predestination he did not defend at all, against Orthodox writers of his own day who wanted the man himself struck off the list of fathers. Writing to a priest in June 1981, he explained where his own fear lay.
If you have read this far and think the Orthodox answer too conservative, that is a reasonable place to stand and we are not going to argue you out of it in an article. Come and see what a faith that believes itself unchanged actually looks like in a room on a Sunday morning. Judgements of that kind are better made from inside a building than from outside one.

> I myself fear the cold hearts of the 'intellectually correct' much more than any errors you might find in Augustine.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 26 June 1981, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 86 "Orthodoxy of the Heart" (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Common questions

Q: Does the Orthodox Church believe doctrine develops?
A: It believes the content of the faith was given whole and cannot be added to, while the language used to state it can and has changed. Orthodoxy therefore speaks of the same faith more precisely expressed under pressure from error, rather than of doctrine unfolding into new teaching. The test, inherited from St Vincent of Lerins, is whether what is said remains the same doctrine in the same sense and the same meaning.

Q: What is the Vincentian canon?
A: It is the rule stated by St Vincent of Lerins around 434 in the second chapter of his Commonitory: Christians should hold the faith that has been believed everywhere, always, and by all, following universality, antiquity and consent. It is a test for distinguishing the Church's faith from novelty. Vincent himself spent most of the book on the hard cases, because the rule is easier to state than to apply.

Q: If nothing changes, why does the Creed use the word homoousios?
A: Because a word was needed that Arius could not sign. The Arian party could accept every scriptural phrase about Christ while meaning by it that he was a creature. Homoousios, of one essence, was adopted at Nicaea in 325 to close that door. It is not a biblical term and had an awkward history, and St Athanasius had to argue for using it. It added nothing to the faith; it protected what was already believed.

Q: What did Newman actually argue?
A: In his Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845), Newman argued that a revelation given once is understood more fully over time within a living community, so that what was implicit becomes explicit. Aware that this could excuse anything, he set out seven notes for telling genuine development from corruption. It is a serious and careful book, and Orthodox disagreement with its conclusions is not a reason to misrepresent its argument.

Q: Why is Orthodoxy wary of the idea of development?
A: For three reasons. It can justify teaching by inference where Orthodoxy wants the witness of the Church's actual prayer and practice. It implies that earlier Christians held the faith less completely, which Orthodoxy denies. And historically it was framed partly to account for doctrines Orthodoxy does not accept, including papal infallibility defined in 1870 and the Immaculate Conception defined in 1854. Orthodox theologians are not unanimous about how sharp the disagreement is.

Q: Is the title Theotokos an example of doctrine developing?
A: Orthodoxy would say it is an example of doctrine being defended. The title was already in Greek Christian prayer before the Council of Ephesus defined it in 431; an ancient prayer using it survives on a papyrus usually dated to the third or fourth century, though the dating is disputed. The council did not create the word, and what it protected was a statement about Christ rather than a new claim about his mother.

### Sources
- St Vincent of Lerins, Commonitory: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3506.htm
- St Vincent of Lerins, Commonitory ch. 23, 'On Development in Religious Knowledge': https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf211.iii.xxiv.html
- First Council of Nicaea (325), the creed and canons: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3801.htm
- Council of Ephesus (431): https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3810.htm
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works, ch. 63 'Super-Correctness': http://orthodoxinfo.com/ecumenism/fsr_63.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works, ch. 86 'Orthodoxy of the Heart': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
- Orthodox Tradition XIV.4: 'Blessed Augustine of Hippo: His Place in the Orthodox Church': http://orthodoxinfo.com/inquirers/bless_aug.aspx
- Works of Fr. Seraphim Rose at azbyka.ru: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/

## What Orthodox Christians Believe Happens in Baptism
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/orthodox-baptism-what-happens.html
Summary: Orthodox Christians believe baptism does something rather than only signifies something. The candidate renounces the devil, turns east to Christ, and is immersed three times in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Saint Paul calls this a burial with Christ and a rising with him (Romans 6:3-5). Sins are forgiven, the Holy Spirit is given in chrismation, and the baptised person is joined to the Church.
==============================================================================

### What you would see if you came to a baptism
A baptism at our parish usually happens on a Saturday, with the church half empty and the afternoon light coming in sideways. Near the middle of the nave stands a large font of warm water. On a small table lie oil, scissors, a white garment and a cross on a cord. The priest wears white. If the one being baptised is an infant, an aunt is standing by with a towel and the whole family is quietly anxious about the water temperature.
The service falls into two halves. In the first, the candidate is prayed over, breathed upon, and asked to renounce the devil; then the water and the oil are blessed and the candidate is anointed. In the second half comes the immersion itself, three times, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Immediately afterwards the newly baptised person is chrismated, clothed in white, given a cross, and a few hairs are cut in token of offering. At the next Liturgy, often the same weekend, he receives communion.

### Buried with him by baptism
Saint Paul does not describe baptism as a badge. Writing to the Romans he asks: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:3-4, RSV). The grammar is the grammar of a funeral, and then of a resurrection.
Orthodox practice takes that language at face value. The font is deep enough to go under. Three immersions answer the three days in the tomb, and the ancient canons treat the number as serious business: Apostolic Canon 50 directs that a bishop or presbyter who does not perform three immersions be deposed. The words spoken over each immersion are the words of Christ's own commission in Matthew 28:19, naming the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
What is being claimed here is not that the candidate has demonstrated something, but that God has done something. The Nicene Creed, said in every Orthodox church every Sunday, includes the line: I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. Not commemorate. Confess. The Church has never taught that the water merely displays a work completed privately beforehand; she teaches that in the water a person is joined to the death and rising of Christ, and comes up out of it belonging to him.

### Facing west, then turning east
Before anyone goes near the water there is a confrontation. The candidate, or the godparent holding the child, is turned to face west, towards the back of the church and the darkness, and is asked three times whether he renounces Satan, and all his works, and all his angels, and all his service, and all his pride. The answer is given three times: I do renounce him. Then the candidate is told to breathe and spit upon him, which visitors always find startling, and which is meant to be.
Only after that does the priest turn the candidate round to the east, where the questions change: Dost thou unite thyself to Christ? I do unite myself to Christ. Asked whether he has united himself, the candidate answers that he has, and worships him as King and God, and then recites the Creed aloud. East is chosen deliberately. Paradise was planted in the east (Genesis 2:8), and the Lord's return is likened to lightning that comes from the east (Matthew 24:27). Orthodox churches are built facing that way, so the whole congregation prays in the direction the new Christian has just turned.

### The case for waiting, stated properly
A great many Christians, including people we know and love in Singapore, baptise only those old enough to ask for it. Their conviction deserves to be stated at full strength rather than brushed past. Faith, they say, is personal and cannot be borrowed; nobody is a Christian on his parents' account. The pattern in Acts is that the word is preached, people believe, and then they are baptised (Acts 2:41; Acts 8:12). A promise made by an adult over a sleeping infant is not that infant's promise, and the day may come when he never makes one himself.
Behind this lies a fear with real evidence behind it: whole countries full of people baptised in infancy who were never taught anything, never returned, and now call themselves Christian the way one might name a birthplace. Believer's baptism is a high view of baptism, not a low one. It has cost people their families. An Orthodox writer who treats it as carelessness has not been listening, and Fr. Seraphim Rose, whose own mother was a Protestant, was blunt about where some of the blame for such misunderstandings lies.

> perhaps it is our fault for not living and teaching the Orthodox Faith in a way they can understand
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Why the Orthodox Church baptises infants anyway
The Orthodox answer begins somewhere other than argument. A child belongs to the Church before he is able to argue about it, in the same way that he belongs to his family, his language and his mother's table before he can defend any of them. Nobody waits for a two-year-old to consent to being fed. The Church has never thought that faith is the single good which must be withheld from a child until he can hold his own in a debate about it.
Scripture is then read in that light. Peter tells the crowd at Pentecost that the promise is to you and to your children (Acts 2:39). Luke reports whole households baptised at once, Lydia's and the Philippian jailer's, and Paul recalls baptising the household of Stephanas (Acts 16:15; Acts 16:33; 1 Corinthians 1:16). Colossians 2:11-12 sets baptism alongside circumcision, which was given on the eighth day to infants who could not consent and did not understand. And there is the plain sentence of the Lord: “Let the children come to me, do not hinder them” (Mark 10:14, RSV).
Early evidence points the same way, though its weight is argued over honestly. Saint Irenaeus of Lyons, writing around 180, speaks of Christ saving all who are born again to God through him, “infants, and children, and boys, and youths, and old men” (Against Heresies II.22.4); readers disagree about how much that sentence proves. Firmer is Saint Cyprian's Letter 64, which records an African council of about the year 253 deciding that baptism ought not to be delayed until the eighth day after birth. By then the question was no longer whether infants were baptised, but how soon.
None of this makes baptism a substitute for faith, and Orthodoxy does not pretend otherwise. A baptised child who is taught nothing has been given a beginning and then abandoned in it. What the Church offers instead is a long apprenticeship: communion from infancy, confession from about the age of seven, the Creed learned by heart, and eventually the day when the young Christian says in his own voice what his godparents once said for him. Grace goes ahead of understanding here, as it does everywhere else in a human life.

### What the godparents actually undertake
At an infant baptism the godparent is not decoration. It is the godparent who faces west and renounces the devil on the child's behalf, who turns east, and who recites the Creed aloud in the child's place. That is, in the first instance, a profession of the godparent's own faith, made in public, and an undertaking to teach the child the faith just professed. The Church asks, therefore, that at least one godparent be a practising Orthodox Christian who goes to confession and communion.
In practice the undertaking runs to a short and unglamorous list, which we ask godparents to read before they agree to it. None of it is heroic. All of it is the sort of thing that happens only because one adult decided years earlier that it would, and then went on deciding it on ordinary Saturdays when there were easier things to do.
- Pray for the godchild by name, daily, for as long as you both live.
- Bring the child to communion, particularly when the parents cannot.
- Teach the Lord's Prayer and the Creed, and see that the child knows the story of his patron saint.
- Give the first icon and the first prayer book, and keep giving books as the child grows.
- Be a second adult the child can talk to, especially in the years when parents are hard to talk to.
- Stand by the family in trouble, which is the part nobody mentions at the font.

### If you were already baptised somewhere else
Converts are received in one of three ways: by baptism, by chrismation after a confession of the Orthodox faith, or, more rarely, by a confession of faith alone. The choice is not made by the convert, and not really by the parish priest either. It belongs to the bishop, who weighs what was done originally, in what words, with what intention, and what the person is coming from.
In most Russian Orthodox practice, including that of our own Exarchate, a person baptised with water in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is not baptised again. Such a convert is prepared as a catechumen, makes a confession of sins, is anointed with the holy myrrh in chrismation, and comes to the chalice. Where the original baptism was not in water, or not in the name of the Trinity, or cannot be established at all, the person is baptised.
Here honesty matters more than tidiness. Practice varies between the local Orthodox Churches, and sometimes between bishops within one of them. Some parishes and monastic communities baptise every convert as a matter of principle, appealing to the strict standard the canons set out. Others receive by chrismation, appealing to the Church's long freedom to act by economy towards those who are coming to her.
So a convert chrismated in one city may one day meet Orthodox Christians who would have done it differently. That difference is real, it is old, and it is argued about among Orthodox themselves rather than settled by a parish website. It is not a verdict on anyone's past or on anyone's sincerity. The practical counsel is simple: raise the question with the priest at the beginning rather than the end, and let the bishop decide it.
Whatever form the reception takes, the point of it is not paperwork, and not a change of club membership. Fr. Seraphim Rose wrote to a catechumen preparing for baptism in May 1979, and the sentence he put at the centre of that letter is worth carrying from the first enquiry to the day the chrism is wiped away.

> You are coming to Orthodoxy to receive Christ, and this you should never forget.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 3 May 1979, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### A door left open
Nothing in this article asks anyone to despise the water that was poured over him as a child, or to think badly of the parents who arranged it, or of the pastor who prayed. Orthodoxy has its own account of what baptism is and does, and has held it consistently for a very long time; saying so plainly is not an accusation against anyone else. Fr. Seraphim Rose, who grew up among Protestants and stayed on good terms with his family after he became a monk, put the attitude he wanted from Orthodox Christians in one sentence.
If any of this interests you, the simplest next step is not a book. Come to a Liturgy at Kovan, stand at the back for as long as you like, stay for tea afterwards, and ask the questions you actually have rather than the ones you think you are supposed to have. Nobody here will hurry you towards the font, and nobody will think less of you for taking years over it.

> We should view the non-Orthodox as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been revealed, as people who are potentially Orthodox
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Common questions

Q: Why does the Orthodox Church baptise infants?
A: Because the Church regards a child as belonging to her before he is old enough to argue about it. Scripture records whole households baptised together (Acts 16:15, 16:33; 1 Corinthians 1:16), Peter says the promise is to you and to your children (Acts 2:39), and Christ tells his disciples not to hinder the children who come to him. Baptism is a beginning, and the child is then raised in what he has been given.

Q: Why three immersions rather than one?
A: The three immersions answer the three days Christ lay in the tomb, and each is made in the name of one Person of the Holy Trinity, following Matthew 28:19. The practice is not merely customary: Apostolic Canon 50 directs that a clergyman who baptises with a single immersion instead of three be deposed. An Orthodox font is therefore built deep enough for a person to go fully under the water.

Q: Will I be baptised again if I was already baptised as a Protestant?
A: Usually not, in Russian Orthodox practice. Someone baptised with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is normally received by chrismation after a period of preparation and a confession of sins. Practice varies between jurisdictions and between bishops, and some communities baptise all converts on principle. The decision belongs to the bishop, so it is worth raising with the parish priest early.

Q: What do Orthodox godparents promise?
A: At an infant baptism the godparent renounces the devil on the child's behalf, turns east, and recites the Creed in the child's place, which is first of all a profession of the godparent's own faith. The undertaking that follows is lifelong: daily prayer for the godchild, bringing the child to communion, teaching the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, and standing by the family. At least one godparent should be a practising Orthodox Christian.

Q: Is baptism by pouring accepted in Orthodoxy?
A: The Orthodox norm is threefold immersion, and parishes build their fonts accordingly. Pouring has been used in cases of genuine necessity, such as serious illness, and baptisms performed by pouring outside the Church are often accepted when converts are received by chrismation. This is a matter on which the practice of local Churches differs, so it is a question for the priest, and ultimately for the bishop, rather than for a website.

Q: What happens immediately after the immersion?
A: The newly baptised person is chrismated, anointed with holy myrrh on the forehead, eyes, nostrils, mouth, ears, breast, hands and feet, with the words: the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. He is then clothed in a white garment, given a cross to wear, and a few hairs are cut as a first offering. Communion follows at the next Divine Liturgy, and infants receive it too.

### Sources
- Orthodox Church in America — The Sacraments: Baptism: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-sacraments/baptism
- Orthodox Church in America — The Sacraments: Chrismation: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-sacraments/chrismation
- OrthodoxInfo — Baptismal Ecclesiology: http://orthodoxinfo.com/ecumenism/ea_ecclesiology.aspx
- OrthodoxInfo — The Church Is Visible and One: http://orthodoxinfo.com/inquirers/church.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works, ch. 84, “Pastoral Guidance”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Azbyka.ru — works of Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose): https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/

## The Eucharist: Real Presence Without Explanation
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/the-eucharist-real-presence.html
Summary: Orthodox Christians believe that at the Divine Liturgy the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ. The change is asked for in the epiclesis, the prayer calling down the Holy Spirit on the gifts. Orthodoxy affirms the reality and deliberately does not define the mechanism, treating it as a mystery to be received rather than a process to be explained.
==============================================================================

### What is claimed, and what is left unsaid
Ask an Orthodox priest what is in the chalice on Sunday morning and he will tell you, without hedging, that it is the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ. Ask him how the bread stopped being bread and he will most likely say that he does not know, that nobody knows, and that the Church has never undertaken to find out. Both answers are serious. The first is a confession of faith the Church will not soften; the second is a refusal she regards as equally important.
That combination puzzles visitors, particularly those who have been taught to expect a religion either to explain its claims or to reduce them. Orthodoxy does neither here. She states the fact and stops. A great deal of what follows is an attempt to show why stopping is not evasion, and why the Church thinks the question “how” belongs to a different order of enquiry from the question “what”.

### John 6, and the disciples who walked away
The sixth chapter of John is where this begins. After feeding the five thousand, Christ tells a crowd that he is the bread of life, and then says something that they find impossible: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (John 6:53, RSV). His hearers object. He does not withdraw the words or explain them away; he repeats them in stronger terms, four times over.
What happens next is the detail that Orthodox readers find decisive. “After this many of his disciples drew back and no longer went about with him” (John 6:66, RSV). Disciples leave, and Christ lets them go, asking the Twelve whether they will leave too. A teacher who had meant only a vivid metaphor had every opportunity to say so, and did not. The Church has therefore read the discourse as meaning what it appears to mean, and has read it at the chalice ever since.

### Paul writing to a congregation that got it wrong
Saint Paul's first letter to Corinth gives the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper, and it is a rebuke. The Corinthians were treating the gathering as a supper club where the rich ate first. His correction turns on what the bread and the cup are: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16, RSV).
From there he draws a conclusion that only makes sense if something objective is present. Whoever eats unworthily is “guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord,” and anyone who eats “without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:27, 29, RSV). He then says that this is why some in the congregation are weak and ill. One does not profane a symbol, and a memorial does not make anyone sick. Orthodoxy takes the warning as evidence about what is being received.

### The epiclesis: the prayer that asks for the change
In the Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, served in this parish most Sundays, the central prayer of the anaphora comes after the words of institution. The deacon and priest bow, and the priest asks God to send down the Holy Spirit upon the assembled people and upon the gifts set forth, and to make the bread the precious Body of his Christ and the cup the precious Blood of his Christ, changing them by his Holy Spirit. The congregation answers Amen three times.
Notice the shape of the request. Nobody in the building claims to perform the change. The priest asks, in the name of the whole assembly, and what is asked for is the action of the Holy Spirit, the same Spirit who overshadowed the Virgin and raised Christ from the dead. Orthodox theology has always laid weight on this prayer, and the epiclesis is one of the places where Eastern and Western liturgical thought developed differently over the centuries.
The consequence is practical. Because the change is asked for rather than produced, the Church has no procedure to describe. She has a petition and an answer. What the faithful see is bread and wine; what they are taught they receive is Christ himself, whole and entire, in each particle and each drop.

### What other Christians hold, and what each view protects
Christians outside Orthodoxy hold a range of positions here, and each of them is trying to guard something the apostolic writings genuinely say. It is worth setting them out properly, at their strongest rather than at their weakest, because a caricature helps nobody and because most readers of this page will have been formed by one of them. What follows is a summary, not a rebuttal.
The memorial understanding, often associated with Zwingli and widespread among evangelical and non-denominational congregations, takes the Supper as an act of remembrance and of covenant loyalty, obeying “do this in remembrance of me.” What it protects is real: the sufficiency of the one sacrifice offered once for all, and the conviction that grace is not manipulated by ritual. Behind it lies a proper horror of superstition.
Reformed teaching, following Calvin, holds that believers truly feed on Christ in the Supper, not by his body descending into the bread but by the Holy Spirit joining the believer to Christ where he is. That view guards two things at once: the reality of the gift, and the bodily ascension of the Lord who sits at the right hand of the Father. It is not a thin doctrine, and those who hold it often speak of the Supper with great reverence.
Lutheran teaching goes further still, affirming that the true Body and Blood are given in, with and under the bread and the wine, though Lutherans generally reject the label consubstantiation as a scholastic intrusion. What that position protects is the plainness of Christ's words at the table. Anglican formularies have carried more than one of these views at the same time. Fr. Seraphim Rose, writing about Christians outside the Orthodox Church, refused to treat such people as strangers.

> there is no reason why we should regard them as totally estranged or as equal to pagans
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Why Orthodoxy stops short of an explanation
Orthodoxy differs from all of these, and the difference should be stated without apology. The Church holds that the gifts are changed, that what lies on the altar after the epiclesis is not bread with something added but the Body of Christ, and that this is true independently of the faith of any particular communicant. That is a real disagreement with the memorial view, and a real disagreement with the Reformed account, and it is not dissolved by good manners.
But the Orthodox reluctance to explain is just as firm. Greek Orthodox confessional documents of the seventeenth century, notably the Confession of Dositheus adopted at the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672, did borrow the term metousiosis in reply to Reformed arguments then circulating. Later Orthodox theologians have generally been wary of treating that word as an endorsement of the Latin scholastic analysis of substance and accidents, and have preferred the older language of mystery.
Saint John of Damascus had already set the tone in the eighth century. In his exposition of the faith he considers the question how the bread becomes the Body, and answers, in substance, that the Holy Spirit does it, that the manner is beyond us, and that it is enough to know the word of God is true (An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, IV.13). The Liturgy itself calls the gifts “the holy mysteries,” and that is not a decorative word. It names a boundary the Church has chosen not to cross.
There is a pastoral reason for the boundary as well as a theological one. A mechanism can be argued about, improved, defended and eventually believed in for its own sake. A mystery can only be approached, and approached in a particular way, with fasting, confession and preparation. Orthodoxy would rather have communicants who tremble a little than communicants who have a satisfactory theory.

### Why the chalice is not offered to every visitor
Orthodox parishes practise what is usually called closed communion. A visitor who is not an Orthodox Christian is asked not to receive the gifts. This is the point at which the most hurt is caused, and it is worth being exact about what it does and does not mean, because it is often heard as a judgement on the visitor's faith, and it is not that.
In Orthodox understanding, the chalice is not a means of building unity but the sign and seal of a unity that already exists. To come to it is to say, publicly, that one holds the faith of this Church, lives under her discipline, confesses her sacraments and is in communion with her bishop. Asking a guest to say all that by an action, when it is not yet true, would be asking him to say something untrue, and it would be unkind as well as untrue.
The practice is also very old. In the second century Justin Martyr wrote that no one is allowed to share the eucharistic food except one who believes the Church's teaching, has been washed in the bath of regeneration, and lives as Christ commanded (First Apology 66). For centuries the catechumens were dismissed by name before the anaphora began, and the deacon's summons “the doors, the doors” survives in the Liturgy still.
It should also be said that Orthodox Christians do not simply walk up either. Communion follows preparation: a rule of prayers, a fast from the previous evening, and in Russian practice confession beforehand. Someone baptised Orthodox forty years ago who has not confessed in a decade is in the same queue of questions as anybody else. The restriction is not a ranking of persons, and where a person stands before God is a separate matter which the Church declines to pronounce upon.

> it is not for us to define the state of those who are outside the Orthodox Church
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### What you can actually do if you come on Sunday
Nobody is turned away from the building, and there is a great deal more to the Liturgy than the few minutes at the chalice. In practice, a visitor at our parish in Kovan can do all of the following without any awkwardness, and it is worth knowing beforehand so that Sunday is not spent guessing.
If you would like to come forward for a blessing at communion time rather than remain in your place, mention it to the priest before the service, since the custom differs between Orthodox parishes and it is easier to arrange than to improvise.
- Stay for the whole service, stand or sit where you like, and leave when you need to.
- Light a candle before an icon and pray in your own words.
- Come forward at the end of the Liturgy to venerate the cross, as everyone does.
- Take a piece of antidoron, the blessed bread cut from the same loaf as the eucharistic Lamb but not consecrated; in Russian parishes it is commonly offered to all who are present.
- Stay for the meal afterwards, which in Singapore is usually better attended than the sermon deserves.
- Ask the priest for a conversation, in English or in Russian, about anything in this article.

### Where this leaves us
The disagreement described here is genuine, and it would be dishonest to end by suggesting that all Christians mean the same thing by the Lord's table. They do not. What can be said is that the Orthodox position is not a claim to have solved the mystery, and that any Orthodox Christian who uses the chalice as a way of feeling superior has misunderstood what he is receiving.
Fr. Seraphim Rose, who came to Orthodoxy from a Protestant family in California, wrote in print against exactly that temptation among converts, and his warning applies to this subject as much as any other. The door at Kovan stands open on Sunday mornings, and the conversation afterwards costs nothing.

> Even when it is worded in a theologically correct manner, this attitude is spiritually wrong
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, “In Defense of Fr. Dimitri Dudko”, *The Orthodox Word* no. 2 (1980), p. 131, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Common questions

Q: Do Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine literally become the Body and Blood of Christ?
A: Yes. The Orthodox Church teaches that after the eucharistic prayer the gifts are the true Body and Blood of Jesus Christ, not a symbol or a reminder of them. What she does not teach is any account of how the change occurs. The reality is confessed and the mechanism is left undefined, which is why Orthodox writers speak of the holy mysteries rather than of a doctrine of the Eucharist.

Q: What is the epiclesis?
A: The epiclesis is the prayer in which the priest asks God to send down the Holy Spirit upon the people and upon the gifts, and to make the bread the Body of Christ and the cup his Blood. It comes after the words of institution in the Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, and the congregation answers Amen. Orthodox theology gives this petition particular weight, since the change is asked for rather than produced.

Q: Does the Orthodox Church teach transubstantiation?
A: Not in the sense of adopting the scholastic analysis of substance and accidents. The Greek term metousiosis does appear in the Confession of Dositheus, adopted at the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 in reply to Reformed arguments, and it is sometimes rendered as transubstantiation. Later Orthodox theologians have been cautious about that reading, preferring to affirm the change while declining to explain it philosophically.

Q: Why can I not receive communion in an Orthodox church?
A: Because Orthodoxy treats the chalice as the seal of a unity that already exists rather than a means of creating it. Receiving is a public statement that one holds this Church's faith, lives under her discipline and is in communion with her bishop. Asking a guest to say that by an action before it is true would be unkind. It is not a judgement on anyone's faith or standing before God.

Q: What is antidoron, and may a visitor take it?
A: Antidoron is blessed bread cut from the same loaf from which the eucharistic Lamb was taken, but it is not consecrated and is not communion. It is distributed at the end of the Liturgy. In Russian parishes it is commonly offered to everyone present, including visitors, though customs differ from place to place, so it is always reasonable to ask the priest or a parishioner first.

Q: Can a non-Orthodox visitor attend the Divine Liturgy?
A: Yes, and visitors are welcome. You may stand or sit where you like, light a candle, pray in your own words, come forward at the end to venerate the cross, take antidoron and stay for the meal afterwards. If you would like a blessing at communion time rather than to remain in your place, it is best to mention it to the priest before the service begins.

### Sources
- Orthodox Church in America — The Sacraments: Holy Eucharist: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-sacraments/holy-eucharist
- Orthodox Church in America — The Sacraments: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-sacraments/the-sacraments
- OrthodoxInfo — “Monogamous Communion”: A Defense of “Closed” Communion: http://orthodoxinfo.com/general/monogamous-communion-a-defense-of-closed-communion.aspx
- OrthodoxInfo — Proper Confession and Communion: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/communionprep.aspx
- OrthodoxInfo — Where Can One Go in an Orthodox Church?: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/holyspace.aspx
- OrthodoxInfo — Worship and the Sacraments: http://orthodoxinfo.com/general/doctrine3.aspx
