## Why Confess to a Priest?
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/confession-in-the-orthodox-church.html
Summary: Orthodox Christians confess their sins aloud to God in the presence of a priest. The Church teaches that God alone forgives sins; the priest stands as a witness and a physician, not as a judge. Confession is understood as healing rather than sentencing. The practice rests on James 5:16 and on the words of Christ to the apostles in John 20:23.
==============================================================================

### The objection, taken at full strength
For many Christians the idea of telling one's sins to another man is not merely strange but objectionable, and the objection is a serious one. Scripture says there is one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5). It invites the believer to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16). It promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just and will forgive them (1 John 1:9). No priest appears in any of those sentences.
Added to that are memories that cannot be waved away: clergy who used what they were told, systems in which access to God was rationed, and the long Reformation argument about whether forgiveness could be made to depend on an institution. Anyone raised with those memories is right to be careful. A reader who arrives at this page suspicious is not being difficult; he is being responsible, and this article is written for him rather than around him.

### Where Orthodoxy agrees with you
Begin with the agreement, because it is larger than most people expect. The Orthodox Church teaches that sins are forgiven by God and by no one else. No priest forgives by any power of his own, and no Orthodox catechism claims otherwise. The Slavonic service book makes the point at the very start of the rite: before anything is said, the priest tells the penitent that Christ stands here invisibly, receiving the confession, and that he himself is only a witness, bearing testimony before God of everything the penitent says.
Orthodoxy also agrees that a Christian should confess his sins directly to God, constantly, without waiting for anyone. The daily prayers of an Orthodox layman are thick with it. Morning and evening rules include open acknowledgement of sin; the prayers before communion are almost entirely confession; the Jesus Prayer itself ends with the words “a sinner.” Nobody is asked to store sins up for a monthly appointment. Fr. Seraphim Rose, writing to a convert who had grown severe about such things, put the priorities in an order worth remembering.
So the disagreement is narrower than it first appears. It is not about whether God forgives, or whether a Christian may speak to him directly. It concerns one question only: whether the ordinary Christian life also includes speaking the thing aloud, once, in front of someone the Church has appointed to hear it.

> The first and important thing is not 'rightness' at all, but Christian love and harmony.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 5/18 June 1979, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### James 5:16 and John 20:23
Two passages carry most of the weight. The first is from James, and its final clause is the one Orthodox writers underline: “Therefore confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16, RSV). The purpose given is not the settling of accounts. It is healing. The verse sits immediately after instructions about calling the presbyters of the church to pray over the sick and anoint them, which is why the Church has never read it as advice about casual conversation between friends.
The second is from the evening of the resurrection. Christ breathes on the apostles and says: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22-23, RSV). Something is entrusted there to particular men, and the Orthodox Church understands that trust to have been handed on. Whatever the phrase means, it is hard to make it mean nothing.
Alongside these stand the plain descriptions of early practice. People came to John at the Jordan “confessing their sins” (Matthew 3:6). At Ephesus “many also of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices” (Acts 19:18, RSV). Public confession before the community is well attested in the first Christian centuries; the private form used today grew out of it, largely through the monasteries, as a gentler arrangement rather than a stricter one.

### Healing, not sentencing
The image the Orthodox tradition reaches for is medical rather than legal. The church is a hospital, the priest is a physician who has been ill himself, and the sins named are symptoms rather than charges. Nothing is being decided about the penitent's eternal fate in those five minutes. Something is being treated.
This changes the tone of everything. A judge wants an admission; a doctor wants an accurate description. A judge is finished when sentence is passed; a doctor asks you to come back. When a priest gives a penance, which in Greek is an epitimia, it is meant as a prescription rather than a fine: a rule of prayer, an act of charity, a habit to break, occasionally a period of abstaining from communion, and always something aimed at the underlying illness.
Saint Gregory the Theologian, preaching on baptism, counted the baptism of tears among the washings God gives, and the Fathers commonly speak of repentance as a second baptism. That is the register. Confession is not a humiliation to be survived but the ordinary means by which a Christian is washed again, and again, for as long as he needs it, which is for life. Fr. Seraphim Rose was insistent that this inner dimension matters more than any external accuracy.

> Being correct is the external side of Christianity. It's important, but not of first importance.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, talk on simplicity, 1979, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 87 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Then why keep a witness at all?
If God forgives and the priest does not, the question sharpens rather than disappears. Why speak the words to a man? The Orthodox answer is not about authority in the first instance. It is about what sin does to a person and what is needed to undo it.
Sin thrives in privacy. Most of us can maintain an entirely sincere private confession that quietly edits the two or three things we do not intend to give up, and we can maintain it for years without noticing. Saying a thing out loud to another human being breaks the editing. It costs something, and the cost is the point: the shame that has to be walked through is itself part of the healing, and it is spent once rather than carried indefinitely.
There is also the matter of not being alone with it. A person who confesses only inwardly can never be told anything in return. He cannot be asked a question, corrected, or reassured that what he has been torturing himself over for fifteen years is not in fact the unforgivable sin. The Church keeps a witness so that the penitent can hear a human voice say that he is forgiven and may go in peace.
And the witness is appointed rather than chosen at random, precisely so that he is bound. He is answerable to his bishop, trained to say little, and held to an absolute seal. Confessing to a sympathetic friend carries no such protection, and friendships have been ruined by less.

### What actually happens, step by step
The practical shape of it is much plainer than people imagine, and in a Russian parish there is no box, no grille and no anonymity. Confession is normally heard during the Vigil on Saturday evening, before the Liturgy on Sunday morning, or by appointment at another time.
What follows is the usual sequence at our parish in Kovan. It is worth reading once beforehand, because most of the anxiety people bring to a first confession turns out to be anxiety about the choreography rather than about the sins, and the choreography takes about a minute to learn.
A first confession may take longer, and that is expected; say so when you come, and ask for a time when the priest is not also trying to begin a service. Confession here is heard in Russian and in English.
- You stand with the priest at an analogion, a sloped stand, usually at the side of the church. On it lie a cross and the Gospel book. Both of you face them; the priest is beside you rather than opposite you.
- Others waiting keep their distance, and the conversation is quiet. If the church is full, ask for a time when it is not.
- The priest may read a short prayer, including the reminder that Christ stands here invisibly and that the priest is only a witness.
- You say your sins simply, in your own words. There is no formula to learn and no required vocabulary. Name the thing and stop; circumstances, explanations and other people's faults are not needed.
- The priest may ask a question or give a short word of counsel. Sometimes he gives a penance, understood as medicine rather than punishment.
- He places his stole over your head and reads the prayer of absolution, then you venerate the cross and the Gospel. Most confessions take a few minutes.

### Preparing, and how often
Preparation does not require a technique. An evening of quiet is enough: the prayers before confession printed in any Orthodox prayer book, a slow reading of the commandments or the Beatitudes, and honesty about where the last weeks actually went. Some people find it helps to write a short list and tear it up afterwards; others find that writing turns into composition, which is a different activity altogether.
Two cautions are worth passing on. Do not confess other people's sins, which is the commonest way a confession goes wrong. And do not deliver a self-analysis; the priest does not need your theory of why you are like this, only what you did and what you would like healed.
Frequency varies between Orthodox Churches and even between parishes. In Russian practice confession customarily precedes communion, so a regular communicant confesses often. Greek practice is generally less frequent. Neither is a rule the individual sets alone; it is worth asking the priest what pattern suits your situation, and a sensible priest will not impose the same pattern on a monk, a nurse on rotating shifts and a mother of three.

### If you have never done this
Three things are usually worth saying to someone considering a first confession. Nothing you bring will be new to the priest; parish clergy have heard the whole human range and are chiefly interested in whether you want to be free of it. The seal is absolute, with no exceptions for family, police, bishops or dinner conversation. And you may stop at any point, ask a question, or say that you have changed your mind and would rather just talk.
Orthodoxy holds this practice as part of the ordinary Christian life, and does not offer it as proof that anyone else's prayers have gone unheard. Where a person stands before God is God's business. What the Church offers is a witness, a prayer and a door out of the room you have been arguing with yourself in. Fr. Seraphim Rose ended a letter to a convert with a wish that serves as well as anything for a closing line here.
If you would like to talk about any of this, without committing yourself to anything at all, the priest at Kovan can be reached through the parish website, and a conversation over tea after the Liturgy is a perfectly normal way to begin.

> May God keep your heart soft and filled with love for Christ and your fellow man
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 25 May 1979, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Common questions

Q: Does the priest forgive sins in Orthodox confession?
A: No. The Orthodox Church teaches that God alone forgives sins. The service book has the priest tell the penitent at the outset that Christ stands there invisibly receiving the confession and that the priest is only a witness. The prayer read at the end asks God to forgive, and the priest acts by the authority entrusted to the apostles in John 20:23 rather than by any power of his own.

Q: Can I not just confess to God alone?
A: You can, and Orthodox Christians do so daily; the morning, evening and pre-communion prayers are full of direct confession to God. The Church adds a witness because sin grows in privacy, because saying a thing aloud breaks the quiet editing we all do, and because a person confessing only inwardly can never be answered, questioned or told in a human voice that he is forgiven.

Q: What actually happens at an Orthodox confession?
A: In a Russian parish there is no box and no screen. You stand with the priest at a sloped stand holding a cross and the Gospel book, usually at the side of the church, both of you facing them. You name your sins in your own words. The priest may ask a question or give counsel, then places his stole over your head and reads the prayer of absolution. It usually takes a few minutes.

Q: How often should an Orthodox Christian go to confession?
A: Practice varies. In Russian tradition confession customarily precedes communion, so a regular communicant confesses frequently; Greek practice is generally less often. There is no single rule that applies to everyone, and the pattern is best settled with the parish priest, who will not ask the same of a monk, of a nurse working night shifts and of a mother of small children.

Q: Is Orthodox confession confidential?
A: The seal of confession is absolute. A priest may not repeat what he has heard to anyone, at any time, for any reason, including to family, to civil authorities or to his bishop. This is one of the reasons the Church appoints a witness rather than leaving people to unburden themselves to friends, since a friendship carries no such protection and has often been damaged by what it was told.

Q: What if I do not know what to say?
A: Say that, first; it is a common opening and the priest will help. Preparation can be as simple as a quiet evening with the prayers before confession from any Orthodox prayer book and a slow reading of the commandments or the Beatitudes. Name what you did rather than explaining why, leave other people's faults out of it, and stop when you have finished. Nothing needs to be eloquent.

### Sources
- Orthodox Church in America — The Sacraments: Penance: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-sacraments/penance
- OrthodoxInfo — Confession: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/pr_confession.aspx
- OrthodoxInfo — A Guide to Confession: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/guide-to-confession.aspx
- OrthodoxInfo — Preparation for Confession: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/selfexam.aspx
- OrthodoxInfo — Proper Confession and Communion: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/communionprep.aspx

- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works, ch. 87, “Simplicity”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_87.aspx

## Chrismation: The Seal of the Gift of the Holy Spirit
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/chrismation-the-seal-of-the-spirit.html
Summary: Chrismation is the Orthodox sacrament in which a newly baptised Christian, infant or adult, is anointed with holy chrism while the priest says, “The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.” It is given in the same service as baptism, never years later. The chrism is consecrated by the patriarch and sent to every parish. Most converts already baptised in another Christian confession are received by chrismation.
==============================================================================

### The minute after the water
Ask a visitor what happens at an Orthodox baptism and you will hear about the water: the three immersions, the white garment, the small cross hung round the neck. What follows a minute later is described far less often, and it is the subject of this article. While the newly baptised is still wet, the priest opens a small vessel, touches it, and anoints the forehead, the eyes, the nostrils, the mouth, the ears, the breast, the hands and the feet, saying each time the same short sentence: “The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.”
That anointing is chrismation. In the Orthodox Church it is a sacrament in its own right, and it corresponds to what many Western Christians know as confirmation. Historically the two are the same act. What separated them was not a quarrel about doctrine so much as a practical problem about bishops, which the two halves of Christendom solved in different ways. The difference is real, and this article will not pretend otherwise; but it is worth understanding before it is argued about.

### Why it follows baptism without a pause
Baptism, in Orthodox understanding, is a death and a rising: the old life is buried in the water and a new one comes up out of it. Chrismation is what the Church does next, and it is understood as the personal Pentecost of this particular Christian — the Holy Spirit given not to the Church in general but to this named person, sealed on this body, at this font. Because the two belong together as burial and breath belong together, Orthodoxy has never wanted a gap between them.
Infants receive the anointing for the same reason. A baby baptised in an Orthodox church is chrismated in the same service and then brought to receive Holy Communion, usually at the next Divine Liturgy. The Church does not treat the Holy Spirit as waiting until the child can account for Him. Nor does it treat the child as a probationary member who will be admitted properly later. Whatever else may be said for or against that practice, it is at least consistent: the whole of Christian initiation is given at once, to the whole person, before anyone has earned it.
There is, in consequence, no later rite. An Orthodox teenager is not confirmed at fourteen. He has been sealed since infancy, and what waits for him is not a second sacrament but confession, communion and the ordinary work of a Christian life.

### What actually happens at the service
For a parish reader, the shape is worth knowing in advance. After the immersions and the clothing in the white garment, the priest reads a prayer asking God to grant the newly baptised the seal of the Holy Spirit, and then makes the anointings described above. The candidate, godparents and priest then walk three times round the font carrying candles while the choir sings the words of Galatians 3:27 — “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” — in place of the usual hymn before the epistle.
Saint Paul’s passage on baptism as burial and rising is read (Romans 6:3–11), followed by the Gospel. Afterwards come two small rites that surprise people who have not seen them: the washing away of the chrism with a sponge, and the tonsure, in which a few hairs are cut in the form of a cross as a first free offering from someone who has nothing else to give. In many parishes these follow immediately; in others they are kept for a later day.
The whole thing takes perhaps an hour, and nothing in it is repeated afterwards. An adult convert received by chrismation will recognise most of the second half of this service, used without the font: the confession of faith, the prayer, the anointings, the epistle and the Gospel. Families usually take the baptismal candle home and light it on the anniversary. It is worth saying, for anyone imagining something austere, that Orthodox baptisms are crowded and cheerful, and that nobody minds a crying infant.

### The chrism itself, and how it is consecrated
Holy chrism is not ordinary oil. It is olive oil compounded with wine and a long list of aromatic substances, and in the Russian Church it is prepared during Holy Week: the cooking begins on Great Monday and continues through Tuesday and Wednesday, with the Gospel read continuously over the vessels while they are stirred. On Great Thursday the Patriarch consecrates it during the Liturgy, and it is then distributed to the dioceses of the Moscow Patriarchate, from which it reaches parishes as far away as Singapore.
This matters more than it may appear. The priest who anoints a convert in Kovan did not make the chrism in his hand; it came to him from his bishop, and to his bishop from the Patriarch. The bishop is therefore present in the act even when he is not in the room. For the same reason, the right to consecrate chrism has long been treated among the Orthodox Churches as one of the marks of a self-governing, autocephalous Church — which is why the annual consecration is reported as news.

### Sealing and anointing in the Scriptures
The language is apostolic before it is liturgical. Writing to Corinth, Saint Paul says that God “hath anointed us”, and adds: “Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 1:21–22, KJV). Saint John writes to his readers, “But ye have an unction from the Holy One” (1 John 2:20, KJV), and returns to “the anointing which ye have received of him” a few verses later. Anointing, sealing and the gift of the Spirit form one cluster of ideas in the apostolic writings, not three separate ones.
Acts records the act as well as the words. When Samaria received the word of God, those who had been baptised had not yet received the Holy Spirit; Peter and John came down, prayed, “Then laid they their hands on them, and they received the Holy Ghost” (Acts 8:17, KJV). Something followed baptism, and it was given by the apostles.
Honesty requires a distinction here. That the apostles laid hands on the newly baptised is in the text. That they used consecrated oil is not; the anointing with chrism is how the Church, as it outgrew the reach of any one man’s hands, continued to do what the apostles did. Orthodoxy holds that the continuity is real, and does not claim that the ritual detail is written in Acts.

### Why East and West came to differ
In both halves of the ancient Church the bishop was the normal minister of this sealing. The difficulty arrived with success. Once there were more congregations than a bishop could visit, something had to give: either the bishop’s hand or the unity of the rite.
Eastern practice kept the rite together and let the presbyter perform the anointing, using chrism the bishop had consecrated. Western practice kept the minister and let the second half wait for the bishop’s visit. In time the waiting hardened into a principle, and confirmation came to be associated with an age at which a Christian could answer for the faith himself. Roman canon law today keeps both threads: the bishop is the ordinary minister, and confirmation is to be conferred “at about the age of discretion unless the conference of bishops has determined another age” (Code of Canon Law, cc. 882, 891).
Two things are worth adding, because they narrow the gap without closing it. An adult baptised in the Roman rite is normally confirmed in the same service, as the ancient pattern requires; and the Eastern Catholic churches chrismate infants exactly as the Orthodox do. Many Protestant communities also keep a rite called confirmation, though it is generally understood differently again — as the moment a Christian raised in the faith professes it publicly as his own, which is a serious and valuable thing and a different question from the one addressed here.
Where Orthodoxy differs, it differs plainly: it has never treated the anointing as the moment a person makes up his mind, but as the moment the gift is given. That is why it can be given to a child who has made up his mind about nothing at all.

### How converts are usually received
Most adults who come to Orthodoxy from another Christian confession are not baptised again. If a person was baptised with water in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, the Orthodox Church ordinarily receives him by chrismation, after a period as a catechumen, with confession of the Orthodox faith and a first confession of sins.
The practice is ancient. Canon 95 of the Council in Trullo (692), whose canons the Orthodox Church receives together with the Sixth Ecumenical Council, sets out how various groups are to be received. Some are received after presenting certificates and renouncing their errors, and then, in the canon’s own words, “we anoint them with the holy chrism on their foreheads, eyes, nostrils, mouth and ears; and as we seal them we say — The seal of the gift of the Holy Ghost.” Others the same canon directs to be received by baptism. The Church has judged case by case from the beginning.
It should be said candidly that there is no single rule applied identically in every Orthodox jurisdiction. Reception is the diocesan bishop’s decision, taken through the parish priest, and a decision to baptise rather than chrismate is a judgment about what is certain, not a verdict on anyone’s previous Christian life. If you are considering this step, the answer to almost every question you have is the same: ask the priest, early, and let him take it to the bishop.
Catechumens often arrive anxious about how much they will have to renounce, or about how much they must know before they are allowed in. The preparation is not an examination, and it is not primarily about acquiring information. Writing in 1979 to someone preparing for reception, Fr. Seraphim Rose put its purpose in a single sentence, and it is still the best summary available.

> You are coming to Orthodoxy to receive Christ, and this you should never forget.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 3 May 1979, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### What the seal is, and what it is not
Chrismation is not a graduation, not a reward and not a certificate of achievement. The seal is placed on people who have done nothing to deserve it — which is exactly why an infant a few weeks old can receive it. Nor is it a charm. Orthodox writers have warned for centuries against treating holy things as though they worked mechanically on someone who is not looking in their direction.
Understood properly, it is a beginning rather than an end. The Spirit is given whole; the learning to live in Him takes the rest of a life, and is done in the ordinary way, through prayer, the Liturgy, confession, and the unremarkable duties of charity. Most of that work looks like nothing at all from the outside.
If you have read this far from another Christian tradition, nothing in it is an accusation. Fr. Seraphim Rose — an American convert whose own mother was a Protestant and whose father had become one — put the matter in a way this parish is glad to borrow, crediting the formulation to Fr. Dimitry Dudko.

> We should view the non-Orthodox as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been revealed, as people who are potentially Orthodox
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### If you want to see it
Baptisms and receptions at the Parish of the Dormition of the Mother of God in Kovan are not private ceremonies. Anyone may stand and watch, and most people find that an hour of watching answers more questions than an evening of reading. If you are enquiring seriously, speak to one of the parish clergy; there is no obligation attached to asking, and no timetable you are expected to keep.
The door that chrismation opens is not a door into a club. It is the door into a life of repentance, which is slower and plainer than most converts expect, and into communion, which is the point of the whole thing.

### Common questions

Q: Is chrismation the same as confirmation?
A: They come from the same apostolic act and do the same thing: they seal the baptised with the gift of the Holy Spirit. The differences are in practice. In the Orthodox Church a presbyter chrismates immediately after baptism, using chrism consecrated by the patriarch, and infants receive it. In the Roman Catholic Church the bishop is the ordinary minister and confirmation is normally conferred at about the age of discretion, though adults baptised at Easter are confirmed at once.

Q: Why are Orthodox infants chrismated instead of waiting until they understand?
A: Because Orthodoxy regards the Holy Spirit as given rather than earned. Baptism, chrismation and Holy Communion form a single act of initiation, and the Church gives the whole of it to the whole person at once. A child understands nothing of his own birth either, yet is born. Understanding follows and is meant to grow for the rest of a life; the gift is not held back until it arrives.

Q: Do converts to Orthodoxy have to be baptised again?
A: Usually not. Someone baptised with water in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit is ordinarily received by chrismation, after preparation as a catechumen and a confession of the Orthodox faith. Practice is not uniform across all Orthodox jurisdictions, and the decision belongs to the diocesan bishop through the parish priest. A decision to baptise is a judgment about certainty, not a verdict on a person’s previous Christian life.

Q: What is holy chrism made of and who makes it?
A: It is olive oil compounded with wine and many aromatic substances. In the Russian Church it is cooked during the first days of Holy Week with the Gospel read continuously over the vessels, and consecrated by the Patriarch on Great Thursday, then distributed to every diocese. A parish priest never consecrates it himself. The right to consecrate chrism is treated among the Orthodox Churches as a mark of an autocephalous Church.

Q: What words does the priest say during chrismation?
A: “The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit,” repeated at each anointing — forehead, eyes, nostrils, mouth, ears, breast, hands and feet. The formula is very old: it appears in Canon 95 of the Council in Trullo in 692 as the words used when receiving certain Christians into the Church, which is the same rite still used for converts today.

Q: Can chrismation be repeated?
A: No. Like baptism, it is given once. Someone who was chrismated as an infant and later drifted away is not re-sealed on returning; he is received back through confession. The only historic exception concerned those who had formally renounced the faith under persecution and returned, and even there the Church’s concern was to restore rather than to repeat. In ordinary parish life the answer is simply once, and for life.

### Sources
- The Orthodox Faith — Chrismation (Orthodox Church in America): https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-sacraments/chrismation
- Council in Trullo (692), Canon 95: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3814.htm
- Russian, Romanian and Bulgarian Churches consecrate chrism on Holy Thursday (OrthoChristian): https://orthochristian.com/169092.html
- Local Churches begin the rite for making holy chrism (OrthoChristian): https://orthochristian.com/145765.html
- Code of Canon Law, Book IV, cann. 879–958 (Holy See): https://www.vatican.va/archive/cod-iuris-canonici/eng/documents/cic_lib4-cann879-958_en.html
- Hieromonk Damascene, ‘Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works’, ch. 84, ‘Pastoral Guidance’: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Counsels of Fr. Seraphim (Rose) to young converts (OrthoChristian): https://orthochristian.com/141493.html
- Parish of the Dormition of the Mother of God, Singapore: https://orthodox.sg/

## Why Orthodox Churches Are Full of Icons
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/why-orthodox-churches-have-icons.html
Summary: Orthodox churches are full of icons because Orthodox Christians believe the invisible God became visible in Jesus Christ, and what has been seen can be depicted. The Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea, 787) permitted images and drew a careful line: icons receive honour and veneration, while worship in the strict sense belongs to God alone. Kissing an icon is a greeting, like kissing a photograph, and the honour passes to the person represented.
==============================================================================

### What a visitor sees first
The first impression is of faces. An Orthodox church has almost no blank wall: a screen of painted panels stands between the congregation and the altar, more panels rest on stands in the body of the church, and the ceiling is usually occupied. Candles burn in front of them in brass sand-boxes. People come in, cross themselves, bow, and kiss the boards. Nobody explains this to newcomers, because for those who grew up with it there is nothing to explain.
Visitors from Reformed, evangelical and non-denominational backgrounds often arrive with a specific verse in mind, and they are right to. The second commandment is not an obscure objection dredged up to be awkward. It is in the Decalogue, it is emphatic, and a Christian who takes Scripture seriously is bound to ask about it. This article tries to give that question the answer it deserves rather than waving it away.

### The commandment, read whole
The text is plain. “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them” (Exodus 20:4–5, KJV). Read on its own, that appears to settle the matter, and no honest account of the Orthodox position can begin by pretending the verse is unclear.
What complicates it is the rest of the same Law. A few chapters later God commands Moses to make two cherubim of gold for the mercy seat, facing one another with outstretched wings (Exodus 25:18–20). Solomon’s temple was carved throughout with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers (1 Kings 6:29). In the wilderness Moses was told to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole, so that anyone bitten might look at it and live (Numbers 21:8–9).
Nor does that end the argument in the other direction. Centuries later Hezekiah broke that same bronze serpent in pieces, because Israel had begun burning incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). Scripture therefore both commands the making of images and records the destruction of one. The commandment is not a prohibition on carving; it is a prohibition on giving to a made thing what belongs to the Maker. The real question is what an image is for, and what is being done in front of it.

### What the Incarnation changed
The Orthodox answer turns on a claim about Christ, not about art. “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14, KJV). Saint Paul calls Christ “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15, KJV). Saint John begins his first letter with a deliberately physical list: that which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled.
Saint John of Damascus, writing in the eighth century while the controversy was raging, put the argument in two steps. First he concedes the objection entirely: “who can make an imitation of the invisible, incorporeal, uncircumscribed, formless God? Therefore to give form to the Deity is the height of folly and impiety.” That, he says, is exactly why images of God were uncommon under the Law. Then comes the turn: after God “became in truth man for our salvation” and lived on earth and was seen, what had been seen could be recorded (*An Exposition of the Orthodox Faith*, Book IV, ch. 16).
So the Orthodox position is not that the second commandment has been repealed. It is that God Himself has supplied the likeness which no human being could have invented. A Christian who paints Christ is not imagining the divine nature; he is depicting a man who was born in Bethlehem and crucified under Pontius Pilate. This is why the icon question has always been treated in the East as a question about whether the Incarnation was real.

### The century the Church argued about it
The dispute was not a quiet one. From about the year 726 the Emperor Leo III began removing images from public places, and for most of the next century imperial policy ran against them. Monks and bishops who defended icons were deprived, exiled and in some cases killed. In 754 a large council meeting at Hieria condemned the making of images altogether, and its supporters believed they were purifying the Church of idolatry.
Those who defended icons argued back on Christological grounds. If Christ cannot be depicted, they said, then either His humanity was not full or His divinity was being confused with it. The argument ran for decades and cost people their lives on both sides.
In 787 the Empress Irene and the Patriarch Tarasius convened a council at Nicaea, which the Orthodox Church counts as the Seventh Ecumenical Council. Iconoclasm returned under Leo V from 815, and was ended for good in 843, when the Empress Theodora and the Patriarch Methodius restored the images. That restoration is still commemorated on the first Sunday of Great Lent as the Triumph of Orthodoxy, when parishes carry their icons in procession.

### What the Seventh Council actually defined
The council did not simply say that icons were permitted. It made a distinction, in writing, and the distinction is the heart of the matter. Images of Christ, of the Mother of God, of the angels and of the saints are to be set up in churches and houses, and “to these should be given due salutation and honourable reverence” — the Greek is *timetike proskynesis* — “not indeed that true worship of faith (*latreia*) which pertains alone to the divine nature.”
Its reason is a principle Saint Basil had stated four centuries earlier: “For the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents, and he who reveres the image reveres in it the subject represented.” An icon is not a terminus. Whatever is offered to it travels on.
Nicaea also answered the scriptural objection directly, by reading the commandment closely. It observed that Scripture says veneration is to be given to God but does not add the word “only”, since the Greek word covers everything from a bow between friends to the adoration of God; whereas when it comes to service, the text does add the restriction. “You shall serve him only,” the council quotes, “for to God alone do we render latria.” Readers who want to check this can read the council’s own words in English translation; the link is below.

### What a person is doing when kissing an icon
Strip away the theology for a moment and watch what actually happens. A woman comes in from the street, puts down her shopping, crosses herself, bows, and kisses the corner of a painted board. She is doing what she would do to her mother at an airport. The council made this point itself, noting that the Greek verb means both to salute and to kiss, and citing David falling on his face before Jonathan and kissing him (1 Samuel 20:41, cited in the council’s text by its Greek numbering).
What is not happening is equally worth stating. Nobody believes the wood can hear. The board is wood, the paint is pigment bound in egg, and if the icon is destroyed the saint is not harmed. An icon is a meeting place, not a residence. The nearest ordinary comparison is the photograph a widow keeps by the bed and touches when she passes, though the comparison is incomplete, because the Church claims something more than sentiment: that the honour genuinely reaches the person, and that the saints are alive and praying.
In practice the gestures are simple, and a visitor is free to do none of them. Orthodox Christians cross themselves twice, kiss the icon — by custom on the hands, the feet or the edge of the garment rather than on the face — and cross themselves again. Candles are lit as a small offering and a prayer left burning. No one is watching to see whether a newcomer joins in.

### Where the objection still has force
It would be dishonest to leave the impression that the danger the commandment names has never touched Orthodox life. It has. People do sometimes treat a particular icon as a charm, or an oil lamp as insurance, and the Church’s own ascetic writers have said so bluntly for centuries. Fr. Seraphim Rose, himself a convert, made the point about religious externals in general in a way that applies exactly here.

> Anything outward … can become a counterfeit.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 63 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### The test the Church applies to itself
The safeguard is the one the council named, and it is testable. Listen to what is said in an Orthodox church and notice who is being addressed. The prayers before an icon of Christ are addressed to Christ. The prayers before an icon of a saint ask that saint to pray to Christ, in the same grammar a person uses when asking a friend to pray for him. No Orthodox prayer is addressed to a painting, and no Orthodox service treats a painting as a source of anything.
That is a claim a visitor can check rather than take on trust. Stand at the back of a Vigil, follow the text, and see whether what is said matches what is described here. If the words and the gestures ever come apart in a particular person, the fault is in the person, and the Church has never pretended otherwise.

### Standing in the doorway
If you come from a tradition that has kept its walls bare out of reverence for the second commandment, nothing here is an accusation against you. That reverence is not a small thing, and the Orthodox Church spent a century fighting over the same worry. Where Orthodoxy has come out differently is on one point: it holds that when God took flesh He made Himself depictable, and the defenders of the icons held that refusing the image would, followed far enough, put the reality of that flesh in doubt. That is the Orthodox reasoning, set out to be weighed rather than pressed.
There is one more thing to say, and it is about us rather than about anyone reading. Arguments about icons are often lost before they begin, because what a stranger meets first is not the theology but the people standing under the paintings. Fr. Seraphim Rose, writing to an enquirer in 1980, put the responsibility where a parish ought to be willing to have it put, and this parish would rather quote him against itself than at anyone else.

> perhaps it is our fault for not living and teaching the Orthodox Faith in a way they can understand
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Common questions

Q: Do Orthodox Christians worship icons?
A: No. The Seventh Ecumenical Council in 787 defined the difference in writing: icons receive salutation and honourable reverence, while *latreia*, worship in the strict sense, belongs to God alone. The council based this on the principle that the honour given to an image passes to the person represented. In practice, Orthodox prayers are addressed to Christ, or ask a saint to pray to Christ; none is addressed to a painting.

Q: How do Orthodox Christians answer the second commandment?
A: By taking it seriously and reading it alongside the rest of the Law. The same God who forbade graven images commanded the golden cherubim of the mercy seat, the carved cherubim of Solomon’s temple and the bronze serpent. The prohibition is against giving a made thing what belongs to the Maker. Orthodoxy adds that in Christ the invisible God became visible, so that a likeness now exists which no one invented.

Q: What is an Orthodox Christian doing when kissing an icon?
A: Greeting someone. The Greek word used by the Seventh Council means both to salute and to kiss, and the council cited David kissing Jonathan. The gesture is the one people use with family: a bow, a kiss on the hands or feet or the edge of the robe, and the sign of the cross. Nobody supposes the wood hears; the honour is understood to travel to the person the icon shows.

Q: What was the iconoclast controversy?
A: A dispute in the Byzantine Empire, beginning about 726 under Emperor Leo III, over whether Christian images were idolatry. Icons were removed and their defenders persecuted; a council at Hieria condemned images in 754. The Seventh Ecumenical Council at Nicaea permitted them in 787. Iconoclasm returned in 815 and ended in 843 under the Empress Theodora, an event still kept as the Triumph of Orthodoxy on the first Sunday of Great Lent.

Q: Are icons necessary, or just traditional decoration?
A: Orthodoxy treats them as neither optional decoration nor objects of devotion in their own right. They are treated as a consequence of the Incarnation and as teaching: the council noted that not everyone can read, and that images put the events of the Gospel where people can see them. A church without icons would not be invalid, but it would be making a statement the Orthodox Church has deliberately declined to make.

Q: Can a visitor attend without venerating icons?
A: Yes, and many do. Orthodox services are public, no one is required to cross themselves, kiss anything or light a candle, and standing quietly at the back is entirely normal. Communion is reserved to Orthodox Christians who have prepared, but everything else in the service is open to anyone who wishes to be there. Questions afterwards are welcome, and the parish clergy would rather answer them than have them go unasked.

### Sources
- The Second Council of Nicaea (787): decree and definition: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3819.htm
- St John of Damascus, An Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book IV, ch. 16, ‘Concerning Images’: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/33044.htm
- The Icon FAQ (Orthodox Christian Information Center): http://orthodoxinfo.com/general/icon_faq.aspx
- Icons — The Orthodox Faith (Orthodox Church in America): https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-church-building/icons
- ‘The Triumph of Orthodoxy and Holy Icons’ (OrthoChristian): https://orthochristian.com/69054.html
- Hieromonk Damascene, ‘Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works’, ch. 63, ‘Super-Correctness’: http://orthodoxinfo.com/ecumenism/fsr_63.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, ‘Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works’, ch. 84, ‘Pastoral Guidance’: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Parish of the Dormition of the Mother of God, Singapore: https://orthodox.sg/
