## Why Orthodox Christians Still Fast
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/orthodox-fasting-why-christians-fast.html
Summary: Orthodox Christians fast on most Wednesdays and Fridays and during four seasons — Great Lent, the Apostles’ Fast, the Dormition Fast and the Nativity Fast — chiefly by setting aside meat, dairy, eggs, fish, wine and oil in varying degrees. Fasting is not a diet and not a way of earning God’s favour. It is training for prayer, undertaken with the whole person, body included, and always relaxed for health and need.
==============================================================================

### “When ye fast”, not “if”
Christ assumes it. In the Sermon on the Mount He does not argue for fasting or against it; He takes it for granted and corrects the manner: “Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast” (Matthew 6:16, KJV). The instruction that follows is not to stop, but to hide it — “anoint thine head, and wash thy face” — so that the fast is seen by the Father and by nobody else.
Asked why His disciples did not fast while John’s did, He answered that the guests at a wedding do not mourn while the bridegroom is with them, “but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast” (Matthew 9:15, KJV). He fasted forty days Himself before His public ministry. The Church at Antioch was fasting and praying when it set apart Barnabas and Saul, and fasted and prayed again before sending them (Acts 13:2–3).
None of this settles any particular rule about food, and the apostolic writings do not give one. What they show is that fasting was assumed rather than invented later, and that the Church went on doing it after the Resurrection as a matter of course. The Orthodox Church has simply never stopped, and has spent the centuries since working out how the practice fits the ordinary year.

### The rhythm of the week and the year
Two days a week carry the memory of Holy Week into every ordinary week: Wednesday, on which Christ was betrayed, and Friday, on which He was crucified. Outside a few fast-free weeks these are kept throughout the year, which means that for an Orthodox household the question of what is for dinner is settled twice a week by the calendar rather than by appetite.
Beyond that there are four fasting seasons, and one of the clearest statements of the rule in English was compiled by Fr. Seraphim Rose for the St Herman Calendar. He lists them as Great Lent, the Nativity Fast, the Apostles’ Fast and the Dormition Fast, together with two single days that are fasts even though they are feasts: the Exaltation of the Cross and the Beheading of the Forerunner, kept as such because of what they commemorate.
This parish, like the rest of the Russian Orthodox Church, keeps the older Julian reckoning, so the dates above fall thirteen days later on the ordinary civil calendar: the Dormition Fast runs from 14 to 27 August, and the Nativity Fast from 28 November to 6 January. Great Lent and the Apostles’ Fast move with Pascha and have no fixed dates at all.
Rather than work this out from first principles, use the parish’s own fasting page at https://orthodox.sg/fasting.html. It gives the rule for today, the degrees of fasting, the seasons, and — because this is Singapore — practical help with reading a hawker centre menu, where an innocent-looking vegetable dish may have been cooked with pork stock or shrimp paste. The page is a guide rather than a ruling; for a particular question, ask the parish clergy.
- Great Lent and Holy Week — seven weeks before Pascha, the longest and strictest of the four.
- The Apostles’ Fast — beginning on the Monday after the Sunday of All Saints and ending on the eve of Saints Peter and Paul; its length varies each year with the date of Pascha.
- The Dormition Fast — a fortnight, 1 to 14 August on the Church calendar, ending with the feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God.
- The Nativity Fast — forty days, from 15 November on the Church calendar until the Nativity of Christ, with the last days stricter than the rest.

### What is actually given up
The strictest days set aside meat, poultry, eggs, dairy, fish, wine and oil. Lighter days restore oil and wine; lighter still, fish as well. The pattern is not arbitrary: the rule lives in the Typicon, chiefly in its thirty-second and thirty-third chapters, and it is relaxed for feasts and vigils, so that the more a day is celebrated, the more consolation is allowed at table.
Two clarifications save a great deal of anxiety. Practice on some foods, shellfish among them, differs between Orthodox traditions and even between parishes, so it is a question for the clergy rather than one to settle from a book. And the standard is a standard, not a verdict. Writing about the rule he had compiled, Fr. Seraphim Rose said plainly that it is not meant to be a straitjacket, nor a source of pharisaical pride for anyone who keeps its letter; it is the measure against which each person judges his own practice and towards which he strives according to his strength and circumstances.
That last phrase — strength and circumstances — is doing real work, and it belongs to the rule itself rather than being a modern concession bolted on to soften it. The Typicon was written for monasteries and has always been applied to families in the world with judgment. A household with young children, shift work and a long commute is not keeping a lesser Christianity by fasting less than a monk; it is keeping the same rule in different circumstances.

### Not a diet, and not a way of earning anything
This has to be said flatly, because it is the commonest misunderstanding and because saying it gently has not worked. Fasting does not earn God’s favour. It purchases nothing, offsets nothing and puts God under no obligation whatever. “But meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse” (1 Corinthians 8:8, KJV). Saint Paul is blunt, and the Church reads him at face value.
Neither is it a health regime. If someone loses weight during Great Lent that is incidental, and a fast kept for the figure has quietly become something else. The prophets were sharper still about fasts kept while the poor went hungry: “Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free” (Isaiah 58:6, KJV).
What fasting is for is smaller and harder. It is training. A person who cannot say no to cheese on a Wednesday has little practice at saying no to anger on a Thursday. The food is the exercise weight, not the point; and the kingdom of God, as Saint Paul says in the same breath, “is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost” (Romans 14:17, KJV).

### Why the body is involved at all
Orthodoxy does not divide a person into a soul that matters and a body that is along for the ride. The body prays: it stands through long services, bows, makes the sign of the cross, prostrates itself in Lent, and is buried in hope of rising. It is baptised, anointed and communed. A Christianity in which the body has nothing to do would be a different religion.
Fasting is the point at which this becomes concrete and slightly uncomfortable. It is also communal rather than private. Across Singapore and across the world the same households are eating the same plain food on the same days, which is why parish life thickens during a fast: there are more services, more confessions, and a great many shared meals of rice and vegetables.
And fasting never travels alone. In the Sermon on the Mount it stands with prayer and almsgiving, and the three are meant to be done together. Fasting without prayer is only a diet with a religious label; fasting without almsgiving is thrift. Fr. Seraphim Rose returned constantly to the ordinary Christian duties — giving alms, visiting the sick, helping those in need — as the daily test of whether any of the rest is real.

### If you are starting
Begin smaller than you think you should. A beginner who keeps Wednesday and Friday faithfully for a year has done more than one who attempts the full Lenten rule in March and abandons it in the second week. Consistency in something modest builds what heroics in something large destroys.
Speak to a priest before you set your rule, and set it in advance rather than deciding at each meal, which turns every meal into a negotiation. Do not announce what you are doing; the instruction to wash your face is practical advice as much as a warning. And when you fail — everyone fails — the response is to begin again at the next meal rather than to write off the season.

> The first and important thing is not ‘rightness’ at all, but Christian love and harmony.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 5/18 June 1979, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Health, age and the blessing of a priest
The fasting rule has always been applied with dispensations, and asking for one is not a failure. Children, the elderly, the sick, the pregnant and nursing, those on medication, diabetics, people doing heavy physical work, travellers and soldiers have all been treated differently, and a parish priest can adjust the rule for any of them. Anyone with a history of disordered eating should say so, and should expect the fast to be modified or set aside.
Hospitality outranks strictness. If you are a guest and meat is set before you, the older Christian instinct is to eat it and say thank you rather than wound a host or make a scene about your own discipline — “eat such things as are set before you” (Luke 10:8, KJV). In a city where families are often mixed and meals are often shared, this comes up constantly, and the answer is usually to ask your priest rather than to improvise a rule of your own.
None of this is a loophole, and a relaxed rule is not a second-class one. It is how the discipline has always been meant to work: a standard held up honestly and without embarrassment, then applied to particular people by someone who knows their circumstances. The alternative — a single rule enforced identically on the frail and the strong — would be easier to administer and much worse for souls.

### The danger nearest to hand
The risk of fasting is not that someone will eat a biscuit. It is pride, and Christ named it in a parable about a man whose fasting was real: “God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are … I fast twice in the week” (Luke 18:11–12, KJV). That man’s fast was genuine. It made him worse. A fast that produces a sharper eye for other people’s eating has gone wrong at the root, however exactly it is kept.
Converts are especially exposed, because a new rule is a visible achievement and the temptation to audit oneself against it is strong. Fr. Seraphim Rose, an American convert who spent his last years writing against precisely this tendency among Western converts, returned to it again and again in his letters. To one young man who had written describing how far he had come, he replied bluntly, and the reply is worth keeping where it can be seen.

> You are too young in Orthodoxy to be evaluating your spiritual growth—that is actually a sign of your pride.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 22 June 1976, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### An open door
Many Christians of other confessions fast, and many do not; Saint Paul told the Romans that the one who eats should not despise the one who abstains, and the one who abstains should not judge the one who eats, “for God hath received him” (Romans 14:3, KJV). That verse is addressed to Orthodox readers of this page at least as much as to anyone else.
If you are curious rather than committed, you are welcome to keep a fast day with this parish and see what it is like from the inside. Come to a Lenten service, eat afterwards with whoever is there, and ask your questions over the food. Most of what is worth knowing about fasting is learned that way rather than from an article.

### Common questions

Q: What can Orthodox Christians eat during a fast?
A: On strict days, no meat, poultry, eggs, dairy, fish, wine or oil — in practice vegetables, grains, pulses, fruit and, by long custom, shellfish. Many days are lighter, allowing oil and wine, or fish as well, especially at weekends and on feasts. The degrees are set out in the Typicon and published in the parish calendar; the parish fasting page at orthodox.sg/fasting.html gives the rule for each day.

Q: Does fasting earn forgiveness or God’s favour?
A: No, and Orthodoxy says so as plainly as it can. Nothing is purchased by fasting and no obligation is placed on God. Saint Paul wrote that food does not commend us to God either way (1 Corinthians 8:8). Fasting is training: a way of learning to refuse something harmless so that refusing something harmful becomes possible. Kept as a transaction, or as a diet, it has quietly turned into something other than a fast.

Q: What are the four Orthodox fasting seasons?
A: Great Lent with Holy Week before Pascha; the Apostles’ Fast, which begins after the Sunday of All Saints and ends on the eve of Saints Peter and Paul; the Dormition Fast, a fortnight in August; and the Nativity Fast, forty days before Christmas. Great Lent and the Apostles’ Fast move with the date of Pascha. In this parish the fixed dates follow the Julian calendar, thirteen days behind the civil one.

Q: What if I cannot fast for health reasons?
A: Then you should not, and you are not doing anything wrong. The rule has always been adjusted for children, the elderly, the ill, the pregnant and nursing, those on medication and those doing heavy work. Speak to a parish priest, who can set a rule that fits your situation. Anyone with a history of disordered eating should say so; in such cases the fast is normally modified or set aside altogether.

Q: How should a beginner start fasting?
A: Modestly and consistently. Keeping Wednesday and Friday for a year is worth more than attempting the full Lenten rule and abandoning it after ten days. Agree your rule with a priest in advance so that meals are not renegotiated one by one, and say nothing about it to anyone. When you fail, and you will, resume at the next meal rather than writing off the whole season.

Q: Why do Orthodox Christians fast on Wednesdays and Fridays?
A: Wednesday recalls the betrayal of Christ and Friday His crucifixion, so the two days carry Holy Week through the ordinary year. They are kept outside a small number of fast-free weeks, such as the week after Pascha and the week after Pentecost. For most Orthodox households this weekly rhythm, rather than the long seasons, is where fasting is actually learned and sustained.

### Sources
- Fasting calendar — Parish of the Dormition of the Mother of God, Singapore: https://orthodox.sg/fasting.html
- Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose), ‘The Rule of Fasting in the Orthodox Church’: https://orthochristian.com/77551.html
- Fr. Seraphim Rose index (OrthoChristian): https://orthochristian.com/141494.html
- Counsels of Fr. Seraphim (Rose) to young converts (OrthoChristian): https://orthochristian.com/141493.html
- Hieromonk Damascene, ‘Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works’, ch. 84, ‘Pastoral Guidance’: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, ‘Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works’, ch. 63, ‘Super-Correctness’: http://orthodoxinfo.com/ecumenism/fsr_63.aspx
- ‘Fasting for Non-Monastics’, Fr. Sergei Sveshnikov (OrthoChristian): https://orthochristian.com/69880.html
- Parish of the Dormition of the Mother of God, Singapore: https://orthodox.sg/


==============================================================================
## Why Orthodox Christians Honour the Mother of God
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/why-orthodox-honour-the-theotokos.html
Summary: Orthodox Christians honour Mary as Theotokos, the one who gave birth to God in the flesh. The Council of Ephesus defined that title in 431 to protect the truth that Jesus Christ is one person, God and man. The honour given her is veneration, not worship; worship belongs to God alone. Orthodoxy asks her prayers and does not receive the Roman Catholic dogma of the Immaculate Conception defined in 1854.
==============================================================================

### The question a visitor asks first
A visitor arrives at the cathedral in Kovan on a Saturday evening, part-way through the vigil. The choir is singing something that repeats, and the repeated line is addressed to a woman. People are queueing to kiss her icon. If that visitor grew up in an evangelical church, a question forms before the service ends, and it is not a frivolous one: has something been placed beside Christ?
The question deserves an answer rather than a reassurance. Most people who raise it are guarding something they are right to guard, namely that Jesus Christ alone saves and that no creature may stand where he stands. Orthodox Christians say the same thing, in those words, every week. So the reply is not that the visitor has misheard, but that the words mean something particular, and the Church chose them for a reason.
Singapore makes the question ordinary rather than academic. Families here are often mixed: a Methodist mother, a Catholic uncle, a daughter who has started attending an Orthodox parish, all at the same table on Christmas Day. What is said about the mother of Christ in that room matters more than what is said in a seminar, and it deserves the same care.

### The title was defined to protect Christ
Theotokos is Greek, usually rendered God-bearer, or the one who gave birth to God. It came before the Church as a live dispute in the fifth century. Nestorius, Archbishop of Constantinople, preferred Christotokos, Christ-bearer, because he thought the older title suggested that the divinity of the Son had a beginning in Mary's womb. He was trying to protect something true.
Cyril of Alexandria answered that a mother does not give birth to a nature; she gives birth to a person. The person born in Bethlehem is the eternal Son of God, who at that moment had taken flesh from her. To withhold the title is therefore to imply two sons, one eternal and one born, which is precisely what the Church could not accept. The Council of Ephesus in 431 settled the matter in Cyril's favour.
So the word is a statement about Christ before it is a statement about Mary. It says that the child in the manger is God. Much of the Reformation kept the title for that reason; the Lutheran Formula of Concord of 1577 confesses her as the mother of God in exactly this christological sense. When an Orthodox choir sings Theotokos, the subject of the sentence is her Son.

### What Luke 1:48 asks of its readers
Scripture puts a prediction in Mary's own mouth. In the Magnificat she says, “for behold, henceforth all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48, RSV). A few verses earlier Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, greets her: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:42, RSV). The greeting and the prophecy sit inside the same chapter, spoken before the child is born.
Orthodox hymnography reads that verse as an instruction rather than a curiosity. Generations were to call her blessed, and the Church's liturgical books are, among other things, the record of generations doing so. Whether that is the right way to read the line is a fair question. It is a question about how to obey a verse, though, not about whether the verse is there.
There is also the scene at the Cross, where Christ gives his mother to the disciple and the disciple to his mother (John 19:26-27). Christians have long read that as more than a domestic arrangement made by a dying son. The woman given to the beloved disciple is given, in him, to the Church.

### Veneration and worship are two different acts
This distinction is not a modern apology invented under pressure; it was made in council. At the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 the Church defined that holy images are to be given “due salutation and honourable reverence, not indeed that true worship of faith which pertains alone to the divine nature”. Two Greek words carry the weight: proskynesis, the honour paid to a person, and latreia, worship, which belongs to God and to nobody else.
A practical test is easier to check than a definition. In an Orthodox church the Eucharist is never offered to a saint, and there is no liturgy addressed to the Mother of God. The Divine Liturgy is offered to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit; she is commemorated within it as the first and best member of the Church. Nothing whatever is sacrificed to her.
Kissing an icon belongs to the same order of act as kissing a photograph of a mother who has died, which nobody mistakes for worship. Orthodox Christians bow before icons, kiss them, and light candles in front of them. What they do not do is offer them what is due to God.
English makes the confusion worse than Greek does. Until quite recently the word worship carried a broader sense in English: the Book of Common Prayer of 1662 has the bridegroom say to his bride, with my body I thee worship, and English magistrates are still addressed as Your Worship. Greek keeps two separate words for two separate things, and the councils used them precisely.

### What the Orthodox Church holds about her
Set out plainly, Orthodoxy holds that Mary is Theotokos; that she is Ever-Virgin, a title used of her in Christian antiquity and taken up by the Fifth Ecumenical Council in 553; that she is all-holy, Panagia, and committed no personal sin; that at the end of her life she fell asleep and was taken to her Son, which the Church keeps on 15 August as the Dormition; and that she prays now for the Church on earth.
Equally worth stating is what the list does not contain. She is a creature. She was saved by her Son and said so: “my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour” (Luke 1:47, KJV). Orthodoxy has never taught that she is a source of grace independent of Christ, or an addition to the Trinity, or a rival court of appeal. Her whole significance lies in whose flesh she gave.
Her role in the Gospel of John shows the pattern Orthodoxy claims she still follows. At the wedding in Cana she notices that the wine has run out, brings the need to her Son, and then turns to the servants with her last recorded words in Scripture: “Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it” (John 2:5, KJV). She points away from herself. That is what Orthodox Christians believe she is doing now.

### What Orthodoxy does not hold: the Immaculate Conception
Many Protestant readers assume that Orthodox and Roman Catholic teaching about Mary are the same thing under two labels. They are not, and this is the clearest place where they part. On 8 December 1854, in the bull Ineffabilis Deus, Pope Pius IX defined that Mary was preserved free from every stain of original sin from the first instant of her conception. The Orthodox Church does not receive that dogma.
One reason is that the question it answers is framed by a Western account of the Fall. Where the Latin tradition came to speak of inherited guilt, Orthodoxy speaks of inherited mortality and corruption: a wounded nature rather than a charge on a record. If what descends from Adam is death rather than guilt, the difficulty the 1854 definition was built to remove does not arise in the same shape, and no exemption is required to keep her pure.
Archbishop John Maximovitch, the hierarch who blessed the founding of Fr. Seraphim Rose's brotherhood, put a second objection. He argued that the dogma belittles the Mother of God rather than exalting her, because it removes her struggle; a holiness that could never have been otherwise is not a victory won. Orthodox tradition holds that she was sanctified and kept from personal sin, and that this was a life lived in freedom, not a condition installed in advance.
A third reason concerns authority. Orthodoxy settles doctrine in council, received by the whole Church over time, and a definition issued by a single see in 1854 is not such a settlement. Orthodox hymns do call her most pure and spotless, and the Church keeps the feast of the Conception of St Anne on 9 December; neither carries the meaning defined in 1854. The difference is real and worth knowing before anyone argues about it.

### The line that troubles visitors most
One refrain unsettles newcomers more than any other, and it is better faced than smoothed over. Through the canon at matins the choir sings, “Most Holy Theotokos, save us.” Heard cold, in English, that sounds like the very thing the objection fears.
What the phrase means, and what Orthodox writers consistently say it means, is: by your prayers, obtain salvation for us from your Son. The verb carries that range in Scripture. Paul writes that he becomes all things to all men “that I might by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22, KJV), and tells Timothy that by watching his doctrine he shall “save thyself, and them that hear thee” (1 Timothy 4:16, KJV). Nobody reads those verses as a rival to Christ.
Honesty requires one more sentence. Compressed liturgical shorthand is hard on a stranger, and a stranger cannot be blamed for hearing it wrongly the first time. A parish that sings that line owes its visitors the explanation without waiting to be asked twice.
Fr. Seraphim Rose made a related point about arguments in general, and he made it against his own side rather than against anyone else's. A parish can be word-perfect about every hymn in its books and still fail the person standing at the back of the church, wondering whether it is safe to ask a question.

> Being correct is the external side of Christianity. It's important, but not of first importance.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, talk on simplicity (1979), in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 87 (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### An invitation rather than an argument
Fr. Seraphim Rose, the American hieromonk whom many enquirers read on their way towards Orthodoxy, was raised Protestant; his mother was a Protestant and his father a former Roman Catholic who had become one. When converts wrote to him armed with sharp arguments for their new faith, he told them to live at peace with their families, and he put part of the blame for Protestant misunderstanding where Orthodox Christians least like to find it.
He also thought that doctrinal accuracy, real as its value is, was not the first thing to be said about a Christian life. A parish that can defend every hymn and cannot love a visitor has answered the smaller question.
None of this asks anyone to agree by the end of the page. It asks only that the words be heard as the Church means them: a title that guards the Incarnation, an honour that Scripture itself predicted, and worship kept for God alone. The vigil is on Saturday evening, and questions afterwards are welcome.

> perhaps it is our fault for not living and teaching the Orthodox Faith in a way they can understand
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### Common questions

Q: Do Orthodox Christians worship the Virgin Mary?
A: No. Orthodoxy distinguishes veneration, the honour given to a person, from worship, which belongs to God alone. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 defined that difference in so many words. The practical test is what happens in church: the Eucharist is offered to the Holy Trinity and never to a saint, and there is no liturgy addressed to the Mother of God. She is honoured and asked to pray.

Q: What does the word Theotokos actually mean?
A: It is Greek for God-bearer, or the one who gave birth to God. The Council of Ephesus affirmed it in 431 against Nestorius, who preferred Christ-bearer. The argument was about Christ, not about Mary: a mother gives birth to a person rather than to a nature, and the person born of her is the eternal Son of God who had taken flesh. The title guards the unity of Christ.

Q: Does the Orthodox Church accept the Immaculate Conception?
A: No. The dogma defined by Pope Pius IX in 1854 holds that Mary was preserved from every stain of original sin from the first instant of her conception. Orthodoxy does not receive it, partly because it does not share the Western account of inherited guilt that the definition presupposes, partly because it was defined by one see rather than received in council. Orthodoxy still confesses her as all-holy and without personal sin.

Q: Why do Orthodox hymns say “Most Holy Theotokos, save us”?
A: The line asks her to obtain salvation for us by her prayers to her Son. Scripture uses the verb in a similar stretched sense: Paul hopes to save some, and tells Timothy that he will save himself and his hearers. The phrase is liturgical shorthand, and it is fair to say that a visitor hearing it for the first time cannot be expected to catch that on their own.

Q: Is honouring the Mother of God found in the Bible?
A: Orthodox Christians point to Luke 1, where Elizabeth calls her blessed among women and Mary herself says that all generations will call her blessed. They also point to the Cross, where Christ entrusts her to the beloved disciple. Whether those passages require the honour the Orthodox Church gives her is a genuine question, but the practice grows out of the text rather than around it.

### Sources
- Council of Ephesus (A.D. 431), acts and canons: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3810.htm
- Second Council of Nicaea (A.D. 787), definition and canons: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3819.htm
- Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (8 December 1854): https://www.papalencyclicals.net/pius09/p9ineff.htm
- St John Maximovitch, An Orthodox Christian Understanding of the Immaculate Conception: https://orthochristian.com/73378.html
- Orthodox Church in America: Sinlessness of Mary: https://www.oca.org/questions/saints/sinlessness-of-mary
- Orthodox Church in America: Original Sin: https://www.oca.org/questions/teaching/original-sin
- Fr. John Breck, “Most Holy Theotokos, Save Us”: https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/most-holy-theotokos-save-us
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84: Pastoral Guidance: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx


==============================================================================
## Asking the Saints to Pray for Us
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/asking-the-saints-to-pray-for-us.html
Summary: Orthodox Christians ask the saints in heaven to pray for them, in the same way they ask fellow Christians on earth. They do not treat saints as additional mediators of salvation: Christ alone gave himself a ransom. The same chapter that names one mediator, 1 Timothy 2, also commands Christians to intercede for one another. Orthodoxy holds that death does not end that mutual prayer.
==============================================================================

### The objection, stated at full strength
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5, KJV). Put at its strongest, the objection runs like this. The heart of the Gospel is that access to the Father was opened by one person at one cost, and that nobody else is needed at the door. To direct a request to a Christian who died in the fourth century looks like reinstalling a chain of intermediaries that the Cross removed.
That is not a weak argument, and in the mouths of most people who make it, it is not a hostile one either. It is the strongest objection brought against this Orthodox practice, and it is usually raised by Christians who are guarding the sufficiency of Christ because they love him. An Orthodox reply that waves it away has not replied at all.
So the honest method is to leave the verse exactly where it is and read the sentences around it, then look at what the rest of the New Testament says about Christians praying for one another, and then say plainly what Orthodox Christians think they are doing.

> In the Protestant world, we have many examples of people with soft hearts, who, for the love of Christ, are kind to other people.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, talk on simplicity (1979), in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 87 (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### What Paul is doing in that paragraph
The paragraph containing the verse opens with a command to intercede. “I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men” (1 Timothy 2:1, KJV). Four verses before he writes that there is one mediator, Paul instructs Christians to stand between other people and God in prayer. If intercession by a creature were a rivalry with Christ, this is the first place it would have to be excluded.
What makes the mediation of Christ unique is stated in the very next line: he “gave himself a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6, KJV). That is an act of a different order from asking. No saint died for anyone's sins, no Orthodox prayer suggests that one did, and the Church's hymns say the opposite several times in every service.
Paul also asks for prayer constantly, and not as a formality. He begs the Romans to strive together with him in their prayers, tells the Thessalonians twice to pray for him, and asks the Ephesians to pray that he would be given words to speak. James states the principle: “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (James 5:16, KJV). Scripture treats the prayers of other Christians as genuinely effective, and singles out righteous ones.

### Asking for prayer is not the same act as praying to
English blurs a distinction that matters here. To pray, in older English, simply meant to ask, which is why characters in Shakespeare say I pray thee to people who are plainly not divine. Orthodox prayers addressed to saints are requests in that older sense, and their grammar shows it: pray for us, intercede for us, entreat Christ our God on our behalf.
What is never asked of a saint is what only God can give. No Orthodox Christian asks a saint for the forgiveness of sins, for the gift of the Holy Spirit, or for the Body and Blood of Christ. Every service ends by referring everything to the Holy Trinity, and every blessing is given in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
In practice the difference is easy to see. A parishioner in Kovan asks the woman next to her at coffee hour to pray about a hospital appointment on Tuesday, and that evening asks St Panteleimon for the same thing. She regards those as two instances of one act, differing only in that one of the two friends is further along than she is.

### Can the departed hear anything?
Underneath the theological objection lies a practical one, and it is often the real question: the dead cannot hear you, so whom exactly are you addressing? Orthodoxy does not answer that the saints are omniscient, because they are not. The answer is that they are alive in Christ, and that whatever they know of us, they know in him rather than independently of him.
Scripture is not silent about this. Christ says of the patriarchs that God “is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him” (Luke 20:38, KJV). He also says that there is “joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth” (Luke 15:10, KJV), which means that particular events in particular lives on earth are known in heaven.
Revelation goes further. Under the altar are the souls of those slain for the word of God, and they cry out with a loud voice, asking God how long it will be until he acts (Revelation 6:9-10). They are conscious, they are aware of unfinished business on earth, and they are asking God to do something about it. Whatever else that passage is, it is intercession offered by people who have died.

### What Revelation shows happening in heaven
Two scenes in Revelation are quoted in almost every Orthodox discussion of this subject, and it is worth reading them slowly. When the Lamb takes the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fall down before him, “having every one of them harps, and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints” (Revelation 5:8, KJV). The prayers of Christians on earth are in the hands of others, in heaven, being offered.
The second scene is plainer still. An angel stands at the altar with a golden censer, and there is given to him much incense, “that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints upon the golden altar which was before the throne”; and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, “ascended up before God out of the angel's hand” (Revelation 8:3-4, KJV).
Whatever one concludes from those verses, they do not describe heaven as a sealed room. They describe creatures in the presence of God handling the prayers of the Church. This is also why an Orthodox service is full of incense, and why Vespers opens with the verse “Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense” (Psalm 141:2, KJV). The censer is a statement about how prayer travels.

### What Christians did before anyone argued about it
The practice is older than the arguments for it, which is usually a sign that it grew rather than being invented. In the shrine beneath the church of San Sebastiano in Rome, visitors scratched requests into the plaster asking Peter and Paul to pray for named individuals; the graffiti are generally dated to the middle of the third century. These are not treatises. They are the handwriting of ordinary Christians.
Manchester holds the oldest known prayer addressed to the Mother of God, the Sub tuum praesidium, on a Greek papyrus. Its date is disputed, with scholars placing it anywhere from the third to the fourth century, and an honest account should say so rather than claim the earliest figure. It asks for her protection and her prayers, and it is still sung in Orthodox churches.
By 787 the practice was old enough that the Second Council of Nicaea described it as received tradition, speaking of honouring the Theotokos, the angels, the apostles, prophets and martyrs, and of seeking their intercessions. For a Protestant reader a council of that date does not settle the question, and it is not offered here as though it did. As historical evidence, though, it shows what Christians were already doing and had long been doing.

### The honest worry: the line really can blur
Here is the part that Orthodox writers should not hurry past. Popular piety does drift, in every century and every country. A saint can be treated as a specialist consulted for one kind of trouble, prayer can slide into bargaining, and the Mother of God can be approached as though she were gentler than her Son, which distorts the Gospel at its centre. Anyone who has spent time in a large parish has seen some of this.
The Church has known it for a long time and has acted. The Synod of Laodicea in the fourth century forbade Christians to forsake the Church of God and invoke angels in separate assemblies, calling that covert idolatry, and the same error appears to be the one Paul warns against in Colossians 2:18. Commentators note that the same council takes the honouring of martyrs for granted elsewhere, so the target is a rival cult rather than intercession as such.
An Orthodox priest draws a conclusion from that history, and it is not a defensive one. Where a parishioner's practice has become superstition, the answer is to correct it, not to explain it away. The distinction between veneration and worship exists precisely because the line is crossable, and nobody draws a line where nobody can stray.

### What is actually being asked
Strip the distortions away and what is left is modest. A Christian believes that the Church is one body, that death did not dismember it, and that asking a member of that body for prayer is not an insult to its Head. Every request made to a saint is a request that they ask Christ, which is why the answer to every such prayer comes from him.
Nobody supposes that asking a friend after church to pray for a sick child sets the friend up as a competitor to Christ. Orthodoxy extends the same ordinary courtesy across the grave, on the ground that the friend who was buried last year is not less alive than the one sitting in the next chair. That is either true or it is not; it is not idolatry either way.
There is also a quieter point. A Christian who asks nobody to pray for him is not closer to Christ for it, only more solitary, and the apostolic writings do not commend solitude of that kind. The letters of Paul are full of people holding one another up. Orthodoxy simply holds that the list of people available to hold you up is longer than the parish register.

### Where this leaves a reader who disagrees
Nothing here asks a Protestant visitor to begin asking the saints for prayer. It asks only that the practice be weighed for what it is rather than for what it resembles from a distance: a request for prayer, addressed to Christians who are alive in Christ, answered by Christ alone.
Fr. Seraphim Rose, the American hieromonk whose books bring many enquirers to this subject, was raised in a Protestant family and wrote at length about how Orthodox Christians should speak to the people they came from. He held the traditional Orthodox teaching that the Church is one and that the sacraments are given in her, and he refused all the same to pronounce on where any individual stands before God.
The parish in Kovan serves the vigil on Saturday evening and the Liturgy on Sunday morning, and the litanies in both include prayers for the living, prayers for the departed, and requests for the prayers of the saints. A visitor is welcome to stand through all of it and agree with only part.

> There is no reason why we cannot call them Christians and be on good terms with them
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### Common questions

Q: Doesn't 1 Timothy 2:5 rule out asking the saints to pray?
A: Orthodox Christians read that verse as excluding any rival mediator of redemption, which is what the next verse describes: Christ gave himself a ransom for all. The same paragraph opens by commanding Christians to make intercessions for all men, so intercession by creatures is not what the verse excludes. Asking a saint for prayer is understood as the same act as asking a friend, not as a second ransom.

Q: Is asking a saint to pray the same as praying to God?
A: No, and Orthodox prayers show the difference in their grammar. Prayers to saints ask them to pray, intercede or entreat Christ. Nothing is asked of a saint that only God gives: not forgiveness of sins, not the Holy Spirit, not the Eucharist. In older English to pray simply meant to ask, which is why the same verb covers both and why the confusion is easy to fall into.

Q: How could a saint possibly hear prayers from all over the world?
A: Orthodoxy does not claim that the saints are omniscient. It holds that they are alive in Christ and that whatever they know of us they know in him. Scripture describes heaven as aware of events on earth: there is joy among the angels over one sinner who repents, and the martyrs under the altar in Revelation cry out about what is still happening below.

Q: When did Christians start asking the saints for prayer?
A: Earlier than the arguments about it. Graffiti in the shrine beneath San Sebastiano in Rome, usually dated to the mid-third century, ask Peter and Paul to pray for named people. The Sub tuum praesidium, a prayer to the Mother of God, survives on a papyrus dated by scholars somewhere between the third and fourth centuries. By 787 a council could describe the practice as long-received.

Q: What about people who take this too far?
A: That happens, and the Orthodox Church says so. Piety can drift into treating saints as specialists, into bargaining, or into imagining the Mother of God as kinder than her Son. The Synod of Laodicea condemned a rival cult of angels in the fourth century. When a parishioner's practice has become superstition, the priest's job is to correct it rather than to defend it.

### Sources
- Second Council of Nicaea (A.D. 787), definition and canons: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3819.htm
- Synod of Laodicea (4th century), canons with commentary: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3806.htm
- Fr. Lawrence Farley, Praying to the Saints: https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/praying-to-the-saints
- Why Do Orthodox Christians Pray to the Saints?: https://orthochristian.com/160499.html
- The Orthodox Faith: Intercessory Prayer: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/spirituality/prayer-fasting-and-almsgiving/intercessory-prayer
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84: Pastoral Guidance: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 87: Simplicity: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_87.aspx
- Counsels of Fr. Seraphim (Rose) to Young Converts: https://orthochristian.com/141493.html

## Why Orthodox Christians Venerate Relics
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/why-orthodox-venerate-relics.html
Summary: Orthodox Christians venerate relics, the bodily remains of saints, because they hold that the Incarnation ended any division between matter and holiness. Scripture records a corpse revived by Elisha's bones and cloths from Paul's body healing the sick. Relics are placed in every altar, and the Liturgy is served on a cloth containing one. Veneration is honour, not worship, which belongs to God alone.
==============================================================================

### There are bones in the altar
Start with the fact rather than the argument. In an Orthodox church, somewhere in or beneath the altar table, there are fragments of the bones of a martyr. On the table itself lies a cloth called the antimension, signed by the bishop, with a relic sewn into it; without that cloth a priest may not serve the Liturgy at all. Every Sunday, the bread and wine are set down on a piece of a dead Christian.
Stated that baldly, it sounds macabre, and there is no point pretending otherwise to a visitor who grew up in a church with clear windows and a wooden communion table. It is one of the practices that divides Orthodox instinct from Protestant instinct most sharply, and it will not be made palatable by softening the description.
What follows is the reasoning, laid out so that a reader can weigh it. It has three parts: what Scripture reports, what the Incarnation is taken to imply about matter, and what the Church has actually done since the second century. The abuses come in too, because leaving them out would be dishonest.

### The objection is old, and it was raised at the time
The worry is not a Reformation invention. In the account of the death of Polycarp of Smyrna, written by his own congregation in the middle of the second century, the authorities are urged not to hand over his body, in case the Christians abandon the crucified one and begin to worship this one instead. The suspicion arrived with the practice, on day one.
In its modern form the objection is stronger and better aimed. It runs roughly so: Scripture nowhere commands the veneration of remains; the Law of Moses treated contact with a corpse as defiling; God deliberately hid the grave of Moses so that Israel would have no shrine; and the history of relics in Christendom is a history of fraud, money and credulity. Behind all of it stands the simplest point of all, which is that a bone is a bone.
None of that is unreasonable, and an Orthodox reply that treats the objection as mere squeamishness has replied to nothing. The response offered here accepts the historical charges, which are true and in places worse than commonly supposed, and disputes only the conclusion usually drawn from them. Fraud in the handling of a thing is an argument about the handlers.

### Two passages Christians have always noticed
The first is in 2 Kings. A burial is interrupted by raiders, and the mourners throw the body into the nearest grave, which happens to be the prophet Elisha's. “And when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet” (2 Kings 13:21, KJV). The narrator reports it and moves on, with no commentary and no warning attached.
Acts supplies the second. “And God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul: so that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them” (Acts 19:11-12, KJV). Earlier in the same book the sick are carried into the street so that Peter's shadow might fall on them (Acts 5:15), and in the Gospels a woman is healed by touching the hem of Christ's garment.
These passages do not command anything, and Orthodox Christians should not claim that they do. What they do is describe a world in which holiness is not sealed inside a person's soul but reaches what they touch and what remains of them. Orthodoxy takes that description seriously instead of treating it as a set of oddities.

### Why Orthodoxy will not treat matter as inert
The deeper reason is the Incarnation. Christianity does not teach that God rescued souls out of a material world; it teaches that God took flesh, was carried in a womb, ate fish, was nailed to wood and rose bodily. After that, the idea that matter is spiritually neutral becomes very hard to hold, and Orthodoxy has never tried to hold it.
That same conviction runs through everything else Orthodox Christians do. Water is blessed and people are immersed in it. Oil is blessed and the sick are anointed with it. Bread and wine are offered and received as the Body and Blood of Christ. Paul tells the Corinthians that their bodies are “the temple of the Holy Ghost” (1 Corinthians 6:19, KJV), which is said of the body, not of the mind.
Relics follow from that, rather than standing on their own. If a body was a temple of the Holy Spirit during a saint's life, and if that body will be raised, then it is not simply rubbish when the soul departs. It is a Christian awaiting the resurrection. Honouring it is of a piece with everything else in the room.

### What the Christians of Smyrna did
The earliest clear account is the one already mentioned. After Polycarp was killed, around the middle of the second century, his congregation gathered his bones, describing them as more precious than exquisite jewels and more purified than gold, and laid them in a fitting place. They then planned to meet there each year, on the anniversary of his death, with joy.
In the same document the congregation draws the distinction on which the whole practice depends, and draws it without being prompted. Christ, as the Son of God, they adore; the martyrs they love as disciples and followers of the Lord. Two different words for two different acts, written down by people who had watched their bishop die a few weeks earlier.
That text matters for the present argument because it is early, it is not defensive theology, and it shows the practice and its safeguard arriving together. Whatever grew up later, this is what the thing looked like at the start.

### The altar, and why the relic is under it
The placing of relics in the altar is not decoration but an argument in furniture. John writes: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Revelation 6:9, KJV). Orthodox and other ancient churches built their altars over the graves of martyrs, and where there was no grave they brought a relic to the table.
Eventually the practice was made a rule. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 ordered that relics be placed, with the accustomed prayers, in churches that had been consecrated without them, and directed that a bishop who consecrated a church without relics be deposed. Behind the sharpness of the canon is a simple conviction: the Church is built on people who died for Christ, and the building should say so.
An antimension carries the same logic down to the parish. It is a cloth bearing an icon of the burial of Christ, containing a relic, signed by the diocesan bishop and given to a particular community. The priest opens it before the Liturgy and folds it away afterwards. A parish serving on that cloth is saying, each week, that it is not a private religious society but part of one Church with a bishop and a memory.

### The abuses were real, and admitting it costs nothing
By the late Middle Ages in the West, relics had become an industry. Pieces of the True Cross multiplied beyond any possibility, bodies were divided and sold, and pilgrimage money shaped what a church claimed to possess. In 1543 John Calvin published a treatise cataloguing the duplications with a cold accuracy that is still uncomfortable reading, and much of what he listed was indefensible.
The Christian East has no clean record here either. Fraud follows money wherever it goes, and an Orthodox writer who presents the abuses as a purely Western problem is not telling the truth. It is worth saying plainly that the Orthodox Church has no interest in defending a forgery and no doctrine that requires any particular relic to be genuine.
What the abuses establish is that the practice can be corrupted, which was never in doubt. They do not establish that the practice is corrupt in itself, any more than simony shows that ordination is wrong. Anything valuable can be sold by someone; the question of whether it was valuable in the first place has to be settled separately.

> As for prejudices—these belong to people, not the Church.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### What veneration looks like on an ordinary day
The practice itself is undramatic. A reliquary is set out on a stand. People come forward in a queue, make the sign of the Cross, bow, kiss the case, and stand for a moment. Some ask the saint to pray for a sick relative. Then they go back to their places, and the service continues towards the Eucharist, which is offered to God alone.
No sacrifice is made to a relic and no prayer is addressed to the bone. The hymns of the day are addressed to Christ, with requests for the prayers of the saint whose memory is kept. If a visitor watched the whole service with a text in hand, the grammar would be consistent from beginning to end.
Something else is worth noticing in a city like Singapore, where many parishioners are far from the graves of their own families. Standing in front of the relics of a Christian who died in Asia Minor in the third century is a way of saying that the family is larger than the one that can be visited at Choa Chu Kang.

### What is being claimed, and what is not
The claim is modest in shape, even if it is strange in practice. Orthodoxy holds that God works through created things because he has always worked through created things, that the bodies of the saints are not discarded matter, and that honouring them honours the Christ who lived in them. It does not hold that relics are magical, that they operate apart from faith, or that any individual relic must be believed genuine.
Fr. Seraphim Rose, an American convert who was raised Protestant and later lived as a hieromonk in the forests of northern California, thought that arguments were rarely what moved people towards the Church. What moved them, he said, was seeing something in Christians that they recognised as worth having, and he put the burden of that squarely on the Orthodox.
That seems the right note to end on. Nobody is asked to agree with this page. Anyone is welcome to come to the cathedral in Kovan on a feast day, watch what is done, and ask the priest afterwards why a church keeps bones on its altar. The answer given will be roughly the one above, at more length and with fewer footnotes.

> If we have the true Christianity, there should be something in our midst that someone who sincerely loves the truth will see and want.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, lecture “Orthodoxy in the USA”, *The Orthodox Word* no. 94 (1980), quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 86

### Common questions

Q: Where does the Bible support the veneration of relics?
A: Scripture does not command it, and Orthodox Christians should not claim that it does. What Scripture reports is a man revived by contact with Elisha's bones, cloths carried from Paul's body healing the sick, Peter's shadow falling on the ill, and a woman healed by touching the hem of Christ's garment. Orthodoxy takes those reports as describing how holiness actually behaves rather than as curiosities.

Q: What is the antimension?
A: It is a cloth laid on the altar table, bearing an icon of the burial of Christ and containing a relic, signed by the diocesan bishop and issued to a particular parish. The Liturgy is celebrated on it, and a priest may not serve without one. It ties every parish altar to a martyr and to a bishop, which is precisely the point of it.

Q: Isn't venerating bones just superstition?
A: It can become superstition, and Orthodox priests correct it when it does. The practice as the Church teaches it is honour paid to the body of a Christian in whom the Holy Spirit dwelt and which will be raised. Nothing is sacrificed to a relic and no prayer is addressed to it. The distinction between veneration and worship was drawn in the second century and has been maintained since.

Q: What about fake relics and the medieval relic trade?
A: Those abuses were real. Calvin's 1543 treatise catalogued duplicated relics with accuracy, and the Christian East has had frauds of its own. No Orthodox teaching requires any particular relic to be authentic, and the Church has nothing to gain from defending a forgery. The abuse of a practice shows that it can be corrupted, not that it was wrong to begin with.

Q: Why are relics placed under the altar?
A: Early Christians celebrated the Eucharist over the graves of martyrs, and Revelation 6:9 describes the souls of the slain as being under the altar. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 required relics to be placed in churches consecrated without them. The arrangement says that the Church rests on those who died for Christ rather than on the people currently occupying the building.

### Sources
- The Martyrdom of Polycarp (c. A.D. 155-160): https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0102.htm
- Second Council of Nicaea (A.D. 787), canon 7: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3819.htm
- The Orthodox Faith: the Altar Table: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-church-building/altar-table
- Metropolitan Onuphry: we pray before the relics of saints because they have the power of life: https://orthochristian.com/96102.html
- On the mysteries and miraculous power of Orthodox holy objects: https://orthochristian.com/99397.html
- John Calvin, A Treatise on Relics (1543): https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/treatise_relics
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 86: Orthodoxy of the Heart: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84: Pastoral Guidance: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx

## The Communion of Saints, Explained
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/the-communion-of-saints-explained.html
Summary: The communion of saints means that the Church is one body on both sides of death. Orthodox Christians hold that those who have died in Christ remain members of the same Church, that they pray for the living, and that the living pray for them. Hebrews 12 describes Christians as already surrounded by a cloud of witnesses. In practice this shapes Orthodox worship, the calendar, and the way Orthodox Christians grieve.
==============================================================================

### The room is fuller than it looks
Walk into an Orthodox church on a weekday morning and you may find eight people, a reader, and a priest. Look at the walls and the count changes. The icons are not illustrations of absent people; they are arranged the way a congregation is arranged, facing in, and the building is designed to make a visitor feel outnumbered.
That is the doctrine in architectural form. Orthodox Christians believe that the Church has members who have died and that those members did not resign. The small congregation at a Wednesday Liturgy is the visible fraction of something much larger, and the service assumes the rest are present rather than remembered.
This article sets out what that belief is, where it comes from, and what changes when a community actually lives by it. Of the practices Protestant visitors find strange, this one is the least contested in principle and the most far-reaching in effect.

### Where the phrase itself comes from
Honesty first: the phrase communion of saints is not Orthodox in origin. It belongs to the Apostles' Creed, a Western creed which the Orthodox Church does not use in its services. What Orthodox Christians confess at every Liturgy is the Creed of Nicaea and Constantinople, finished in 381, which says instead: one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church.
The Latin phrase, sanctorum communionem, is also famously ambiguous, and commentators have long pointed out that it can mean either the communion of holy persons or communion in holy things. Both senses turn out to matter, because in Orthodox practice the fellowship of the saints and the sharing of the Eucharist are not two topics but one.
It helps to remember what the apostolic writings mean by saints. Paul addresses ordinary, quarrelling congregations as saints: those at Rome are called to be saints, those at Corinth are called saints, and so are the Philippians. The word marks people set apart in baptism, not an elite. On that usage, the communion of saints includes the reader who overslept and the visitor at the back.

### Hebrews 12, and the tense of the verbs
The text Orthodox Christians reach for first is Hebrews. After the long roll of the faithful in chapter 11, the writer turns to his readers: “Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight” (Hebrews 12:1, KJV). The Greek word for witnesses is the one that gives us martyrs, and it carries both senses at once, those who testified and those who watch.
A few verses later the same chapter becomes startling. “But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn... and to the spirits of just men made perfect” (Hebrews 12:22-24, KJV). The tense is not future. The readers are told they have already arrived.
Orthodox worship takes that sentence at face value and builds accordingly. If Christians assembling on earth have come to the heavenly Jerusalem, to angels and to the spirits of the righteous, then a church service is a meeting of two congregations that turn out to be one.

### Death does not dismember the body
The underlying claim is about what kind of thing the Church is. Paul calls it a body, and says of that body that “whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26, KJV). Bodies do not shed limbs at funerals, and Orthodoxy has never been able to see how a member of Christ could stop being one by dying.
Christ's own argument about the resurrection points the same way. Of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, long buried, he says that God “is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him” (Luke 20:38, KJV). Paul adds that neither death nor life can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus, and separation from Christ's love would be the only thing that could sever the connection.
From those two convictions everything else in this article follows. If the departed are alive in Christ, and if the living are joined to Christ, then the living and the departed are joined to one another. It is not a mystical extra. It is the ordinary consequence of taking the metaphor of the body literally.

### What it does to worship
The clearest picture is in the service of preparation before the Liturgy. The priest cuts a square from the first loaf, the Lamb, which will become the Body of Christ. From other loaves he cuts small particles: one for the Theotokos, others for the ranks of saints, then particles for living people whose names have been handed in, and particles for the departed. All of them are placed on one dish, around the Lamb.
At the end of the Liturgy those particles are put into the chalice, with a prayer that the sins of all those commemorated may be washed away by the precious Blood of Christ. A visitor watching from the nave will not see it happen. What is being enacted on that small dish is the whole of this doctrine: living and dead, in one company, gathered around one centre who is Christ.
The calendar says the same thing more slowly. Every day of the year carries the memory of particular Christians, and the Sunday after Pentecost is kept as the Sunday of All Saints, so that the Church's first act after receiving the Holy Spirit is to point at the people the Spirit produced. A congregation that keeps that calendar is being introduced to its own relatives, one day at a time.

### What it does to grief
Orthodoxy does not ask the bereaved to stop grieving, and any presentation of it that suggests otherwise has gone wrong. Paul writes that Christians should not sorrow “even as others which have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13, KJV), which regulates the sorrow rather than forbidding it. At the grave of a friend four days dead, knowing what he was about to do, Jesus wept.
What the Church offers instead is work to do. There are prayers on the third, the ninth and the fortieth days after a death, and on the anniversary. There is the panikhida, a short memorial service that can be served in a home or at a graveside. There are memorial Saturdays through the year, when whole parishes read out long lists of names, and in Russian practice there is Radonitsa in the weeks after Pascha, when families take the Paschal greeting to the cemetery.
Small details carry a good deal of this. Boiled wheat is brought for memorial services, because of the grain that must fall into the ground and die before it bears fruit. At the end the congregation sings Memory Eternal, which is not a wish that the dead be remembered by us, since our memories are short, but a prayer that they be held in the memory of God, which is not.
Grief handled this way does not become smaller, but it stops being private. A widow in the parish has somewhere to take her husband's name on a Saturday morning, and a hundred other people say it out loud with her.

### Where Christians differ here, and where they do not
A great deal of this is shared ground, and it would be dishonest to stage a disagreement that is not there. Most Protestant Christians confess the communion of saints, hold that believers who have died are with Christ, and expect to see them again. The hymn about the saints of God who toiled and fought and lived and died for the Lord they loved is sung in a great many churches on the first of November.
The difference is about whether the relation is active now, and in both directions. Orthodoxy holds that the saints pray for the Church on earth and that the Church on earth prays for its departed, and it puts both into its services every week. Many Protestant traditions hold that the departed are with Christ and leave it there, partly out of a real concern that traffic across that boundary would crowd Christ out of the middle.
That concern deserves a straight answer rather than a debating point. In the Orthodox Liturgy the whole company, living and departed, is arranged around one thing, and it is not a saint. If the arrangement ever stops pointing at Christ, the arrangement has failed, and the Church's own hymns are the first witnesses against it.

> these people are warm, loving people who obviously love Christ
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, lecture “Orthodoxy in the USA”, *The Orthodox Word* no. 94 (1980), quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 86

### The feast this parish is named for
This parish is the Parish of the Dormition of the Mother of God, and the feast it carries, kept on 15 August in the church calendar, is a death. Dormition means falling asleep. The Church spends a fortnight preparing for it, fasts before it, buries an icon-shroud with hymns borrowed from Holy Friday, and then sings about it for days afterwards with unmistakable happiness.
The icon of the feast explains the whole argument at a glance. The apostles stand around a bier; behind it Christ stands holding a small child wrapped in white, which is his mother's soul. The roles from the Nativity are reversed, and the point is made without a word: she once held him as an infant, and now he holds her. This is what the Church thinks dying in Christ looks like.
Fr. Seraphim Rose, who came to Orthodoxy from a Protestant family in California, spent much of his last years telling Orthodox converts how to speak to the people they had left behind. He held the traditional Orthodox teaching about the Church without softening it, and refused to draw conclusions about where any individual stands before God, preferring a formula he had from Fr. Dimitry Dudko.
Anyone is welcome at the vigil on Saturday evening and at the Liturgy on Sunday morning in Kovan. Bring the names of your own dead if you like; they can be given to the priest before the service, and they will be read. That is not a request to agree with everything on this page. It is an ordinary courtesy extended by one part of a family to another.

> We should view the non-Orthodox as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been revealed, as people who are potentially Orthodox
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### Common questions

Q: What do Orthodox Christians mean by the communion of saints?
A: They mean that the Church is a single body whose members include both the living and those who have died in Christ. The departed are held to be alive in him, aware, and praying for the Church on earth, while the Church on earth prays for them. The phrase itself comes from the Apostles' Creed; the Orthodox Church confesses instead the Creed of 381, but holds the same reality.

Q: Does Hebrews 12:1 actually teach this?
A: It describes Christians as surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, using a word that means both those who testified and those who watch. A few verses later the same chapter tells its readers that they have already come to the heavenly Jerusalem, to innumerable angels and to the spirits of just men made perfect. Orthodox worship takes that present tense seriously and is built around it.

Q: How is this different from what most Protestants believe?
A: Much of it is shared: that believers who die are with Christ, and that Christians will see one another again. The difference is whether the relationship is active now and in both directions. Orthodoxy prays for its departed and asks the prayers of the saints at every service. Many Protestant traditions hold that the departed are with Christ and stop there, out of concern for Christ's uniqueness.

Q: Does Orthodoxy expect the bereaved not to grieve?
A: No. Paul tells Christians not to sorrow as those who have no hope, which shapes grief rather than forbidding it, and Christ wept at the grave of Lazarus. Orthodoxy gives grief a structure instead: prayers on the third, ninth and fortieth days, memorial services at the graveside, memorial Saturdays through the year, and the singing of Memory Eternal, a prayer that God will remember.

Q: Can I have my departed relatives commemorated at an Orthodox service?
A: Names of the departed are written down and given to the priest before the Liturgy, and particles are taken out for them at the service of preparation. Practice about commemorating the non-Orthodox varies between parishes and is a question for the parish priest rather than for a website. Asking is entirely normal, and the answer will be given plainly.

### Sources
- The Orthodox Faith: the Church: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/doctrine-scripture/the-symbol-of-faith/the-church
- The Orthodox Faith: the Funeral: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-sacraments/funeral
- Orthodox Church in America: Prayers for the Departed: https://www.oca.org/questions/deathfunerals/prayers-for-the-departed
- The Orthodox Faith: Pentecost: https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-church-year/pentecost-the-descent-of-the-holy-spirit
- Second Council of Nicaea (A.D. 787), definition: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3819.htm
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84: Pastoral Guidance: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 86: Orthodoxy of the Heart: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
