## The New Religious Consciousness: What Fr. Seraphim Rose Saw in 1975
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/the-new-religious-consciousness.html
Summary: The new religious consciousness is Fr. Seraphim Rose's 1975 phrase for a widespread appetite for spiritual experience detached from repentance and the Cross. Writing in Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future, he argued that intensity of feeling is no proof of grace. His positive test is the one the Fathers use: real Christian experience makes a person humbler, soberer and readier to suffer for others.
==============================================================================

### A phrase from a book published in 1975
In April 1975 a small monastic press in northern California printed a book called Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future. Its author was Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose), an American who had taken a master's degree in Oriental languages at Berkeley, spent years among the seekers of San Francisco, and then gone to live as a monk in the forest at Platina. Chapter V of that book carries a title which has outlived most of the rest: "The 'New Religious Consciousness': The Spirit of the Eastern Cults in the 1970s".
He set the phrase inside inverted commas because it was not his own coinage. It was in the air around him. The following year two Berkeley sociologists, Charles Glock and Robert Bellah, edited a volume under exactly that title for the University of California Press. Believers and unbelievers alike could see that something was shifting in American religious life, and both were reaching for a name.

### What he was actually looking at
The chapter is reportage before it is argument. Its five sections walk through scenes that a Californian of the period could have attended on a free afternoon: Hare Krishna devotees chanting in San Francisco, Guru Maharaj-ji filling the Houston Astrodome, tantric yoga in the mountains of New Mexico, zen training in northern California. Only in the fifth section, "The New 'Spirituality' vs. Christianity", does he begin to draw conclusions.
None of this was foreign material to him. Before his baptism he had studied at the Academy of Asian Studies in San Francisco under Alan Watts, and he had been a genuinely serious student of Eastern thought rather than a hostile tourist in it. When he writes about the attraction of these movements he is describing something he had felt. That is worth keeping in view, because it changes the tone of the chapter from denunciation to recognition.
Behind the individual scenes he thought he could see one shape. Each promised contact with a reality deeper than the ordinary one. Each offered a technique for reaching it. And each, in his reading, offered that contact on terms that asked nothing of the seeker's moral life.

### The diagnosis: experience without repentance
This is the heart of it. What he named was not a doctrine but an appetite — for states, for felt presence, for the transcendent as something a person can be given rather than something a person is remade by. Peace and contentment were being offered as products, quickly and at no moral cost, and he thought Christians had begun to shop in the same market under Christian labels.
His answer was not to deny that the experiences happened. It was to deny that they proved anything. An experience can be vivid, unforgettable, even benevolent in its feel, and still tell you nothing whatever about its source. Against the promise of quick arrival he set a description of Christian life that reads almost harshly by comparison, and that he meant to apply to himself before anyone else.

> Christian spirituality is formed in the arduous struggle to acquire the eternal Kingdom of Heaven
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future*, ch. VIII §2 (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Fifth Edition, 2004)

### A necessary note on who wrote which chapter
Anyone who quotes this book should know that it is a compilation as well as an argument, and that its opening chapters are not by Fr. Seraphim at all. Attributions to him circulate widely and are often wrong. The printed bylines of the Fifth Edition are these:
Fr. Seraphim himself wrote the Preface, the Introduction, Chapters IV to VIII and the Epilogue "Jonestown and the 1980s", and he compiled and edited the whole. The chapter on the new religious consciousness is his. The argument about whether Christians and non-Christians worship the same God, which is quoted from this book more often than anything else in it, belongs to Fr. Basile Sakkas, and quoting it as Fr. Seraphim's is simply a mistake of fact. In the Introduction he describes those borrowed chapters in the third person, as an editor would:

> The first three chapters offer a general approach to non-Christian religions and their radical difference from Christianity, both in theology and in spiritual life.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future*, Introduction §4 (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Fifth Edition, 2004)
- Chapter I, "The 'Monotheistic' Religions" — by Fr. Basile Sakkas, reprinted from La Foi Transmise, 5 April 1970
- Chapter II, "The Power of the Pagan Gods" — by "A Convert to Orthodoxy"
- Chapter III, "A Fakir's 'Miracle' and the Prayer of Jesus" — by Archimandrite Nicholas Drobyazgin
- Preface to the Fifth Edition and the Epilogue to the Fifth Edition — by Hieromonk Damascene

### Why the edition matters
The book has been reprinted nine times since 1975, through five editions, the fifth appearing in 2004. Its text has not stayed identical across those printings, and the changes touch questions about the Church that are not incidental. Sergei Chapnin has publicly asked which version is genuinely Fr. Seraphim's own, who authorised the revisions, and on what authority.
That question has not been settled, and this parish is not in a position to settle it. The practical consequence for a reader is simple and worth observing everywhere: name the edition you are quoting. Everything cited on this page is from the Fifth Edition of 2004.
None of this is a reason to distrust the book. It is a reason to read it as a document with a history, written by a man in his early forties in a particular decade, revised after his death by people who loved him, and quoted ever since by readers who mostly do not know which parts are his.

### The positive criterion: humility and the Cross
Strip away the furniture of the 1970s and what remains is a test, and the test is not about which movement to avoid. It is about what genuine Christian experience looks like from the inside. The Fathers whom Fr. Seraphim was drawing on are consistent here: grace makes a person quieter, more self-suspicious, more patient with others and more willing to be inconvenienced for them.
The measure is the Cross, which is why the criterion cannot be intensity. "If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me" (Matthew 16:24, RSV). An experience that leaves a person more certain of their own advancement has failed the test, however vivid it was. An ordinary Tuesday spent forgiving someone has passed it, however flat it felt.
Saint Paul tells the Philippians to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling (Philippians 2:12). That phrase, fear and trembling, is the opposite register from the one the new religious consciousness was working in, and the difference is not a difference of temperament. It is a difference about what a human being is for.

### This is not a verdict on anybody's neighbours
It would be easy to read Chapter V as a list of people to be suspicious of, and some readers have done exactly that. It is not how its author asked to be read at the end of his life. In November 1980 a catechumen wrote to him, distressed by the words she saw Orthodox writers using about other Christians, and asked whether she might still call her Protestant and Catholic family Christians. His answer, which he credited to Fr. Dimitry Dudko, has become the most quoted thing he ever wrote:
In the same years he put the matter in print rather than in a private letter. Convert harshness, he wrote in The Orthodox Word, is spiritually wrong even when it is worded in a theologically correct manner, and it drives away from the Church people who would otherwise have been drawn to it. He also thought part of the reason others have not seen Orthodoxy is that we have not lived it in a way they could recognise. His own mother was a Protestant and his father a former Roman Catholic who became Protestant, and his counsel to converts was to live at peace especially with their own families.

> We should view the non-Orthodox as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been revealed, as people who are potentially Orthodox
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### What a reader in 2026 might make of it
Half a century on, the particular scenes have dated. The ashram has become the retreat centre and the app. Breathwork, plant medicine, silent weekends, sleep optimisation, the quantified interior life: much of what is now sold as wellness makes the same offer the chapter described, which is transcendence without repentance, and makes it at scale and for a subscription fee. The appetite has not gone anywhere. It has been industrialised.
Other parts of the book have worn less well. The chapter on unidentified flying objects reads strangely now. Academic readers have found the whole book polemical and thin on the scholarship of world religions, and that criticism is fair to record. Fr. Seraphim's own standing in the Church is likewise unsettled: he is locally venerated in some places, and in December 2025 the Synod of Bishops of the Russian Church Abroad established a commission to study his life, legacy and veneration. He is not a canonised saint of the Russian Church, and this parish does not call him one.
The part that survives is the question he was asking, and it is a question anyone can use. Not: is this exotic, or foreign, or new? But: does this ask anything of me? Does it make me easier to live with?

### Turning the question inward
The most useful thing about this diagnosis is that it works just as well on Orthodox Christians, and Fr. Seraphim applied it to us first. A person can want the singing, the incense, the beauty of an old rite and the pleasure of belonging to something ancient, and want all of it for exactly the reasons Chapter V describes. He said as much repeatedly, and admitted to being suspicious of a church full of correct icons, because the people in it might simply be following a fashion.
So the article ends where the discipline actually begins, which is with the writer and not the reader. If you have come here from a congregation where Christ is loved and the singing is warm, nothing on this page is aimed at you. The Orthodox Church makes a large claim about herself, and we have not tried to soften it. But the test she applies first is to her own members, on an ordinary weekday, in confession. You are welcome to come and watch how that goes.

### Common questions

Q: What did Fr. Seraphim Rose mean by the new religious consciousness?
A: He meant the widespread appetite, visible in the 1970s, for spiritual experience sought for its own sake and detached from repentance, obedience and the Cross. He described it in Chapter V of Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future through four scenes he could observe in California and Texas. His objection was not that the experiences were unreal, but that intensity of experience proves nothing about its source.

Q: Did Fr. Seraphim Rose write all of Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future?
A: No. He wrote the Preface, the Introduction, Chapters IV to VIII and the Epilogue on Jonestown, and compiled the book. Chapter I is by Fr. Basile Sakkas, Chapter II by an anonymous convert to Orthodoxy, and Chapter III by Archimandrite Nicholas Drobyazgin. In the Fifth Edition of 2004 the preface and the closing epilogue are by Hieromonk Damascene. Attributing those chapters to Fr. Seraphim is a common and avoidable error.

Q: Is this an attack on other Christians or on other religions?
A: It is not intended as one, and Fr. Seraphim himself set limits on that kind of writing. He held that harsh polemic was spiritually wrong even when technically accurate, and that Christians outside Orthodoxy should be treated as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been shown. The criterion described here is applied by Orthodox Christians to their own prayer and their own experience before it is applied to anyone else's.

Q: Should Fr. Seraphim Rose be called Saint Seraphim?
A: Not at present. He is locally venerated in some places, and in December 2025 the Synod of Bishops of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia created a commission to study his life, legacy and veneration. That study has not concluded. The correct and courteous forms are Fr. Seraphim Rose and Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose), and this parish uses those.

Q: How does this apply in 2026?
A: The specific movements of the 1970s have mostly dispersed, but the appetite he described is now served by an enormous wellness industry offering calm, presence and inner transformation as purchasable experiences. The Orthodox test has not changed with the market. Ask whether an experience has made you humbler, more patient and readier to carry someone else's burden. If it has not, it has told you nothing about God.

### Sources
- Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future — full English text: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/orthodoxy-and-the-religion-of-the-future/
- St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood — publisher's edition page: https://www.sainthermanmonastery.com/product-p/orf.htm
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84 'Pastoral Guidance': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 86 'Orthodoxy of the Heart': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
- OrthoChristian — index of materials on Fr. Seraphim Rose: https://orthochristian.com/141494.html
- ROCOR Synod establishes a commission on Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose): https://orthochristian.com/174495.html
- Patriarchal Exarchate of South-East Asia: https://exarchate.asia/


==============================================================================
## Spiritual Deception: What the Fathers Call Prelest
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/spiritual-deception-prelest.html
Summary: Prelest, from the Greek plani, is the Orthodox term for self-delusion in prayer: mistaking one's own imagination, feelings or vanity for the action of God. The Fathers teach that grace makes a person humbler and soberer, never more impressive to himself. Visions and warm feelings are therefore not accepted as evidence. The safeguards are confession, obedience to a counsellor, watchfulness, and steady distrust of one's own spiritual states.
==============================================================================

### A word with no comfortable English equivalent
The Greek is plani, wandering or going astray. The Slavonic and Russian word is prelest, and it is the more telling of the two, because in ordinary modern Russian prelest simply means charm or loveliness. You would use it of a child or a summer evening. The same word, in the language of the ascetic Fathers, means being taken in — the state of a person who has mistaken something in himself for the presence of God.
English translators reach for "spiritual delusion", "spiritual deception", or "self-deception", and none of them quite carries the double sense. The condition is not merely an error. It is an error that feels beautiful from the inside. That is what makes it dangerous, and that is why the tradition has so much to say about it.

### Where the teaching comes from
This is not a recent anxiety, nor a Russian one. It comes out of the Egyptian and Palestinian deserts of the fourth century onward, where people who prayed for a living discovered what happens to a mind left alone with itself for twenty years. Saint John Climacus devotes a long step of The Ladder of Divine Ascent to discernment. Saint Gregory of Sinai warns against admitting images into prayer at all. The whole collection assembled by Saint Macarius of Corinth and Saint Nicodemus of the Holy Mountain and printed at Venice in 1782 is called, in full, the Philokalia of the Neptic Fathers — the fathers of watchfulness.
The teaching reached Russian readers largely through Saint Paisius Velichkovsky, who translated the Philokalia into Slavonic at the end of the eighteenth century, and then through Saint Ignatius Brianchaninov (1807–1867), a bishop of the Caucasus and Black Sea whom the Russian Church canonised in 1988. His book The Arena and his writings on the Prayer of Jesus are the most systematic modern treatment of the subject in any language, and they are the books Fr. Seraphim Rose leaned on hardest.

### The two shapes it takes
Saint Ignatius describes the condition in two broad forms. The first arises from praying wrongly: from deliberately working up images, warmth in the chest, sensations of sweetness, and then taking these self-produced effects for grace. The body is obliging. It will supply almost any sensation asked of it often enough, and the person who has taught himself to expect consolation will reliably receive some.
The second form he calls opinion, and it is the worse of the two because it needs no visions at all. It is the settled conviction of having arrived — of standing further along than others, of having understood, of being someone whose spiritual judgements can be trusted. A person in this condition may pray very little and still be thoroughly deceived. It is available to bishops, to converts of six months, and to people who write articles for parish websites.

### Why visions and warm feelings are not treated as evidence
An outsider often finds this the strangest feature of Orthodox practice. A tradition drenched in icons, incense, chant and the language of mystical union turns out to be cold-eyed about religious experience to a degree that startles people. Told that someone has seen a light in prayer, an experienced Orthodox priest is far more likely to ask what the person has eaten and how much they have slept than to rejoice.
The reason is a piece of reasoning, not a temperament. If the criterion of a genuine experience were its intensity, then whatever can produce intensity can produce the criterion — fatigue, grief, longing, suggestion, music, a crowd, and, the Fathers add without embarrassment, spirits that are not God. Intensity is therefore useless as a test, because it is available from too many sources. Something that cannot be counterfeited is needed instead.
What the tradition puts in its place is not another experience but a direction of movement. Does this leave the person humbler, quieter, less interesting to himself, more patient with the tedious, more willing to be wrong? Grace, on this account, is recognised by its fruit in ordinary conduct over months, not by its taste in the moment. The old counsel about visions follows from that: do not accept and do not reject, but carry on with what you were told to do, and tell your confessor.

> Anything outward … can become a counterfeit.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 86 (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### The discipline is aimed at ourselves first
It matters a great deal how this teaching is used, because it can be picked up by the wrong end and turned into a weapon. Used as a diagnostic instrument for other people's prayer, it becomes a permission slip for contempt, and it then produces, with some reliability, the second form of the condition in the person holding it. There is a grim symmetry here that the Fathers saw clearly.
Orthodox practice is itself the first thing under suspicion. The Jesus Prayer taken up as a technique, fasting kept as a performance, a taste for old chant and correct icons, the pleasure of belonging to something ancient and unusual in a city like Singapore, the quiet satisfaction of knowing more than the people in the pew behind you: every one of these is flagged in the literature by name. Fr. Seraphim said he was suspicious of a church with nothing but good icons, because the people there might be following a fashion.
Fr. Seraphim made the same point more sharply in a letter written in 1981, during an argument about whether a Western Father had erred in his theology. His correspondent wanted the errors catalogued. The reply refused to treat that as the urgent question, and it is the sentence to keep if only one is kept:

> I myself fear the cold hearts of the 'intellectually correct' much more than any errors you might find in Augustine.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter to Fr. Michael, 26 June 1981, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 86 (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### The safeguards
None of the protections the Church offers is dramatic, and that is deliberate. They work by keeping a person's interior life from becoming a private matter, and by keeping the ordinary duties in front of the exalted ones. Fr. Seraphim, asked repeatedly by young Americans how to find a God-bearing elder, answered that such guidance is not given to our times and pointed instead to what Saint Ignatius calls life by counsel: a counsellor gives advice which is then tested in experience, rather than commands.
- Confession — spiritual experience described out loud, to a priest who knows you, loses most of its power to flatter.
- Counsel — a settled relationship in which someone else's judgement about your prayer outweighs your own.
- Watchfulness, nepsis — attention to what is actually arriving in the mind, without arguing with it or entertaining it.
- The appointed prayers — words given by the Church rather than composed in the moment, which do not bend to your mood.
- Ordinary duties first — giving alms, visiting the sick, helping those in need, which are hard to perform while admiring yourself.
- A working distrust of your own spiritual states, held without anxiety, as a pilot distrusts his inner ear in cloud.

### What this teaching does not say
It does not say that feeling is bad, or that consolation is suspect in itself. God does console, often at the point where a person can bear no more, and the Church's own hymns are not exactly restrained. Pascha night in a packed church at two in the morning is not a sober occasion, and no one asks it to be. The Fathers are not describing a religion of grey suspicion.
Nor does it say that God gives no visions. The Lives of the Saints are full of them. What the tradition says is narrower and more practical: that you are not the right judge of your own, that seeking them is the surest way to be given something false, and that a person who is not looking for them is in far less danger than a person who is. Saint Nicetas, who shut himself away to pursue exactly such gifts, is the standing example of how that ends.

### A writer who applied it to himself
Fr. Seraphim's best-known use of this material is in The Soul After Death, published in 1980, and in Chapter VII of Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future, where section 5 is headed simply "Spiritual Deception". What is worth noticing is how he wrote when the criterion was turned on his own work. In the preface to The Soul After Death he separates what the Church teaches about life after death, which he presents as settled, from his own readings of particular modern cases, which he does not.
That sentence was tested almost immediately. His presentation of the aerial toll-houses was publicly attacked, chiefly by Deacon Lev Puhalo, and the dispute went to the Synod of Bishops of the Russian Church Abroad. The Synod found that the teaching contains nothing contrary to piety, acknowledged that the vivid form given to it in one saint's Life has no direct scriptural basis, and then forbade further public controversy in periodicals. The teaching itself is old and widely attested in Orthodox liturgical and dogmatic sources; the manner of its presentation has genuinely been disputed among Orthodox writers, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

> Concerning these interpretations, of course, there is room for a legitimate difference of opinion among Orthodox Christians.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *The Soul After Death*, Preface (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, 1980; 2009 printing)

### Why a stranger might find this useful
If you have arrived here from a tradition where a strong experience of God is welcomed and given thanks for, the Orthodox habit of interrogating such experiences can look ungrateful, even faithless. It is worth saying plainly that Orthodoxy does make large claims for itself, and that this article has not tried to soften them. But the discipline described here is not a claim about you. It is a house rule, applied indoors, and applied first to the people who wrote it down.
Anyone is welcome to see how it works in practice. Come to a service at the Dormition parish in Kovan and watch what happens after: the queue for confession, the ordinary business of asking forgiveness of people you will see again next week. That is where the tradition thinks the real test of anyone's prayer is administered, and it is a test most of us fail quietly and often.

### Common questions

Q: What does prelest mean?
A: Prelest is the Slavonic and Russian term for spiritual delusion, translating the Greek plani, a wandering or going astray. It describes the state of a person who has mistaken his own imagination, emotion or vanity for the action of God. The ordinary modern Russian sense of the word is charm or loveliness, which captures the difficulty exactly: the condition is pleasant from the inside, which is why it is hard to detect in oneself.

Q: Why are Orthodox Christians suspicious of visions and strong feelings in prayer?
A: Because intensity is a poor test. Fatigue, grief, longing, music, suggestion and a crowd can all produce powerful religious feeling, so the presence of feeling proves nothing about its source. The Fathers replace that test with a slower one: whether a person is becoming humbler, quieter, more patient and more willing to be wrong. Visions are neither accepted nor rejected outright, but reported to a confessor and otherwise left alone.

Q: Is this teaching used to criticise other Christian traditions?
A: It should not be. The literature on prelest is ascetic literature, written by monks for monks about their own prayer, and every Orthodox practice is named in it as a possible occasion of delusion: the Jesus Prayer, fasting, a taste for correct icons, the satisfaction of belonging to something ancient. Used to diagnose other people it reliably produces the very condition it describes, which the Fathers call opinion.

Q: Who is the main Orthodox writer on spiritual deception?
A: Saint Ignatius Brianchaninov (1807–1867), bishop of the Caucasus and Black Sea, canonised by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1988. His book The Arena and his writings on the Prayer of Jesus set out the subject more systematically than any other modern treatment. He draws on the earlier Philokalic tradition, particularly Saint John Climacus and Saint Gregory of Sinai, and he was the chief inspiration for Fr. Seraphim Rose's own work on the subject.

Q: What are the practical safeguards?
A: Regular confession, so that the interior life is not a private matter; a settled relationship with a priest or counsellor whose judgement about your prayer outweighs your own; watchfulness over what arrives in the mind; using the prayers the Church appoints rather than improvising to suit a mood; putting ordinary duties such as almsgiving and visiting the sick ahead of exalted ones; and a calm, unanxious distrust of your own spiritual states.

Q: Does Orthodoxy teach that religious emotion is bad?
A: No. God consoles people, often when they can bear no more, and Orthodox worship is not a restrained affair — the Paschal night service is anything but sober. The teaching is narrower than it first appears. It says that you are not a reliable judge of your own experiences, that deliberately seeking them is the surest way to be given a counterfeit, and that the safe position is not to be looking.

### Sources
- What is Prelest?: https://orthochristian.com/114593.html
- The Basics of Spiritual Life, Based on the Writings of St. Ignatius (Brianchaninov): https://orthochristian.com/53476.html
- Champion of the Arena — Bishop Ignatius Brianchaninov: https://orthochristian.com/35220.html
- Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future — full English text: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/orthodoxy-and-the-religion-of-the-future/
- The Soul After Death — full English text: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/the-soul-after-death/
- The 1980–81 Synodal review of the toll-houses controversy: http://orthodoxinfo.com/death/tollhouse_debate.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 86 'Orthodoxy of the Heart': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
- Fr. Seraphim Rose's introduction to Blessed Paisius Velichkovsky: http://orthodoxinfo.com/phronema/intro_bpv.aspx

## What the Word Ecumenism Has Actually Meant
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/what-ecumenism-has-meant.html
Summary: Ecumenism has carried at least three distinct meanings: practical co-operation between Christians in charity and relief; formal theological dialogue between churches; and a proposed unity that treats doctrinal difference as secondary. Orthodox wariness attaches to the third sense, not to friendship or dialogue. Orthodox churches have taken part in ecumenical dialogue for over a century and continue to do so, while declining to treat the content of the faith as negotiable.
==============================================================================

### One word doing three jobs
Most disagreements about ecumenism are not disagreements at all. They are two people using one word for different things and discovering, some minutes in, that neither can make sense of the other. It is worth separating the senses before anything else is said, because the Orthodox position is quite specific about which of them it objects to, and quite specific about which it does not.
The word itself is older than the argument. It comes from the Greek oikoumene, the inhabited world, and in Christian usage it long meant something with no controversial edge whatever. The councils at Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon are called ecumenical because they were councils of the whole inhabited Christian world rather than of one province. An Orthodox Christian uses the word in that sense every time the Creed is discussed.

### The first sense: working together
The plainest meaning is practical. Christians of different confessions co-operate in relief after an earthquake, in hospital chaplaincy, in prison visiting, in feeding people, in defending the unborn or the trafficked, in running a food bank. No doctrinal claim is made or implied. Two groups who disagree about the sacraments carry the same boxes into the same warehouse.
Nothing in Orthodox teaching forbids this, and a good deal in the Gospel requires it. The Samaritan in the parable was not asked about his ecclesiology before he was commended. In a city like Singapore, where Orthodox Christians are a very small community among many larger Christian bodies, this kind of co-operation is simply a feature of ordinary life, and no one at this parish regards it as a compromise.

### The second sense: theological dialogue
The second meaning is formal conversation between churches about what divides them, conducted by appointed theologians over decades, producing agreed statements which the churches then receive, qualify or decline. This is slower and less photogenic than it sounds, and it has been going on for a very long time.
Orthodox involvement is not a recent or marginal thing. In 1920 the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople issued an encyclical addressed to the churches of Christ everywhere, proposing a league or fellowship of churches — a document usually treated as one of the founding texts of the modern movement. Orthodox churches were present at the formation of the World Council of Churches in Amsterdam in 1948. The Russian Orthodox Church joined in 1961. Bilateral dialogues with Roman Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Reformed and Oriental Orthodox have run, with interruptions, ever since.
There have been symbolic moments too. On 7 December 1965 Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople and Pope Paul VI simultaneously expressed regret for and lifted the anathemas of 1054 — an act of mutual courtesy which removed a mutual condemnation without restoring communion, and which was careful to say so. It is a good illustration of what dialogue can and cannot do.

### The third sense: unity on the terms of indifference
The third meaning is the one that generates the heat. It is the proposal, in its various forms, that the divisions between Christians concern matters of secondary importance; that the existing confessions are branches of a single tree, none of them simply the Church; and that unity may therefore be achieved by mutual recognition and shared communion without first resolving what is actually believed.
Stated that baldly, few people would sign it. But something close to it has been advanced at various points in the last century, sometimes as a theory about the Church and sometimes as an operating assumption about how quickly things ought to move. Impatience is understandable. Division between Christians is a scandal, it is visible to the whole world, and it has lasted a very long time.
It is this third sense, and only this one, that Orthodox wariness is about. The objection is not to friendship, not to conversation, not to praying for other Christians, and not to admiring them. It is to a particular account of what the Church is.

### Why the third sense is a difficulty for Orthodoxy
Orthodox ecclesiology does not work as a federation. The Church is understood as one thing, visible and identifiable, not as an invisible fellowship distributed across institutions which are all partial. That is a large claim, it is made plainly, and softening it would not be honest. It is the claim reaffirmed at the Holy and Great Council held in Crete in 2016.
From that claim a particular order follows. Communion at one chalice is not a means of reaching agreement; it is the expression of an agreement already reached. Orthodox Christians therefore do not receive communion in other churches and do not offer it, and this is not a judgement on the devotion of the people there. It follows from what the act is held to mean. Where unity of faith is absent, the sign of unity would be saying something untrue.
Nor does the difficulty concern only the sacraments. If the differences are secondary, then the councils that defined them were settling secondary matters, and the martyrs who died over them died over details. The Orthodox instinct is that the content of the faith was given, not developed by negotiation, and that it is not the Church's to trade.

### What Fr. Seraphim Rose wrote in 1975
Fr. Seraphim Rose's Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future, published in April 1975, is the book most often cited in English-language arguments about this, and it is also the book most often misquoted. Its Introduction contains a distinction that most of its readers overlook. He separates what he calls Christian ecumenism, which he regards as resting on a real if imprecise sense of common Christianity, from dialogue with non-Christian religions, which he treats as something else entirely.
Of the first of these he writes a sentence that is worth reading twice, because the adjectives in it are not decoration. He is not conceding a point grudgingly before returning to attack. He is stating what he takes the position to be, in the voice of a man describing people he has known and whose motives he does not doubt:
The word sincere is doing real work there, and so is the word understandable. He is describing an error, and he says so, but he is describing it as the error of people trying to do something decent. That is not the sentence of a man who thought Protestants and Roman Catholics were acting in bad faith.
Two cautions belong with any use of this book. First, Chapters I, II and III are not by Fr. Seraphim: they are by Fr. Basile Sakkas, by an anonymous convert to Orthodoxy, and by Archimandrite Nicholas Drobyazgin respectively, and the preface and closing epilogue of the Fifth Edition are by Hieromonk Damascene. The chapter that argues about whether Christians and non-Christians worship the same God is Fr. Basile's, not his. Second, the text has altered between editions, including at points bearing on the Church, and this has been publicly questioned. Name the edition. This page uses the Fifth Edition of 2004.

> 'Christian' ecumenism at its best may be seen to represent a sincere and understandable error on the part of Protestants and Roman Catholics
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future*, Introduction §2 (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Fifth Edition, 2004)

### What has changed since 1975
A reader should not assume that the situation Fr. Seraphim described in 1975 is the situation now. A good deal has moved since then, in both directions, and an honest account of the word has to say so rather than freeze the picture at the year a well-known book happened to appear.
Orthodox dissatisfaction with the World Council of Churches grew through the 1990s, and the Georgian and Bulgarian Orthodox Churches withdrew from it in the late 1990s. Rather than let the matter drift, the Council created a Special Commission on Orthodox Participation at its assembly in December 1998. The commission reported in 2002, and its central recommendation was structural: decisions would be reached by consensus rather than by majority vote, so that a minority could not be outvoted on matters of conscience. That method was tested in 2005 and applied at the assembly of 2006.
Then in June 2016 the Holy and Great Council met in Crete and adopted a document on relations with the rest of the Christian world. It holds two things together without embarrassment. It states that the Orthodox Church is the one holy catholic and apostolic Church, and it also records that she accepts the historical names of the other Christian churches and confessions not in communion with her, that she has taken part in the ecumenical movement from its beginning, and that she considers this participation consistent with her own tradition rather than foreign to it.
Four autocephalous churches did not attend that Council — Antioch, Russia, Georgia and Bulgaria — for a range of reasons, some of them unrelated to this document, and the reception of the Council's texts across the Orthodox world has been uneven. That, too, belongs in a fair account. A reader who is told only that the Council spoke has been told half of what happened.
So the argument continues, and it is worth being clear about its character. It is an argument among Orthodox Christians, conducted by bishops and theologians who are not in bad faith on either side, about how to hold a strong claim about the Church together with a real obligation of charity. It is not a settled consensus, and anyone who presents it as one is simplifying.

### What this means for an ordinary friendship
Most people who read a page like this are not deciding the policy of a synod. They have a Methodist colleague, or an Anglican mother, or a husband who was raised Baptist and still is. The question is practical: what am I allowed to say and do?
Fr. Seraphim answered that question directly in a letter of November 1980, written to a catechumen who was distressed by the language she had seen other Orthodox writers use. He gave the exclusive claim about the Church without softening it, and then set a boundary on what may be inferred from it:
From that boundary the rest of his counsel follows, and it is unremarkable advice which is nevertheless hard to live up to. Call them Christians. Be on good terms with them. Keep the peace at home above everything, since the person most likely to be wounded by a convert's new vocabulary is a mother or a spouse. He held that a harsh tone was warranted only where someone was actively trying to take away the Church's flock or alter her teaching.

> it is not for us to define the state of those who are outside the Orthodox Church
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### Where that leaves a reader
Three senses, then, and they deserve three different responses. Co-operation in works of mercy needs no defence. Theological dialogue has Orthodox participation stretching back more than a century and continues with the support of the Council of 2016. Unity purchased by treating the content of the faith as secondary is the thing Orthodox Christians decline, and the reason is not coldness but a particular understanding of what the Church is.
Saying that plainly is not the same as saying it unkindly, and Fr. Seraphim, who spent the last years of his life arguing with fellow converts about precisely this, would have insisted on the difference. He thought a cold correctness drove people away from the Church who would otherwise have come. If you have read this far and disagree with the third paragraph of every section, you are still welcome at the Dormition parish in Kovan on a Sunday morning, and no one will ask you where you stand before offering you tea.

> There is no reason why we cannot call them Christians and be on good terms with them
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood)

### Common questions

Q: What does ecumenism mean?
A: The word comes from the Greek oikoumene, the inhabited world, and it has carried at least three senses in modern usage. It can mean practical co-operation between Christians in charity and relief. It can mean formal theological dialogue between churches about what divides them. And it can mean a proposed unity that treats doctrinal difference as secondary. These are different projects, and arguments about ecumenism usually turn out to be arguments about which one is meant.

Q: Are Orthodox Christians opposed to ecumenism?
A: Orthodox churches have taken part in ecumenical dialogue for over a century, were present at the founding of the World Council of Churches in 1948, and the Holy and Great Council of 2016 affirmed that participation. Orthodox wariness attaches to the third sense of the word: unity achieved by treating what Christians believe as a secondary matter. Co-operation in works of mercy and honest theological conversation are not in dispute.

Q: Why can a non-Orthodox Christian not receive communion in an Orthodox church?
A: Because of what Orthodox Christians understand the act to be. Communion at one chalice is not treated as a means of reaching agreement but as the expression of an agreement already reached in faith. Where that agreement is absent, receiving together would be saying something that is not yet true. The practice is not a judgement on anyone's sincerity or devotion, and Orthodox Christians likewise do not receive in other churches.

Q: What did Fr. Seraphim Rose say about ecumenism?
A: In the Introduction to Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future, published in 1975, he distinguished ecumenism among Christians, which he described as at its best a sincere and understandable error on the part of Protestants and Roman Catholics, from dialogue with non-Christian religions, which he treated as a different matter altogether. Readers should note the edition, since the text has changed between printings, and that Chapters I to III are by other authors.

Q: Has anything changed since Fr. Seraphim wrote in 1975?
A: A good deal. The Georgian and Bulgarian Orthodox Churches left the World Council of Churches in the late 1990s. The Council created a Special Commission on Orthodox Participation in December 1998, which reported in 2002 and led to decision-making by consensus rather than majority vote. In 2016 the Holy and Great Council in Crete adopted a document on relations with other Christians, though four autocephalous churches did not attend.

Q: Can an Orthodox Christian pray with Protestant family members?
A: Ordinary prayer together with family, grace at table, praying for someone who is ill, is not the same question as concelebrating a service or receiving communion, and pastoral practice on the wider question varies. Fr. Seraphim's counsel to converts was to call other Christians Christians, be on good terms with them, and keep peace at home above all. Any specific question is best put to your own parish priest.

### Sources
- Relations of the Orthodox Church with the Rest of the Christian World: https://www.holycouncil.org/rest-of-christian-world
- Orthodox participation in the World Council of Churches: https://oikoumene.org/en/about-us/self-understanding-vision/orthodox-participation
- Final report of the Special Commission on Orthodox Participation in the WCC: https://www.oikoumene.org/resources/documents/final-report-of-the-special-commission-on-orthodox-participation-in-the-wcc
- Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future — full English text: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/orthodoxy-and-the-religion-of-the-future/
- St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood — publisher's edition page: https://www.sainthermanmonastery.com/product-p/orf.htm
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84 'Pastoral Guidance': http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 63 'Super-Correctness': http://orthodoxinfo.com/ecumenism/fsr_63.aspx
- Patriarchal Exarchate of South-East Asia: https://exarchate.asia/

## Eastern Religions and the Western Seeker
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/eastern-religions-and-the-western-seeker.html
Summary: Eugene Rose, later Fr. Seraphim Rose, took degrees in Oriental Languages, helped the philosopher Gi-ming Shien translate the Tao Teh Ching, and read René Guénon before entering the Orthodox Church in 1962. He held that every sincere religion reaches for ultimate reality, but that God gives Himself fully in Jesus Christ and in the Church — while refusing to pronounce on where any individual soul stands.
==============================================================================

### He learned the language before he formed the opinion
Eugene Rose graduated from Pomona College in 1956 with a degree in Oriental Languages. He had learned to read Chinese, ancient and modern, because he wanted the sages without a translator standing between him and the page. His parents had expected a scientist, and his teachers a brilliant career in mathematics. He gave that up for a question he could not put down: whether there is anything real underneath the life everyone around him was living.
At the Academy of Asian Studies in San Francisco he studied under its dean, Alan Watts, then the best-known populariser of Zen in the English-speaking world. The teacher who marked him more deeply was a Chinese philosopher on the same faculty, Gi-ming Shien, described in the biographical note printed in Fr. Seraphim's own books as a true representative of the Chinese tradition rather than a Western interpreter of it. Together the two of them worked on rendering the Tao Teh Ching out of the old characters.
Berkeley came next. He took his master's degree in Oriental Languages there in 1961, and during those years he visited Eastern temples — not as a tourist collecting impressions, but as a man looking for somewhere to stand. From Gi-ming, and from the French metaphysician René Guénon, he had absorbed a principle he kept for a long time: that if a religion is to be entered at all, it must be entered in its traditional and orthodox form, whichever religion that turns out to be.

### What he admired, and why it is worth saying first
It is easy to assume that a Christian writer who ends up disagreeing with Buddhism never understood it. That is not what happened here, and the honest thing is to say so before anything else. He knew these traditions from inside their texts, in their own languages, under teachers who belonged to them. Whatever he wrote later, he wrote as a man who had been held by them once, and who never pretended otherwise.
Their seriousness impressed him permanently. The Chinese sages taught him that strength can look like suppleness and that the yielding thing outlasts the rigid thing, and he believed that for the rest of his life. Hindu metaphysics offered him an account of reality far more ambitious than the flattened materialism of 1950s California. Zen offered discipline without sentimentality. None of that was a mistake, and he did not afterwards describe it as one.
Speaking in May 1981 to a comparative religion class at the University of California, Santa Cruz — a room full of students who had tried gurus, Tibetan and Zen Buddhism, shamanism and hallucinogens — he began not by correcting them but by granting the premise of their search. There is only one serious reason to study religion, he told them: to come into contact with a reality deeper than the ordinary one, which changes, rots away and leaves nothing behind.

> Every religion that is sincere tries to open up contact with this reality.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *God's Revelation to the Human Heart*, §1 “The Search” (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Second Edition, 2014)

### The search ended in a way he had not planned
One day in the early 1960s he walked into a Russian Orthodox church in San Francisco. By his own later account he went in the way he had gone into the Buddhist temples: to look at another tradition, one that Guénon's circle had named as the most authentic surviving form of Christianity. What met him there was not a conclusion he reached by argument. It was a recognition — the search, he wrote afterwards, was simply over, although the service was strange to him and in a language he did not know.
Naming the change took him longer than having it. Truth, he came to think, was not an abstraction to be mastered by a capable mind but someone personal, sought and loved by the heart. He was received into the Orthodox Church on the Sunday of the Prodigal Son, 25 February 1962. Nineteen years later, standing in front of the Santa Cruz students, he put the same thing not as a memory but as a rule about how God is known at all.

> God's revelation is given to something called a loving heart.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *God's Revelation to the Human Heart*, §2 “Revelation” (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Second Edition, 2014)

### What he concluded, stated plainly
Here is the part that cannot be softened without dishonesty. Fr. Seraphim did not conclude that the traditions climb one mountain by different paths. He concluded that Jesus Christ is God become man; that the Church He founded still exists and is the Orthodox Church; and that the fullness of communion with God is given there and is not on offer elsewhere. That is the traditional Orthodox position, he held it to the end, and this parish holds it too.
Such a claim is hard, and we will not dress it up as something milder. What it is not, though, is a claim about anyone's intelligence, sincerity, family or worth. Many Orthodox Christians reached Orthodoxy precisely because they found other traditions more serious than the Christianity they had been shown as children; Fr. Seraphim was one of them. The claim is about who Christ is. It is not a ranking of the people who have not yet met Him.
Second, and less often quoted, he set a firm limit on how far the claim may be pressed. Asked where particular souls stand before God, he declined to answer — not out of vagueness, but on principle. In a letter of 27 November 1980, written to a catechumen who was distressed by the harsh language she kept meeting in Orthodox books and who wanted to know whether she could still call her family Christians, he laid down the rule he kept himself.

> it is not for us to define the state of those who are outside the Orthodox Church
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### The book people quote, and who wrote which part of it
Nearly every argument about Fr. Seraphim and the Eastern religions comes back to one book: *Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future*, first published in April 1975 and now in its Fifth Edition (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, 2004). Anyone quoting it should know how it is assembled, because it is a compilation he edited as well as wrote, and the name on the cover does not describe every page inside.
The distinction is not pedantry. Some of the sharpest sentences about Hinduism that circulate online under his name belong to Chapter II, which he selected and printed but did not compose. It is also worth knowing that the text has changed between editions and that this has been publicly questioned by at least one Orthodox critic, so the responsible habit is to name the edition you are citing, every time. This article cites the Fifth Edition of 2004.
- Chapter I, on whether Christians and non-Christians have the same God, is by Fr. Basile Sakkas, reprinted from *La Foi Transmise* (1970).
- Chapter II, on Hinduism, is signed “By a Convert to Orthodoxy” — a woman who had practised Hinduism before becoming Orthodox.
- Chapter III, on a fakir's miracle and the Prayer of Jesus, is by Archimandrite Nicholas Drobyazgin.
- The Preface, the Introduction, Chapters IV to VIII and the epilogue “Jonestown and the 1980s” are Fr. Seraphim's own work.
- The Preface and Epilogue to the Fifth Edition are by Hieromonk Damascene, written long after Fr. Seraphim's death in 1982.

### How he wrote about a Zen monastery
His own chapters are the fairest test of how he handled a tradition he had left behind. Chapter V reports at first hand on Zen training at a monastery in northern California, and the report is not a hatchet job. He notes that the community forbids fortune-telling and psychic practice, that it warns students against drifting from teacher to teacher, that it has little patience with merely academic religion, and that it demands hard work and the banishing of flattering illusions about oneself.
More striking still, he writes that the young monks there discuss the spiritual life in a tone so sober and knowledgeable that it sounds like the conversation of serious young Orthodox converts, and that an Orthodox Christian reading them might well recognise himself and say that only grace had placed him elsewhere. He judged Zen the most intellectually sophisticated and the most spiritually sober of the Eastern movements then arriving in America, and he took its teaching of compassion seriously rather than caricaturing it.
Where he finally disagrees is not about the quality of the people or the rigour of the discipline. His objection is that an ideal reached by human effort, however high it goes, is not the same thing as the God who came down and looked for us; and that a path which relies on experience alone has no way of telling one kind of experience from another. You may think that wrong. It is at least an argument about the thing itself, made by someone who had been in the room.

### He went on quoting Lao Tzu to his monks
A man who had repudiated his old studies would simply have dropped them. He did not. In 1979, seventeen years after his baptism and two years after his ordination to the priesthood, he gave an informal talk on simplicity to the brothers and sisters gathered at his monastery, and he taught them out of Lao Tzu, introducing him plainly as a philosopher who was not a Christian.
The oak trees on the ridge above the monastery, he said, are hard and unbending, and their limbs come down in every storm; the pines bend, and stay standing. Then he turned the image on his own people: a man so certain of himself that he will take your head off over a disagreement is not showing strength but weakness, because he needs to convert you in order to be sure of his own belief.
Whatever else that is, it is not the behaviour of someone who thought the Chinese sages were beneath his notice. He had read them at twenty; he was still teaching from them at forty-five, to monks, in a forest, as a priest.

### If your family is Buddhist, Hindu or Taoist
In Singapore none of this is abstract. It is the question of what happens at home — whose altar, whose joss sticks, who is expected at the temple for the anniversary of a death, what a son does at his father's funeral. Orthodox Christians in this city live inside families where most of the people they love are Buddhist, Hindu, Taoist or of no particular religion, and this parish has no wish to make that harder than it already is.
Fr. Seraphim's own family were Protestants, and his conversion was not easy for them. What he told converts was to live at peace, especially with their own families; that calling people names accomplished nothing; and that when the non-Orthodox have not seen the truth of the Church, part of the reason may well be that we have not lived it in any way they could recognise. He kept that last accusation pointed at himself and never removed it.
So the claim stands, unsoftened, and it is not a claim that anyone owes us agreement. If you have read this far out of curiosity about what the Orthodox actually hold, you are welcome to keep reading, and you are welcome to come and stand quietly at the back of a service in Kovan and watch. Nobody will ask you to sign anything. It is the same door Eugene Rose walked through in San Francisco, as a man who had come only to look.

### Common questions

Q: Did Fr. Seraphim Rose really study Eastern religions seriously?
A: Yes. He took a BA in Oriental Languages from Pomona College in 1956 and an MA in the same field from the University of California, Berkeley, in 1961, having learned both ancient and modern Chinese. He studied at the Academy of Asian Studies in San Francisco under its dean, Alan Watts, and helped the Chinese philosopher Gi-ming Shien translate the Tao Teh Ching from the old characters.

Q: Did he think Buddhism and Hinduism are worthless?
A: No, and he did not write as if they were. He granted that every sincere religion is trying to make contact with a deeper reality, and in his own chapter on a Californian Zen monastery he praised its sobriety, its hard discipline and its refusal of psychic practice. His disagreement was about whether an ideal reached by human effort can be the same as the God who comes to meet us in Christ.

Q: Is the chapter on Hinduism in Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future by Fr. Seraphim?
A: No. Chapters I, II and III of that book carry other bylines: Chapter I is by Fr. Basile Sakkas, Chapter II on Hinduism is signed “By a Convert to Orthodoxy”, and Chapter III is by Archimandrite Nicholas Drobyazgin. Fr. Seraphim wrote the Preface, the Introduction, Chapters IV to VIII and the Jonestown epilogue, and edited the rest. The Fifth Edition's own preface and epilogue are by Hieromonk Damascene.

Q: Does the Orthodox Church say that Buddhists and Hindus are damned?
A: The Church teaches that salvation is in Jesus Christ and that the fullness of life with God is given in His Church; it does not issue judgments on individual souls. Fr. Seraphim held the exclusive claim firmly and at the same time wrote that it is not for us to define the state of those outside the Orthodox Church, returning that question to God. Orthodox Christians are asked to love their neighbours, not to sort them.

Q: How should an Orthodox Christian in Singapore treat a Buddhist or Taoist family member?
A: With honour and peace. Fr. Seraphim's counsel to converts was to live at peace especially with their own families, to drop the habit of name-calling, and to remember that our own failure to live the faith well is part of why others have not recognised it. Practical questions about funerals, family altars and festivals are best brought to a parish priest, who will answer them case by case rather than by rule.

Q: Is Fr. Seraphim Rose a canonised saint?
A: Not at this time, and this parish does not use the title. He is properly called Fr. Seraphim Rose or Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose). He was locally canonised in a Georgian diocese in 2023, and in December 2025 the Synod of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia established a commission to study his life, legacy and veneration. The wider question is open and under discussion.

### Sources
- Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future — full English text: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/orthodoxy-and-the-religion-of-the-future/
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84 — “Pastoral Guidance”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 87 — “Simplicity”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_87.aspx
- God's Revelation to the Human Heart — publisher's page: https://www.sainthermanmonastery.com/God-s-Revelation-to-the-Human-Heart-p/grhh.htm
- Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future — publisher's page: https://www.sainthermanmonastery.com/product-p/orf.htm
- Counsels of Fr. Seraphim (Rose) to Young Converts: https://orthochristian.com/141493.html
- ROCOR establishes a commission on the life and veneration of Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose): https://orthochristian.com/174495.html

## Discernment of Spirits: How Religious Experience Is Tested
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/discernment-of-spirits-charismatic.html
Summary: Orthodox Christians test religious experience rather than trusting it, following the apostolic command to try the spirits (1 John 4:1). The patristic criteria are humility and distrust of oneself, quiet sobriety rather than excitement, the fruits shown over years, the counsel of a confessor, and agreement with Scripture read with the Fathers. Fr. Seraphim Rose applied these tests first of all to Orthodox Christians.
==============================================================================

### Try the spirits
The apostolic instruction is blunt, and it is addressed to believers. Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world (1 John 4:1, KJV). St John is not writing to sceptics who doubt that anything spiritual exists. He is writing to Christians who were having experiences, and telling them that having the experience settles nothing by itself.
Most of us instinctively do the opposite. Something happens in prayer — warmth, tears, a sudden certainty, a sense of being addressed — and the sheer intensity of it seems to be its own credential. The stronger it felt, the truer it must have been. Orthodox tradition does not accept that inference, and it has a large, unglamorous body of teaching about how sincere people go wrong here. It assumes from the outset that going wrong is ordinary.

### The word the Fathers use
Greek and Russian ascetic writers have a term for the condition: prelest, usually rendered as spiritual deception or delusion. English has no exact equivalent, which is part of the difficulty. Prelest is not lying and it is not insanity. It is the state of a person who has mistaken something else — his own imagination, his nerves, his vanity, or an intelligence that is not his own — for the grace of God, and who is often the last to suspect it.
Fr. Seraphim Rose set out the teaching chiefly from Bishop Ignatius Brianchaninov, the nineteenth-century Russian hierarch whose collected works gather the older Fathers on this subject. Bishop Ignatius distinguishes two forms. The first and rarer is spectacular: a person reaches for high spiritual states or visions before he has been purified, relying on his own judgment, and receives visions accordingly. The second is commoner and much quieter: a heart that wants the enjoyment of holy feelings while it is not yet fit for them.
Note where that leaves the reader. The dangerous case in this teaching is not the obvious fraud; it is the devout person with good intentions. Bishop Ignatius, quoted by Fr. Seraphim, says that we are all in some measure deceived, that knowing this is the best protection there is, and that the worst deception of all is to believe oneself free of deception. The criteria that follow exist because of that sentence, not in spite of it.

### First: humility, which in practice means distrust of oneself
The older texts are startlingly unsentimental. St Anthony the Great counselled that when any vision presents itself one should not take fright but ask it, firmly, who it is and where it has come from; a manifestation from God will calm the fear, while a deception wavers when it meets a steady soul. Bishop Ignatius adds that if great saints were sometimes nearly deceived by spirits appearing in the form of angels, we are in no position to assume we would do better.
His practical counsel, drawn from the same Fathers, is therefore to decline such perceptions altogether: not to enter into conversation with an apparition, not to dwell on it, to make the sign of the Cross and acknowledge oneself unfit for that kind of communion. St Gregory of Sinai is quoted to the same effect — the mind readily forms whatever images it desires, and those who do not watch themselves closely are the ones it forms them for.
There is a consoling corollary that gets quoted far less often. On this teaching, God is not offended by the cautious person who refuses something out of fear of being deceived, even if what was refused had in fact been sent by Him. Caution is treated as good sense, not as ingratitude. That is worth holding on to if you are the sort of person who worries about having failed a test you did not know you were sitting.

### Second: peace, and the kind of peace it has to be
Grace, in the patristic accounts, is recognised less by its intensity than by its quietness. It leaves a person sober, collected, aware of his own sins and not especially interested in describing what happened to him. The counterfeit tends to leave excitement, a warm sense of having been singled out, and a strong wish to tell somebody. That is a criterion about aftermath rather than about the moment itself, which is precisely why it takes patience to apply.
The same caution extends to the physical phenomena that often accompany religious feeling. Fr. Seraphim, following St John of the Ladder, notes that tears have many different causes, some of them good and some not, and that a person should not trust his own tears until his soul has been purified; the Ladder is similarly wary of religious laughter. None of this means the body is irrelevant to prayer. It means the body is not evidence.

### Third: the fruits, measured in years
By their fruits ye shall know them (Matthew 7:16, KJV) is the criterion everyone remembers and almost nobody applies properly, because fruit takes seasons. The question is not what a person felt on the night, or even in the month afterwards. It is what he is like five years later: whether he is gentler or harder, whether he forgives faster, whether he has become more patient with dull people, whether he still thinks the experience was mainly about him.
Fr. Seraphim applied this test in public, and it is instructive that he applied it favourably to Protestants. Speaking in 1980 about a non-Orthodox Christian community in Eureka, California, from which several of his own spiritual children had come, he noted approvingly that they believed in spiritual struggle and the training of the soul, that they made themselves forgive one another and hold no grudges, and that they took people in off the streets. He said plainly that this was not the fullness of Christianity as the Orthodox have it, and equally plainly that it was good as far as it went.

> In the Protestant world, we have many examples of people with soft hearts, who, for the love of Christ, are kind to other people.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, talk on simplicity, 1979, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 87 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Fourth: somebody other than you has to look at it
This is the criterion that modern readers like least, and it is the one the tradition insists on most. A person cannot reliably assess his own spiritual state, because the faculty doing the assessing is the one under suspicion. The remedy is not a guru. Asked about finding a God-bearing elder, Fr. Seraphim answered that such guidance is not given to our times, and pointed instead to what Bishop Ignatius calls life by counsel: a counsellor gives advice, which you then test in your own experience, rather than commands.
In ordinary parish life this means a confessor — a priest who knows you over years, to whom you can say what happened and who is permitted to be unimpressed. It is a slow, unglamorous arrangement, and it works mainly by removing the private echo chamber in which spiritual self-assessment goes wrong. Fr. Seraphim wrote to one convert who was busy grading his own progress with a frankness that has aged well.

> You are too young in Orthodoxy to be evaluating your spiritual growth—that is actually a sign of your pride.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 22 June 1976, in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Fifth: Scripture and the Fathers, together and not selectively
The final criterion is the longest memory. Scripture itself warns that Satan is transformed into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14, KJV), which is a warning about attractive experiences rather than repulsive ones. St John Cassian, writing in the fifth century on the gifts of the Spirit, observed that wonders are sometimes worked precisely in order to inflate the man who believes he possesses a gift, and so prepare him for a heavier fall. The Ladder of St John warns that even the interpretation of Scripture can be suggested to a beginner by something that does not wish him well.
Reading the Fathers as a whole, rather than mining them for a sentence that endorses what you already experienced, is what makes this a criterion at all. Nobody does that alone or quickly. It is the ordinary work of a lifetime in the Church, which is why the tradition ties discernment to the sacraments, to confession and to time, rather than to a technique anyone could learn in a weekend.

### The charismatic movement, and how to read what he wrote about it
The longest chapter of Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future — Chapter VII, in the Fifth Edition (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, 2004) — is about the charismatic revival then spreading through Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations. Before summarising his argument, the parish wants to say what Fr. Seraphim also said: that the people in those meetings were in the main sincere and well-meaning Christians who loved Christ and wanted more of God. Nobody reading this should be left with the impression that their sincerity is in question here.
His argument runs as follows. The criterion for judging a spiritual experience is not the experience but the attitude taken towards it; the category of prelest was largely absent from the Western spiritual manuals of the period, so the movement had no inherited tool for the job; and when he laid the published testimonies of participants alongside Bishop Ignatius, he found the pattern of the second, quieter form of deception. His conclusion was severe, and we will not disguise it: he judged the movement a counterfeit of the Church's own spiritual life, and he wrote about it sharply.
Two honest qualifications follow. His tone in that chapter is harder than almost anywhere else in his writing, and many Orthodox readers who accept his criteria still find the tone difficult. He knew the danger himself and named it in print in 1980, writing about converts who had grown too free with the words heresy and heretic, and about the smugness that can hide inside a technically accurate position.

> Even when it is worded in a theologically correct manner, this attitude is spiritually wrong
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, “In Defense of Fr. Dimitri Dudko”, *The Orthodox Word* no. 2 (1980), p. 131, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Criteria, not verdicts
Which brings us to the reader. Everything above is a set of criteria. It is not a ruling on your prayer meeting, your conversion, or the night something happened that you have never been able to explain to anyone. This parish does not know what happened to you, has no way of knowing, and is not going to tell you. Anyone who offers you a confident diagnosis of an experience he was not present for is doing something the Fathers did not do.
What the tradition offers instead is a way of testing, worked out over centuries by people who took the risk of self-deception seriously and who applied it to themselves before anyone else. The right use of these criteria is slow and inward: wait; do not build your life on a single hour; tell somebody older in the faith than you are; and watch what you are like in five years. That is unexciting counsel. It was also given to the best disciples the Fathers had.
One last thing should be said, because the testing can sound like suspicion of God. It is not. Fr. Seraphim's own account of the Christian life was that it is formed in the hard struggle to acquire the Kingdom of Heaven (*Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future*, ch. VIII §2, Fifth Edition, 2004), which is a very different thing from nervousness. Caution about our own impressions exists to protect something, not to shrink it. If you have had an experience you cannot account for, you are welcome to bring it to a priest in Kovan, who will not be shocked and will be glad you asked.

### Common questions

Q: What does 1 John 4:1 mean by testing the spirits?
A: It means that a Christian is expected to examine spiritual experiences rather than accept them on the strength of how they felt. The verse is addressed to believers, not to sceptics, and assumes that sincere people can be misled. Orthodox tradition has developed that command into a set of working criteria: humility and self-distrust, sobriety, the fruits over time, the counsel of a confessor, and agreement with Scripture read together with the Fathers.

Q: What is prelest?
A: Prelest is the Slavonic and Russian term used in Orthodox ascetic writing for spiritual deception or delusion — the state of someone who has taken his own imagination, emotion or vanity, or an intelligence that is not God's, for the grace of God. It is not lying and it is not madness. Bishop Ignatius Brianchaninov describes two forms: a spectacular one involving visions, and a commoner one involving exalted religious feelings sought before the heart is ready.

Q: Does the Orthodox Church say charismatic experiences are demonic?
A: The Church tests such experiences by the criteria above rather than issuing blanket rulings on individuals. Fr. Seraphim Rose, in Chapter VII of Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future, reached a severe conclusion about the movement of the 1970s as a movement, while stating that its participants were often sincere and well-meaning Christians. His criteria can be studied and used without treating his conclusion as a judgment on any particular person's prayer.

Q: How do I know whether an experience in prayer was from God?
A: Usually you do not know at once, and the tradition says that is the right state to be in. Do not build on it, do not repeat it to an audience, and do not decide it means something about your progress. Tell a confessor, and pay attention to the fruits over the following years: whether you are humbler, more patient, quicker to forgive. Caution is not ingratitude; the Fathers say God is not offended by the careful.

Q: Do I need a spiritual father to practise discernment?
A: You need someone other than yourself. Fr. Seraphim held that God-bearing elders are not given to our times and pointed instead to what Bishop Ignatius Brianchaninov calls life by counsel: a counsellor gives advice that you test in experience, rather than commands you obey blindly. In parish life this normally means a regular confessor who knows you over years. It is deliberately ordinary, and it removes the private echo chamber in which self-assessment goes wrong.

Q: Is testing experience a sign of a cold faith?
A: It is not meant to be. The same tradition that warns against trusting spiritual feelings also insists that the heart, not the mind, is where God is known, and Fr. Seraphim said repeatedly that being correct is the external side of Christianity and not the most important one. Discernment exists to protect a real love of Christ from being spent on a counterfeit, in the way a careful doctor protects a patient he likes.

### Sources
- Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future — full English text: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/orthodoxy-and-the-religion-of-the-future/
- The Soul After Death — full English text: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/the-soul-after-death/
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84 — “Pastoral Guidance”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 86 — “Orthodoxy of the Heart”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 87 — “Simplicity”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_87.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 63 — “Super-Correctness”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/ecumenism/fsr_63.aspx
- The Soul After Death — publisher's page: https://www.sainthermanmonastery.com/product-p/sad.htm
- Counsels of Fr. Seraphim (Rose) to Young Converts: https://orthochristian.com/141493.html
