## Who Was Fr. Seraphim Rose?
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/who-was-fr-seraphim-rose.html
Summary: Fr. Seraphim Rose (1934–1982) was born Eugene Dennis Rose in San Diego and raised Protestant. He abandoned religion as a student, studied Chinese philosophy at Pomona and Berkeley, and entered the Orthodox Church in San Francisco in 1962. He founded a brotherhood and a printing press, was tonsured a monk in 1970, ordained priest in 1977, and died at Platina, California, aged forty-eight.
==============================================================================

### A boy from San Diego
Eugene Dennis Rose was born in San Diego on 13 August 1934. His mother, Esther, came of a Norwegian family and was a Protestant; his father, Frank, of Dutch and French descent, had grown up Roman Catholic and became a Protestant for his wife's sake. Frank kept a sweet shop for a while, then worked for General Motors, and ended his working life as a janitor at a sports stadium. It was an ordinary American household, and the faith in it was ordinary Protestant faith.
The boy was not ordinary. He left San Diego High School in 1952 at the top of his class, and the people around him assumed he would go into science or mathematics. What he actually wanted, by the time he reached Pomona College in southern California, was something he would have found hard to explain to a careers master: not a profession, but an answer. He wanted to know what was really there.

### The years he would not describe
At Pomona he put aside the religion of his childhood. It had struck him as thin, and he went looking for reality in Western philosophy instead. The search widened into the bohemian life of 1950s California. He read Nietzsche until the sentences had a kind of electricity in them, and he experimented deliberately with breaking down ordinary reasoning, on the theory that logic was the wall and unreason the door through it.
None of it worked. Hieromonk Damascene, who edited his early writings and later wrote his biography, records that when Eugene was asked years afterwards to describe that period, he would say only that he had been in hell. He drank. He shouted at the God he had publicly pronounced dead. This is worth stating plainly, because his later books are sometimes read as the work of a man who had never doubted anything. He had doubted everything, and it had very nearly finished him.

### Chinese philosophy, and where it left him
He graduated from Pomona in 1956 with a degree in Oriental Languages, having learned Chinese, both ancient and modern, in order to read the sages without a translator between. In San Francisco he enrolled at the Academy of Asian Studies, whose dean was Alan Watts, then the most widely read interpreter of Zen in English. The teacher who mattered, though, was a quieter man: Gi-ming Shien, a Chinese philosopher whom Eugene regarded as a true representative of the tradition, and with whom he worked on a rendering of the Tao Te Ching from the ancient characters.
From Gi-ming Shien, and from the French writer René Guénon, he took a principle that would eventually decide his life: that a man ought to hold to the traditional, orthodox form of a religion rather than assemble a private one out of pieces he liked. He took his master's degree at Berkeley in 1961. And the wisdom of the pre-Christian philosophers, profound as he found it, left him unsatisfied — and unable to say why.

### A Russian church in San Francisco
He went to an Orthodox service the way a scholar goes anywhere: to look at one more tradition. Describing it many years later, in a passage printed at the back of The Soul After Death, he said that something happened to him in that Russian church which had not happened in any Buddhist or other Eastern temple — something in his heart told him that this was home, and that the search was over. He did not understand the service. It was in a language he did not know. He kept going back.
What reached him slowly, over months of standing at the back and learning the customs, was an idea that his whole education had not prepared him for: that truth might not be an abstract thing sought by the mind at all, but something personal, even a Person, sought and loved by the heart. That, he wrote, was how he met Christ. He was received into the Orthodox Church on 25 February 1962, the Sunday of the Prodigal Son, in the Russian cathedral of the Mother of God “Joy of All Who Sorrow” in San Francisco. He was twenty-seven.

### Archbishop John
The archbishop of San Francisco in those years was John Maximovitch, a small, stooped hierarch who had come by way of Shanghai and the Philippines, slept sitting up, went barefoot, and was regarded in his own lifetime as a wonder-worker. The Church canonised him in 1994 as St John of Shanghai and San Francisco. Eugene became his disciple. When Archbishop John began a course of theological classes in the city, Eugene attended every one and finished at the head of the class, although the lectures were delivered in Russian and he was the only American convert in the room.
Much of what is best in Fr. Seraphim's later writing came from this man rather than from any book. Lecturing to students at Santa Cruz twenty years afterwards, he was asked what it was about Archbishop John that drew people to him, and said the answer was always the same: he loved, and he gave himself away for others, and that is why things were shown to him.

> God's revelation is given to something called a loving heart.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, *God's Revelation to the Human Heart*, §2 “Revelation” (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Second Edition, 2014)

### A bookshop and a letterpress
In 1963, with a young Russian named Gleb Podmoshensky and with Archbishop John's blessing, Eugene founded a brotherhood named after St Herman of Alaska, the monk who had come from Valaam to Kodiak Island in 1794 and is counted the first saint canonised in America. The following year the two of them opened an Orthodox bookshop in San Francisco. In January 1965 they brought out the first number of a small bimonthly magazine, The Orthodox Word, setting and printing it themselves on a simple letterpress.
That magazine is the key to the man. He was never a professional theologian and held no academic post after Berkeley. He was, in the most literal sense, a publisher: a man who translated lives of saints out of Russian, set the type, read the proofs, and posted the result to a few hundred subscribers. Almost everything he wrote appeared there first, in instalments, written for readers many of whom he knew by name.

### The forest at Platina
Archbishop John died in 1966. The two brothers, who had his blessing for the plan, began looking for land in the wilderness of northern California, and in 1969 they moved to a secluded mountainside near the small town of Platina, carrying the printing equipment up with them. On 27 October 1970 both were tonsured as monks. Eugene was given the name Seraphim, after the Russian ascetic St Seraphim of Sarov; Gleb was named for St Herman.
Ordination followed in 1977 — deacon in January, priest in April, at the hands of Bishop Nektary of Seattle, a disciple of the Optina elders. From then on he was a hieromonk, a monk who is also a priest. His last years were not the solitude he had gone to the mountain to find: letters arrived in sacks, and people came, and he answered them. A short and sudden illness took him on 2 September 1982. He was forty-eight years old.

### Why a Protestant reader might find him worth reading
There are Orthodox writers who address Protestant readers from a considerable height, as if calling down from a wall. Fr. Seraphim is not one of them, and the reason is biographical. He had stood where such a reader stands. He was raised in a Protestant home and left it, not out of indifference, but out of a demand for something more real than he believed he had found there. He knew from the inside what it costs to want the truth badly enough to walk away from the faith you were handed.
His family never followed him. His mother remained a Protestant to the end, and his counsel to converts on this subject ran in the opposite direction from what people expect of him. Writing on 27 November 1980 to a catechumen distressed by the name-calling she had met in Orthodox books, he told her there was no reason she could not call her Protestant and Roman Catholic relatives Christians and be on good terms with them, recognising that they had at least faith in Christ in common, and that she should “live in peace especially with our own families”.
To another correspondent, a catechumen preparing for baptism in May 1979, he wrote a single sentence that sits oddly with his reputation for severity. It is the plainest thing he ever said about why a person should become Orthodox at all, and it is probably the fairest test to apply to any convert — or, for that matter, to him.

> You are coming to Orthodoxy to receive Christ, and this you should never forget.
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 3 May 1979, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### A note on what to call him
One practical matter, because a reader meets it within about ten seconds of searching his name. Fr. Seraphim is widely venerated, and it is common to see him written of as “St Seraphim of Platina”. That title runs ahead of the Church. He was locally canonised in the Georgian diocese of Akhalkalaki in February 2023, but a local glorification does not bind the wider Church, and in the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia — the jurisdiction in which he lived and served — the question remains open.
Matters have been moving. In December 2025 the ROCOR Synod of Bishops established a commission, headed by Bishop James of Sonora, to study his life, legacy and veneration. In May 2026 the Synod was reported to have approved the opening of canonisation proceedings, although that report should be treated as provisional. As this page is written, in September 2026, the matter has not concluded.
For that reason this parish writes “Fr. Seraphim Rose” or “Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose)”, which is what he was called in his lifetime and what the Church's own documents still call him. The process has also drawn public criticism from some Orthodox writers, who fear his name is being attached to causes he did not take up. Readers who want the current position should check it with the Synod rather than rely on any web page, this one included, which may have been written before the next decision was taken.
Whatever is decided, the books will be what they have always been: the work of a man who looked very hard for the truth, in places most people never look, and who believed at the end that the truth had found him.

### Common questions

Q: What was Fr. Seraphim Rose's real name?
A: He was born Eugene Dennis Rose in San Diego, California, on 13 August 1934, and used that name until his monastic tonsure on 27 October 1970, when he received the name Seraphim after St Seraphim of Sarov. Books written before 1970, such as Nihilism, are published under “Eugene (Fr. Seraphim) Rose” for that reason. After his ordination in 1977 he was correctly styled Hieromonk Seraphim.

Q: Was Fr. Seraphim Rose raised Orthodox?
A: No. He was raised Protestant in San Diego; his mother was a Protestant and his father, brought up Roman Catholic, became a Protestant when he married. Eugene rejected that faith as a student and spent several years in philosophical despair before entering an Orthodox church in San Francisco out of curiosity. He was received into the Orthodox Church in February 1962, at twenty-seven.

Q: Is Fr. Seraphim Rose a saint?
A: That is not settled. He was locally canonised in a Georgian diocese in February 2023, and he is widely venerated by individual Orthodox Christians. Within the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia, a Synodal commission was established in December 2025 to study his life and veneration, and proceedings were reported to have been opened in May 2026. Until the Church concludes, “St Seraphim of Platina” is premature; write Fr. Seraphim Rose, and check the current status.

Q: What did Fr. Seraphim Rose write?
A: His best-known books are The Soul After Death (1980) and Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future (1975). Published after his death were God's Revelation to the Human Heart, The Place of Blessed Augustine in the Orthodox Church, Genesis, Creation and Early Man, and Nihilism, written before his tonsure. He also edited The Orthodox Word from 1965 and translated a great deal of Russian hagiography into English.

Q: Who was Archbishop John Maximovitch to him?
A: Archbishop John Maximovitch was the Russian hierarch of San Francisco who received the young convert as a disciple, blessed the founding of the St Herman of Alaska Brotherhood in 1963 and the publishing work that followed, and blessed the eventual move to the wilderness. He died in 1966 and was canonised in 1994 as St John of Shanghai and San Francisco. Fr. Seraphim regarded him as the living argument for everything he later wrote.

### Sources
- OrthoChristian — Fr. Seraphim (Rose) index: https://orthochristian.com/141494.html
- “Counsels of Fr. Seraphim (Rose) to Young Converts”: https://orthochristian.com/141493.html
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 84 — “Pastoral Guidance”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_84.aspx
- St. Herman of Alaska Monastery — The Soul After Death: https://www.sainthermanmonastery.com/product-p/sad.htm
- Azbyka.ru — works of Fr. Seraphim (Rose): https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Serafim_Rouz/
- ROCOR Synod establishes commission on Hieromonk Seraphim (Rose), 13 December 2025: https://orthochristian.com/174495.html
- Local canonisation in the Georgian diocese of Akhalkalaki, February 2023: https://orthochristian.com/151232.html

## Fr. Seraphim Rose Against Religious Harshness
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/correctness-disease-against-polemics.html
Summary: Fr. Seraphim Rose held the traditional Orthodox teaching that the Church is one and the sacraments are given in her, and he said so plainly. He also refused to judge any individual outside the Orthodox Church, accepted that Protestants genuinely meet and love Christ, thought calling them heretics did no good, and wrote in print that harsh convert polemic is spiritually wrong even when it is theologically accurate.
==============================================================================

### A blog with a rule, and where the rule comes from
Everything written on this site follows a rule, and the parish thought it more honest to set the rule out in one article than to leave readers to work it out for themselves. The rule is not a house style. It comes from a letter written in a cabin in northern California on 27 November 1980, and from an article published earlier the same year in a small Orthodox magazine with a few hundred subscribers.
Put simply: the Orthodox Church makes a large claim about herself, and these pages will state that claim plainly, because blurring it would be a discourtesy to anyone who has come here to learn what Orthodox Christians actually hold. But the claim will not be turned into a weapon against the person reading it. That is not a modern compromise between conviction and politeness. It is Fr. Seraphim Rose's own position, and he argued for it in print in the last two years of his life.

### Four things, held at the same time
He is easy to misrepresent, and he gets misrepresented in both directions. Some quote his sharpest sentences and present him as a man whose chief interest was in telling other Christians where they stood. Others quote his kindest and turn him into something he would have refused to be called. He held four things together, and dropping any one of them produces a different man.
- The Orthodox Church is the Church founded by Christ, and the sacraments are given in her. He stated this without qualification and repeated it.
- It is not for us to say where any particular soul outside that Church stands before God. He refused this question every time it was put to him, and referred it to God.
- Christian life outside Orthodoxy is real. He believed that Protestants are genuinely born again in Christ, that they love Christ, and that in some respects they put Orthodox Christians to shame.
- Harsh convert polemic is a spiritual illness, and it does more damage to the Church than the errors it attacks.

### The sentence he put into print
In 1980 Fr. Seraphim published a defence of Fr. Dimitry Dudko, a Moscow priest then under pressure from the Soviet authorities, in The Orthodox Word, the magazine he edited and printed himself. Part of the article turned aside to address his own readers. Among Western converts to Orthodoxy, he wrote, there is a temptation to speak too freely of heresy and heretics, and to use the errors of the non-Orthodox as an excuse for what he called “pharisaic smugness” about our own Orthodoxy. Then came the judgment.
Read that slowly, because it is easy to skim past. He is not saying the harsh convert has his facts wrong. He concedes the theology may be correct, word for word, and condemns the attitude anyway. The sentence continues by naming the consequence: this attitude, he wrote, helps to drive away from the Orthodox Church many who would otherwise have been drawn to it.
The provenance matters. This was not a private remark caught in someone's memoir, nor a line from a letter released after his death. He published it, over his own name, in the journal he had founded and ran. It is the strongest thing he said on the subject and the easiest to verify.

> Even when it is worded in a theologically correct manner, this attitude is spiritually wrong
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, “In Defense of Fr. Dimitri Dudko”, *The Orthodox Word*, no. 2 (1980), p. 131; quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### The letter of 27 November 1980
The other central text is a letter, and its occasion is worth knowing. A catechumen had written to him in distress. She had been reading Orthodox authors and had met words like “Papists” and “heretic”, and she told him that as a member of a race which had been subjected to a great deal of name-calling, she despised the habit and did not wish to take it up herself. She wanted to know whether she was allowed to call her Protestant and Roman Catholic relatives Christians. She mentioned St Innocent of Alaska, who had been notably kind to the Franciscan priests he met in California.
His answer begins with pleasure rather than correction. He was happy to receive the letter, he told her, because her attitude showed that within the truth of Orthodoxy to which she was drawn she wanted to find room for a loving and compassionate attitude towards those outside it — and that, he said, is what Orthodoxy teaches. He then set out his position in numbered points. The points are not soft.

### What he claimed, and what he refused to claim
He begins where the Orthodox Church begins. Orthodoxy is the Church founded by Christ for the salvation of mankind; in the Orthodox Church alone is grace given through the sacraments; and if salvation is difficult enough inside the Church, it must be harder outside her. That is the traditional Orthodox teaching, stated without a cushion. This site is not going to pretend he said something milder, because a reader who follows the citation will find the passage in ten minutes and will rightly conclude that we were managing him.
Then comes the turn. Everything he wrote about other Christians over the following two years swings on it, and it is stated in a single clause, without argument or apology, as though it were simply the obvious consequence of believing that God is the judge of souls and we are not.
If God wishes to grant salvation to someone who is a Christian in the best way he knows, Fr. Seraphim went on, that is up to God and not to us. Notice what kind of distinction this is. The Church teaches where the sacraments are given; she has not been given the task of issuing findings about particular souls, and he would not issue any. He held the doctrine and declined the verdict, and he did not regard that as inconsistent.

> it is not for us to define the state of those who are outside the Orthodox Church
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### What he said about Protestant Christians
In the same letter he wrote that he could himself accept the experience of Protestants being born again in Christ. He had met people, he said, who had changed their lives entirely through meeting Christ, and he would not deny their experience merely because they were not Orthodox. He called such people beginning Christians, and held that they could not have the fullness of Christianity until they were united to the Orthodox Church. He did not take the first half back in order to say the second.
Elsewhere he went further. Several of his own spiritual children had come out of an evangelical community in Eureka, California, and in a lecture that year he described them to an Orthodox audience with open admiration: warm, loving people who obviously love Christ, who believed in spiritual struggle, who made themselves forgive one another rather than nurse grudges, and who took homeless people in off the street. In this, he said, they are an example of what we ought to be, only more so.
Speaking about simplicity the year before, he made the same point to his own side. The Protestant world, he observed, has many examples of people with soft hearts who are kind to others for the love of Christ; that is basic Christianity, and no Orthodox Christian should imagine that he may be cold and hard and correct and still be a Christian. The warning is pointed inwards, not outwards.
There is one criticism of Protestant teaching in the letter, and he makes it without heat. He thought that the idea that a person who is saved need do nothing further, because Christ has done it all, stands in the way of seeing the Orthodox emphasis on struggling for one's salvation after it has been given, and he cited St Paul: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12, RSV). That is a real difference, and other articles here will take it up at length.
Having named it, though, he moved straight on. Almost all the religious Christmas carols, he remarked in the next breath, are perfectly good, and they are sung by Orthodox Christians in America — some of them, he added with evident amusement, in the strictest monasteries. The difference was stated once, accurately, and then he stopped pressing it.

### Potentially Orthodox
The letter ends with a formulation that Fr. Seraphim does not claim as his own. He credits it to Fr. Dimitry Dudko, the Moscow priest he had defended in print that same year, and he offers it as the conclusion of the whole argument. It is the sentence that sets the register for this entire site, and it is worth having in front of you in his own words.
Notice that the sentence does not stop there. It continues into a parenthesis, and the parenthesis is the part that costs the writer something: “(if only we ourselves would give them a better example!)”. The exclamation mark is his. He is not congratulating Orthodox Christians on their position; he is suggesting that the reason others have not seen what the Church is may have a great deal more to do with us than with them.
He had already said as much, more soberly, a few paragraphs earlier. Of Christians outside the Orthodox Church he wrote that they do not yet have the full truth — perhaps because it has not yet been revealed to them, or perhaps because it is our fault, for not living and teaching the Orthodox faith in a way they can understand. On his account, the likeliest point of failure in the whole encounter is the Orthodox side of it.
In a lecture the same year he made the positive version of the point. If the Orthodox Church really holds the fullness of Christianity, he argued, then there ought to be something visible in the common life of her people that a person who sincerely loves the truth would recognise and want. That is a considerably more demanding standard than winning an argument.

> We should view the non-Orthodox as people to whom Orthodoxy has not yet been revealed, as people who are potentially Orthodox
> — Fr. Seraphim Rose, letter of 27 November 1980, quoted in Hieromonk Damascene, *Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works*, ch. 84 (St. Herman Press, 2003)

### Correctness disease
He had a name for what he was against. He called it “super-correctness”, and sometimes “correctness disease”: a narrowness he watched spreading among converts and Western-born Orthodox during the 1970s, which offered simple answers to complicated questions and a party line on every possible subject. Many converts, he wrote, grasp at correctness like a baby's bottle, and he thought they could save their souls better by being a little incorrect but humbler.
What made the diagnosis unusual was where he located the danger. Others of his generation were warning that the Church was becoming lax; he thought the deeper trouble ran the other way, that the real loss was the savour of Orthodoxy, and that strictness will not save anyone who no longer has the taste and feeling of the faith. Reading a letter from a priest who argued that destitute Orthodox Christians in Uganda should not be helped because they belonged to the wrong jurisdiction, he asked how such cold-hearted elitism could possibly be fought.
Being correct, he told an audience in 1979, is the external side of Christianity: important, but not of first importance. Of the man who would take your head off over a disagreement he made a remark that is hard to forget — that such a person is displaying weakness, because he is so unsure of himself that he has to convert you in order to be certain he believes it himself. Anyone who has argued about religion on the internet will recognise the portrait.

### Especially our own families
One biographical fact anchors all of this. Fr. Seraphim's own family were Protestants. His mother remained a Protestant; his father had been brought up Roman Catholic and became a Protestant when he married. Their son entered a Russian church in San Francisco at twenty-seven and spent the rest of his life writing about the Orthodox faith, and they did not follow him. He was not theorising about other people's relatives.
So when he told the catechumen that there was no reason she could not call her family Christians and be on good terms with them, recognising that they had at least their faith in Christ in common, and that she should “live in peace especially with our own families”, he was describing his own practice. He also drew the one line he thought polemic could properly cross: a harsh tone is called for, he wrote, only when someone is actively trying to take away our flocks or change our teaching. Outside those two cases, no.
That is the register these pages will try to keep. We will tell you what the Orthodox Church has held, including at the points where it differs from what you may have been taught, and we will not file the differences down until nothing is left of them; that would waste your time and insult your intelligence. What we will not do is treat you as an opponent. Fr. Seraphim thought the argument was never the thing that persuaded anybody anyway — that what persuades is seeing something, in the life of the Church, worth wanting. The door is on the latch, and it opens outwards.

### Common questions

Q: Did Fr. Seraphim Rose believe non-Orthodox Christians are saved?
A: He refused to answer that question about any individual, and said so repeatedly. He held the traditional Orthodox teaching that the Church is one and that the sacraments are given in her, and he did not soften it. But he wrote that it is not for us to define the state of those outside the Orthodox Church, and that if God grants salvation to someone who is a Christian in the best way he knows, that is God's affair and not ours.

Q: What did Fr. Seraphim Rose mean by “correctness disease”?
A: It was his name for a narrowness he saw spreading among converts in the 1970s: simple answers to complicated questions, a party line on every subject, and a taste for being right that had displaced the love of Christ. He also called it “super-correctness”. He wrote that converts grasp at correctness like a baby's bottle and could save their souls better by being a little incorrect but humbler.

Q: Did he think Orthodox Christians should call other Christians heretics?
A: No. He wrote that the word has a definite meaning and function, but that it is used far too freely, that few non-Orthodox Christians today are consciously heretics, and that it really does no good to call them that. In print he went further, saying that convert harshness is spiritually wrong even when worded in a theologically correct manner, and that it drives away people who would otherwise have been drawn to the Church.

Q: Was Fr. Seraphim Rose an ecumenist?
A: No, and he would have rejected the label. He wrote a book criticising the ecumenical movement of his day and held that the Orthodox Church is the Church founded by Christ. What he refused was the use of that conviction as a licence for contempt. His position was exclusive about the Church and generous about persons, and he did not think the two were in tension.

Q: Where can I read the letter of 27 November 1980?
A: It is printed in full in Hieromonk Damascene's biography, Father Seraphim Rose: His Life and Works (St. Herman Press, 2003), in chapter 84, “Pastoral Guidance”, and that chapter is reproduced by permission at orthodoxinfo.com. The recipient's name is withheld. Copies circulate online under the title “The Proper View of Non-Orthodox Christians”; cite the biography and the letter date rather than the reposts.

Q: Why does this parish blog make so much of one letter?
A: Because it settles a question every enquirer eventually asks: whether a Church that believes something definite about herself can speak to outsiders without contempt. Fr. Seraphim answered yes, in writing, while holding the demanding version of the doctrine. That combination is the editorial standard for these pages, and naming its source lets readers check whether we are keeping to it.

- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 86 — “Orthodoxy of the Heart”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_86.aspx
- Hieromonk Damascene, Father Seraphim Rose, ch. 87 — “Simplicity”: http://orthodoxinfo.com/praxis/fsr_87.aspx

==============================================================================
## Nihilism and the Question of Truth
URL: https://orthodox.sg/blog/nihilism-and-the-modern-heart.html
Summary: Nihilism: The Root of the Revolution of the Modern Age was written in San Francisco in the early 1960s by Eugene Rose, before his monastic tonsure, and published in 1994. It argues that nihilism is not a fringe extremism but the underlying assumption of the modern age — that there is no absolute truth — and traces four stages by which a civilisation arrives there.
==============================================================================

### A book written in a basement
In the early 1960s, in a basement flat near downtown San Francisco, a young man sat at a desk covered with stacks of books and folders of notes. Little daylight reached the room. A murder had been committed there some years before he moved in, and neighbours said something unpleasant still hung about the place; the tenant had covered one wall with icons and kept a red lamp burning in front of them. His name was Eugene Rose. He had been baptised into the Orthodox Church a short while earlier and would not be tonsured a monk for another eight years.
What he was writing was meant to be enormous: a chronicle in fourteen chapters called The Kingdom of Man and the Kingdom of God. Only the seventh chapter was ever finished in typescript. That chapter is the book we now have under the title Nihilism: The Root of the Revolution of the Modern Age, published by his brotherhood in 1994, twelve years after his death, and correctly attributed on the title page to “Eugene (Fr. Seraphim) Rose”, because the man who wrote it was not yet Fr. Seraphim.

### What the word actually means
The word has been worn smooth by use. Most people hear it and picture something loud: a terrorist, a wrecked gallery, a young man in black declaring that nothing matters. Rose begins by clearing those away. Such things, he says, are the spectacular surface of the problem and not the problem. He wants the mentality underneath, the one that produces them and also produces much quieter people.
For the definition he goes to the man he regarded as the fountain of philosophical nihilism, and quotes him directly. Nietzsche's sentence runs: “That there is no truth; that there is no absolute state of affairs — no ‘thing-in-itself.’ This alone is Nihilism, and of the most extreme kind.” Rose notes that most of us have heard the same doctrine in its domesticated form, in the sentence that all truth is relative. Then he draws the conclusion that gives his book its shape.

> the question of Nihilism is, most profoundly, a question of truth; it is, indeed, the question of truth
> — Eugene (Fr. Seraphim) Rose, *Nihilism: The Root of the Revolution of the Modern Age*, ch. I “Introduction: The Question of Truth” (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Second Edition, 2020)

### Two sentences that cannot be said
The most bracing passage in the book is also the shortest, and it is a piece of ordinary logic that anyone can check. Two statements are in wide circulation: all truth is empirical, and all truth is relative. Rose points out that the first is not itself an empirical statement — no experiment establishes it — and the second is itself an absolute claim. Each destroys itself in the act of being made. Whatever else follows, this much does: if there is any truth at all, it cannot be merely relative.
From this he draws a corollary with wider consequences. The first principles of any system of knowledge cannot be established by that system, because they are what the system begins from; they must be given in advance. The coherence and uniformity of nature, the reliability of reason to draw conclusions from observation, the assumption that what one person knows another can know too — none of these is a laboratory result. They are held, and held reasonably, but they are held by faith in the plain sense of the word.
He is careful here, and it is worth being careful with him. He is not attacking science, and he is not scoring a debating point against scientists. His argument is that everyone, in every age, stands on something not proved by the methods they use afterwards, and that the interesting question is never whether a person has faith but what his faith is resting on.

### Four stages, and the first is the quietest
The body of the book traces a sequence Rose calls the nihilist dialectic: four stages, each following from the first denial rather than opposing it. He is explicit that they overlap, that they are not simply chronological, and that no one is a pure example of any of them; most people are a mixture of at least two.
Of these, the first is the one he treats at greatest length, and the one likeliest to describe the air a reader is breathing. He describes a civilisation that still speaks, on formal occasions, of eternal verities and human dignity and Christian civilisation, while nobody in the room takes the words with entire seriousness. They have become ornaments of language, evoking a memory of a time when they meant something definite. Nothing has been denied. The meaning has simply been allowed to leave.
Whether his four-stage scheme is the right map of modern intellectual history is a fair question, and a reader is free to think it too tidy. The observation underneath it is harder to dismiss: that outright denial is rare, and that beliefs usually die by being kept on as decoration.
- Liberalism — not a political party but a temper of mind, in which truth is neither attacked nor defended but quietly moved off the centre of the table. The old words are kept and the old meanings are allowed to drain out of them.
- Realism — the narrowing of the real to what can be measured, so that anything else becomes decoration or sentiment.
- Vitalism — the substitution of vivid experience for truth, once truth has been given up: intensity as a criterion, feeling as evidence.
- The nihilism of destruction — the open turn against order itself, which the twentieth century saw at a scale nobody had imagined.

### He was describing a country he had lived in
This is the point at which the book stops being an essay. Eugene Rose was not a spectator of the condition he was analysing. He had rejected the Protestant Christianity of his boyhood as thin, gone looking for reality in Western philosophy and then in the religions of the East, and arrived at nothing. He read Nietzsche until the sentences had a charge in them. He experimented deliberately with breaking down logical thought, on the theory that reason was the obstacle.
Hieromonk Damascene, who edited the manuscript, records that when Eugene was asked long afterwards to describe those years he would say only that he had been in hell. He drank. He hammered on the floor and shouted at the God he had announced was dead. Once, drunk, he wrote that he was sick, as all men are sick who are absent from the love of God.
That sentence is the key to the tone of the whole book. He is not standing above the nihilist and describing him; he is describing something he had been. It also explains an odd generosity in his later writing about atheists.
He thought that a furious, hating atheism — the kind that grapples with God and accuses Him of injustice — is a spiritual condition rather than the absence of one, and that it has more than once ended in the sight of the One the atheist was actually looking for. The danger, in his reading, was never the great deniers. It was the people for whom Christ had quietly become a word.

### Neither apology nor diatribe
Rose sets out his method at the start by naming two ways of getting it wrong. The first is diatribe: condemning Nazism for its barbarism, or the avant-garde for its pessimism, which he thinks leaves the root untouched, since error is defeated only by truth and most criticism of nihilism never reaches the question of truth at all.
The second is the opposite, and he handles it more carefully, because he feels its pull. It is easy to see the nihilist as a casualty of a sick civilisation — and there is something in that, he grants, since an age whose best as well as worst minds turn to nihilism is plainly ill. But sympathy is not a diagnosis, and he warns against a particular slide.
He will not let anyone off on the ground of being a victim, himself included; there is no such thing, he says, as an entirely innocent victim. This is not a comfortable book about how everyone is doing their best. It is also not a book that enjoys the discomfort it causes, which is a rarer thing.

> to allow sympathy for an unfortunate person to pass over into receptivity to his ideas
> — Eugene (Fr. Seraphim) Rose, *Nihilism: The Root of the Revolution of the Modern Age*, ch. I (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Second Edition, 2020)

### Is it true, or does it work for me?
Here is where a book from 1962 becomes a question for a reader in 2026, and the question is not a rebuke to anyone. It is simply the fork in the road. There are two ways to ask about a religion. One is: is this true — is the world in fact like this, whether or not I find it congenial? The other is: does this work for me — does it steady me, suit my temperament, fit the life I have?
The second question is not wicked, and everybody asks it. The trouble Rose identifies is what happens when a culture forgets that the first question was ever asked. Once truth has moved off the centre of the table, religion survives as a preference, and preferences are chosen by fit. A faith held that way cannot ask anything of you that you did not already want, because the moment it does you will change it for one that suits better.
Orthodox Christianity asks the reader to take the first question seriously, and it is fair to say plainly what that involves. It means the claim that God became man in a particular place under a particular governor, that He rose, and that the Church He founded has handed on His teaching rather than invented it, is either so or not so. It is not being offered as a style of spirituality, or as a set of practices that some people find helpful.
Many Christians of other traditions would say exactly the same about their own convictions, and in saying it they are asking the question Rose cared about. That is real common ground, and it is worth more than it usually gets credit for.

### Beyond nihilism
The last chapter turns to the optimistic version of modern man: the idealists, the scientists pushing back frontiers, the young people working for peace and brotherhood and confident of the future. Rose takes them seriously and declines to sneer. His criticism is narrow and specific. Their faith and their hope are directed entirely at this world, and the goods of this world pass away; a hope pinned wholly to things that end is a hope that will not survive the things ending.
Against that he sets an inversion he knows will sound like a paradox, and which he introduces almost apologetically, aware that it lays him open to the charge of having a nihilism of his own. The Christian, he says, is in an ultimate sense a nihilist too — but the other way round.
The difference, as he puts it, is that one nothingness proceeds from an abyss and the other from abundance, and that calling the Christian's poverty nihilism is really only a literary device, since what it is in practice is fullness. He adds a warning that many readers will find hard, and which is nonetheless the logic of his whole argument: the human mind will not stay empty, and the man who cannot believe in Christ will end by believing in Antichrist. One may dispute the conclusion. The premise — that nobody actually manages to believe nothing — is not easy to refute.

> to him, in the end, the world is nothing, and God is all
> — Eugene (Fr. Seraphim) Rose, *Nihilism: The Root of the Revolution of the Modern Age*, ch. V “Beyond Nihilism” (St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood, Second Edition, 2020)

### How to read it, and whether to
Nihilism is his hardest book, and it is not the place to begin. It is early, unrevised, philosophical in a way his later writing is not, and it carries the marks of the years it came out of. Fr. Seraphim himself later thought his earliest pieces rather abstract. A reader wanting his voice at its warmest should start with God's Revelation to the Human Heart, a lecture he gave to students at Santa Cruz in 1981, which is forty-odd pages long and is mostly stories.
But the short book has one thing the later ones do not. It is the record of a man mapping the country he had just escaped from, while the roads were still fresh in his memory, and it is written to people still living there. He did not think that modern men could come to Christ fully until they had first seen how far they had gone from Him — until, as he put it, they had faced the nihilism in themselves.
That is the offer, and it is an offer rather than an accusation. If the question of whether anything is finally true has stopped being a live question, there is a book by a Californian in a basement who found that it was still live, and nearly died of it, and came out the other side into a small dark church in San Francisco where the service was in a language he did not yet understand. The door of that church was not locked. It generally is not.

### Common questions

Q: Who wrote Nihilism: The Root of the Revolution of the Modern Age?
A: Eugene Rose, before his monastic tonsure, wrote it in San Francisco in the early 1960s as the seventh chapter of an unfinished work called The Kingdom of Man and the Kingdom of God. It was published as a book by the St. Herman of Alaska Brotherhood in 1994, twelve years after his death, under the name “Eugene (Fr. Seraphim) Rose”, which is how pre-monastic work is correctly attributed.

Q: What does Fr. Seraphim Rose mean by nihilism?
A: He takes the definition from Nietzsche, whom he quotes: that there is no truth and no absolute state of affairs. Nihilism in his sense is therefore not primarily violence or despair but a position about truth, held most often without being noticed. Its popular form is the sentence that all truth is relative, which he argues is self-contradictory, since that sentence is itself offered as an absolute.

Q: What are the four stages of nihilism he describes?
A: Liberalism, in which truth is quietly displaced from the centre while its vocabulary is retained; realism, which admits only what can be measured; vitalism, which substitutes intensity of experience for truth; and the nihilism of destruction, which turns against order itself. He insists the stages overlap, that they are not neatly chronological, and that no individual is a pure specimen of any one of them.

Q: Is Nihilism a good book to start with?
A: Probably not. It is early, philosophical, and demanding, and Fr. Seraphim later judged his earliest writing somewhat abstract. God's Revelation to the Human Heart, a short lecture he gave at Santa Cruz in 1981, is a gentler introduction, and The Soul After Death is the book most readers meet first. Nihilism rewards a reader who already wants the argument about truth taken seriously.

Q: Does Orthodoxy claim science and faith are opposed?
A: No, and this book does not argue that. Its point is narrower: that the first principles of any system of knowledge, including the sciences, cannot be proved by that system and must be taken as given. Fr. Seraphim held that everyone stands on something unproved, so the real question is never whether a person has faith but what that faith rests upon.
